course.title: Electrical Power Systems: From Generator to Socket
course.description: How electrical power is carried from a power station to a power point and kept in balance on the way, with Australia's National Electricity Market as the working example. You calculate power, power factor, three-phase loads and transformer losses, and judge how grids are held at 50 Hz, protected, and changed by solar and batteries.
course.audience: A curious adult or a student who has done simple DC circuits and the physics of induction. They know voltage, current, resistance and power, and that a transformer changes voltage by a turns ratio, but not what RMS, power factor or three-phase mean in practice, and not how a whole grid is run. The course explains protection and household safety so that learners understand it, and it never teaches electrical work, which the regulator's household pages leave to licensed electricians.

paragraphs: How electrical power is carried from a power station to a power point and kept in balance on the way, with Australia's National Electricity Market as the working example. You calculate power, power factor, three-phase loads and transformer losses, and judge how grids are held at 50 Hz, protected, and changed by solar and batteries.
outcomes: You'll be able to read an AC supply: convert between peak and RMS values, read a period, a frequency and a phase angle, and check a voltage against Australia's 230 V tolerance.
You'll be able to find the real, reactive and apparent power of a load and size a power factor correction for a lagging load.
You'll be able to find the line and phase voltages, currents and power of a balanced three-phase load.
You'll be able to rate a transformer, find its efficiency from its losses, and estimate how line loss changes when the voltage changes.
You'll be able to relate poles, speed and frequency for generators and motors, and compute the slip of an induction motor.
You'll be able to predict how grid frequency moves when generation is lost, put the layers of frequency control in order, and read a NEM dispatch.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Electronics Foundations, Physics II: Waves, Electricity and Magnetism, and Heat, Trigonometry.

modules.title: Power from an alternating supply
modules.description: What an AC value means, and how real, reactive and apparent power and power factor decide what a supply has to carry.

modules.title: Three-phase supply, transformers and transmission
modules.description: The three-phase system, the real losses of transformers, and why the path from power station to socket climbs to high voltage and comes back down.

modules.title: Machines and frequency
modules.description: How generators and motors lock to the supply frequency, what inertia does, and how the National Electricity Market holds 50 Hz.

modules.title: Faults, protection and safety
modules.description: What fuses, breakers, relays, earthing and safety switches each protect, and how a fault that protection handles correctly can still spread.

modules.title: Renewables and storage on the grid
modules.description: What inverters give and do not give a grid, what limits rooftop solar on a street, and how storage and curtailment answer variability.

concepts.title: RMS value
concepts.summary: The effective value of an AC voltage or current is the DC value that produces the same heating, and for a sine wave it is 0.707 of the peak.

concepts.title: Period and frequency
concepts.summary: The period is the time of one cycle and the frequency is the number of cycles per second, so 50 Hz has a 20 ms period.

concepts.title: Phase difference
concepts.summary: Two waves of the same frequency can cross zero at different times, and the shift is measured in degrees of a 360 degree cycle.

concepts.title: Real power
concepts.summary: Real power P, in watts, is the average of voltage times current over a cycle and is the part that does work.

concepts.title: Reactive power
concepts.summary: Reactive power Q, in var, is energy that moves back and forth between the source and the magnetic or electric fields of the load, with no net transfer.

concepts.title: Apparent power
concepts.summary: Apparent power S, in volt-amperes, is RMS voltage times RMS current, and S squared equals P squared plus Q squared.

concepts.title: Power factor
concepts.summary: Power factor is real power divided by apparent power, the cosine of the phase angle, and is lagging for inductive loads such as motors.

concepts.title: Current and line loss
concepts.summary: For the same real power at the same voltage, current rises as 1 divided by the power factor and line loss as 1 divided by its square.

concepts.title: Power factor correction
concepts.summary: A capacitor supplies the reactive power an inductive load needs, close to the load, so that it does not have to flow from the generator.

concepts.title: Three phases
concepts.summary: Three conductors carry the same frequency and voltage amplitude one third of a cycle (120 degrees) apart, so that their currents cancel in a balanced load.

concepts.title: Star and delta
concepts.summary: In a star connection the line voltage is 1.73 times the phase voltage, and in a delta connection the line current is 1.73 times the phase current.

concepts.title: Three-phase power
concepts.summary: A balanced load takes P = root three x line voltage x line current x power factor, and the power is constant through the cycle.

concepts.title: kVA rating
concepts.summary: A transformer is rated in kVA because voltage and current set its heating, whatever the power factor of the load.

concepts.title: Core and copper loss
concepts.summary: Core loss (hysteresis and eddy currents) is present whenever the transformer is energised; copper loss is I squared R in the windings and rises with the square of the load.

concepts.title: Efficiency
concepts.summary: Efficiency is output power over input power; distribution transformers typically reach 98 to 99 percent.

concepts.title: The voltage ladder
concepts.summary: Power is stepped up at the power station, carried on high-voltage lines, stepped down at substations to distribution voltage and again to 230/400 V for customers.

concepts.title: Loss against voltage
concepts.summary: For the same power and line, current falls as voltage rises and the resistive loss falls as the square of the current, so loss falls as 1 over the voltage squared.

concepts.title: Limits and HVDC
concepts.summary: Insulation, corona loss at very high voltage and reactive current on AC lines limit AC; HVDC wins on very long lines, submarine cables and links between grids that are not in step.

concepts.title: Synchronous speed
concepts.summary: A machine with P poles on a supply of frequency f has a rotating field that turns at N = 120 f / P revolutions per minute.

concepts.title: Synchronous machines
concepts.summary: A synchronous generator or motor locks into step with the field and turns at exactly synchronous speed; its field current sets voltage and reactive power, not frequency.

concepts.title: Slip
concepts.summary: An induction motor's rotor must turn slower than the field to have any current induced, and slip is the percentage difference.

concepts.title: Frequency as the balance signal
concepts.summary: In a synchronous grid every generator turns in step, so excess load slows them all and excess generation speeds them all, and the frequency shows the imbalance of the whole grid.

concepts.title: Inertia
concepts.summary: The spinning mass of synchronous generators supplies or absorbs the imbalance at once, which slows the first change in frequency and gives controls time to act.

concepts.title: Rate of change of frequency
concepts.summary: ROCOF, in hertz per second, is how fast frequency moves; it is larger when there is less inertia, for example when inverter-based generation replaces synchronous machines.

concepts.title: Layers of control
concepts.summary: Inertia acts at once, governor droop responds automatically, automatic generation control adjusts within several tens of seconds, reserves reach their promised output within about ten minutes, and replacement reserve takes 30 to 60 minutes.

concepts.title: Droop
concepts.summary: A governor with 4 percent droop changes output by 25 percent of its rating for each 1 percent change in speed, so generators share a frequency change in proportion to their size.

concepts.title: NEM dispatch and FCAS
concepts.summary: AEMO dispatches the cheapest offers every 5 minutes, sets the price at the highest offer needed, and buys regulation and contingency frequency control services to hold 49.85 to 50.15 Hz.

concepts.title: Fault current
concepts.summary: A short circuit can draw many times the circuit's rated current, so the protection has to interrupt far more than the normal load.

concepts.title: Fuse, breaker and relay
concepts.summary: A fuse melts and is replaced, a breaker opens and can be reset, and a protective relay senses the fault and tells a breaker to open.

concepts.title: Coordination and zones
concepts.summary: Only the device closest to the fault should clear it, and protective zones overlap so that no fault falls between two of them.

concepts.title: Automatic disconnection
concepts.summary: Exposed metal parts are connected to earth so that a fault to them becomes a current large enough for the breaker or fuse to clear.

concepts.title: Safety switch (RCD)
concepts.summary: A residual-current device compares the current out on the line with the current back on the neutral and opens when the difference, typically 30 mA, shows a leak to earth, within about 30 milliseconds.

concepts.title: What each device does
concepts.summary: Circuit breakers protect wiring from overload and short circuit, safety switches protect people from leakage shocks, and surge diverters protect equipment from voltage spikes; none replaces the others.

concepts.title: Cascading failure
concepts.summary: A cascade is a chain in which each failure loads or disturbs the next, so that a local fault becomes a system event.

concepts.title: Trigger, weakness and response
concepts.summary: The trigger starts the event, weaknesses decide how far it spreads, and protection that operates correctly can still end in a blackout.

concepts.title: Restoring a grid
concepts.summary: A black start restarts generators with their own small sources, and restarting a state uses system restart services and the interconnectors.

concepts.title: Grid-tie inverter
concepts.summary: A grid-tie inverter converts DC to AC matched to the grid's voltage, frequency and phase, and disconnects quickly if the grid goes down.

concepts.title: Two-way flow and voltage rise
concepts.summary: Rooftop solar makes distribution networks carry power in both directions, and midday export raises voltage along a feeder until inverters back off or trip.

concepts.title: Export limits
concepts.summary: Networks limit exports with a fixed static limit or a flexible limit that applies only when the local network needs it.

concepts.title: Power against energy
concepts.summary: A battery's power rating, in MW, is how fast it can deliver, and its energy rating, in MWh, is how long it can do so; the ratio is its duration.

concepts.title: What storage is for
concepts.summary: Batteries react within fractions of a second and suit frequency services and peak shaving, while pumped hydro is the largest form of grid storage and runs at an efficiency of 75 to 85 percent.

concepts.title: Curtailment
concepts.summary: Curtailment is an intentional cut in generation; it can be cheaper than building the lines or storage needed to use every megawatt-hour.

lessons.title: Reading an AC supply

steps.headline: The heating value of a wave

lead.text: The [[power|The energy a part transfers each second, in watts. For a resistor $P = V^2/R$. Met in 'How much energy a circuit moves' in Electronics Foundations.]] in a resistor at any instant is $v^2/R$, where $v$ is the voltage across it at that instant, so the heat that a wave delivers follows the *square* of the voltage. Squaring turns a negative voltage into a positive one, which is why a supply that swings below zero for half of every cycle still heats the resistor all the time.

Finding the steady voltage that would heat equally takes three steps, which the name lists in reverse: square the voltage at each instant, average those squares over one cycle, and take the square root to return to volts. The result is the **root mean square** value, written **RMS**, and it is the voltage of the DC supply that gives the same heating, which is how the US Department of Energy's electrical science handbook defines the effective value of an alternating quantity.

The highest voltage that a sine wave reaches is its **peak** value $V_p$, and the whole height from its lowest point to its highest is the **peak-to-peak** value, $2V_p$. For a sine wave the three steps of the RMS calculation can be carried out exactly. Squaring a wave of peak $V_p$ gives $V_p^2\sin^2\theta$, and a squared cosine is the same curve moved a quarter of a cycle along, so the two curves have the same average. Together they add up to $V_p^2$ at every angle, because $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$, so each has an average of $V_p^2/2$, and its square root gives the conversion in both directions.

afterFigure.text: In the figure a supply of 230 V RMS reaches 325 V at its peaks and covers 650 V from its lowest point to its highest, while a 12 V supply follows the same proportions on a smaller scale. Two other averages of the wave can be found, 0.637 of the peak over a half cycle and zero over a whole cycle, and neither tells how much heat a supply gives, which is why the RMS value is the one that gets quoted.

diagram.alt: One cycle of a sine wave with horizontal lines at its peak, its RMS value and its negative values, and a bracket for the peak-to-peak value, drawn for a 230 V supply and for a 12 V supply.
diagram.caption: One cycle of a sine wave with its peak, RMS and peak-to-peak levels. Use the buttons to compare the two supplies.

lead.text: Unless a figure says otherwise, an AC voltage or current that is quoted is an RMS value, a convention that the handbook adopts in every example it works and that the supply standards follow. Australia's nominal supply voltage is therefore **230 V RMS**, a figure adopted in 2000 in place of the earlier 240 V.

The voltage delivered may stray from the nominal value, and the allowed band is a **tolerance**, a percentage of 230 V. From 2000 the standard allowed a rise of 10 percent and a fall of 6 percent, and from 2022 it allows 10 percent either way. A rise of 10 percent is 23 V, so the upper limit under both rules is 253 V and the two rules differ only at the bottom. The voltage at an appliance may sit below the limits, because of the drop in the wiring of the installation.

The supply's frequency is the number of cycles in each second, and in Australia it is held close to 50 hertz, so one [[period|The time one cycle takes, the reciprocal of the frequency. Met in 'Things that repeat' in Physics II: Waves, Electricity and Magnetism, and Heat.]] lasts $1/50 = 0.020$ s, or 20 ms. A cycle also spans 360 degrees of the wave, which makes each millisecond $360/20 = 18$ degrees, and a time can be turned into an angle by dividing it by 20 ms and multiplying by 360.

That conversion lets two waves of the same frequency be compared. When both cross zero going upward, but at different times, the gap between the crossings written as an angle is called the **phase difference**. The wave that crosses first is said to *lead* and the other to *lag*, and when the angle is zero the waves are *in phase*, as in the first view of the figure.

afterFigure.text: At 60 degrees the current crosses zero 3.3 ms after the voltage, and at 120 degrees 6.7 ms after, since each 18 degrees is 1 ms. The same angle describes the gap between any pair of the supply's waves, whether they are two voltages, two currents, or a voltage and a current.

diagram.alt: A voltage wave and a current wave of the same frequency, drawn with no shift, with the current shifted later by 60 degrees, and shifted later by 120 degrees, with the zero crossings marked.
diagram.caption: The current follows the voltage by 0, 60 or 120 degrees of a 360 degree cycle. Use the buttons to change the shift.

steps.headline: Find the phase difference when a load's current crosses zero 3 ms after the voltage does, on a 50 Hz supply.

workedSteps.text: At 50 Hz one cycle takes 20 ms, so a delay of 3 ms is a fraction of a cycle.
A whole cycle is 360 degrees, so the fraction is multiplied by 360.
The current crosses zero after the voltage, so the current lags.

lead.text: A [[phase difference|The gap between two waves of the same frequency, written as an angle. Met earlier in this lesson.]] is found by turning the delay into a fraction of a cycle.

steps.headline: At 50 Hz a load's current crosses zero 4 ms before the voltage does. Find the phase difference and say which wave leads.

workedSteps.text: One cycle takes 20 ms, so the 4 ms gap is a fraction of a cycle.
Turn that fraction of a cycle into degrees.
Decide which wave leads and which lags.

lead.text: A phase difference between a load's current and voltage is a property of the load. A heater or a filament lamp is resistive, and its current is in phase with the voltage. A coil, as in the windings of a motor or a transformer, stores energy in a magnetic field and returns it later in the cycle, and that makes the current *lag*, whereas a capacitor stores energy in an electric field and makes the current *lead*. The handbook condenses this into the memory aid "ELI the ICE man": in an inductive circuit (L) the current (I) lags the voltage (E), and in a capacitive circuit (C) the current leads.
A phase angle is therefore normal for any load built from coils, and it is no sign of a fault. What it changes is how much of the current does useful work, which is the subject of the next lesson.

reveal.text: The conversion runs in both directions: a time becomes an angle by dividing by the period and multiplying by 360, and an angle becomes a time by the reverse.

lessons.orientation: Read the peak, RMS, period and frequency of an AC supply from a rating or a waveform, and say what a phase angle between voltage and current means for a load.
lessons.nextAction: Find the real, reactive and apparent power of a load, and say which one a cable or transformer must be sized for.

blocks.text: A heater element with a resistance of 23 Ω takes $230^2/23 = 2300$ W when it is connected to a steady 230 V supply. Connected to a power point it also takes 2300 W, although the voltage at a power point is a wave that passes through zero twice in every cycle and spends much of its time well below 230 V.

A single number describes a wave that is not steady at all, and the way it does so decides how every rating on an AC supply is read, from the label on a heater to the limits that the supply itself must keep to.

intro.promise: By the end you'll convert between peak and RMS values, read a period and a phase angle from a wave, and check a supply voltage against Australia's tolerance.
intro.whyItMatters: Every rating on an AC supply is an RMS value, and the angle between voltage and current decides how much of that supply does useful work.

recap.keyIdea: An AC voltage is quoted by its RMS value, the steady DC voltage that heats equally, and a sine wave's peak is 1.414 times that value.

blocks.text: The RMS value comes from squaring the wave, averaging over a cycle and taking the root, which for a sine wave makes it 0.707 of the peak, so the 230 V nominal supply of Australia peaks at about 325 V. The allowed band around 230 V was a rise of 10 percent and a fall of 6 percent from 2000, and has been 10 percent either way since 2022.

At 50 Hz a cycle lasts 20 ms and covers 360 degrees, so each millisecond of delay between two waves is 18 degrees of phase difference. A current that lags the voltage points to a load with coils in it, and the angle is an ordinary property of such a load.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson multiplies voltage by current at each instant, and shows how a current that is out of phase with the voltage splits the power into a part that does work and a part that moves back and forth.

lessons.title: Real, reactive and apparent power

lead.text: Multiplying the voltage by the current at every instant gives the instantaneous power, and the figure draws that product for three loads on the same supply. In a resistor the voltage and the current change sign together, so their product never falls below zero and energy always flows towards the load. In an ideal coil the current lags by 90 degrees, and the product is positive for a quarter of a cycle and negative for the next, so the energy that flows in during one quarter flows back out during the following one.

afterFigure.text: The third view, a load whose current lags with a cosine of 0.8, lies between the two. Its product is positive for more of the cycle, and by more, than it is negative, so a net flow of energy goes to the load while some goes back and forth. A real load, with resistance as well as coils, behaves like this, which is why both kinds of power are found in the same circuit.

diagram.alt: Three views of voltage, current and their product over one cycle. For a resistor the product stays above zero. For a coil whose current lags by 90 degrees it is above zero for half the time and below for half. For a load lagging with a cosine of 0.8 the part above zero is larger than the part below.
diagram.caption: The product of voltage and current at each instant, for three loads on the same supply. Use the buttons to compare the areas above and below the axis.

lead.text: The average of the product over one cycle is the energy that the load takes each second and keeps, and it is called the **real power** $P$, also known as active power. It is measured in watts. Written with [[RMS|The steady value that heats equally, 0.707 of the peak of a sine wave. Met in 'Reading an AC supply'.]] values for the voltage $V$ and current $I$, and with $\varphi$ for the angle by which the current lags, it is

For a resistor $\varphi$ is zero and $P = VI$, the product that the course Electronics Foundations used for power. For an ideal coil $\varphi$ is 90 degrees, the cosine is zero, and no power is kept at all.

The energy that moves back and forth in the third view has a measure of its own, the **reactive power** $Q$, which is $VI\sin\varphi$ and is counted in volt-amperes reactive, written var. A coil gathers energy into its magnetic field while its current builds up and gives it back as the field collapses, and a capacitor does the same with its electric field, so over a whole cycle no net energy is delivered by Q.

That does not make Q harmless. The current that carries the energy back and forth flows along the same wires and heats them as any current does, even though the load keeps none of the energy. Reactive power is therefore energy that goes out and returns, and the supply still has to carry the current that it needs.

The product of the RMS voltage and the RMS current, with no angle in it, is the **apparent power** $S$, measured in volt-amperes (VA). Since $P = S\cos\varphi$ and $Q = S\sin\varphi$, the three powers are the sides of a right triangle with $S$ as its slope, and Pythagoras gives
The ratio $P/S$, which is the cosine of the angle, is called the **power factor**, and the next lesson takes it up.

afterFigure.text: With the real power held at 1.8 kW, a cosine of 0.9 needs 2.00 kVA from the supply, and a cosine of 0.6 needs 3.00 kVA, so the same useful power calls for 50% more apparent power as the angle grows. P and Q meet at a right angle, which is why S is not the sum of the two.

diagram.alt: A right triangle with the real power P along its base, the reactive power Q upright and the apparent power S as its slope, drawn for the same real power of 1.8 kilowatts at two phase angles, with the values of Q and S written beside it.
diagram.caption: The power triangle for a real power of 1.8 kW. Use the buttons to change the phase angle and watch S and Q grow while P stays the same.

steps.headline: A coil of reactance 50 Ω in series with a 200 Ω resistor carries 2 A. Find P, Q and S.

workedSteps.text: Only the resistor keeps energy, so P takes the same form as in Electronics Foundations.
The reactive power has the same form with the reactance in place of the resistance.
P and Q are the sides of the triangle, so S is the slope.
The cosine of the angle is P over S, which shows how small the angle is.

lead.text: The coil's opposition to the alternating current is its **reactance**, measured in ohms like resistance. This is the series circuit that the DOE handbook works as its example.

steps.headline: A load draws 10 A from a 230 V supply, and its current lags with cos φ = 0.8. Find S, P and Q.

workedSteps.text: The apparent power is the voltage times the current.
The real power is the part of S along the base of the triangle.
The reactive power is the part along the upright side, and its sine follows from the cosine.

lead.text: Cables, transformers and generators all heat with the current they carry, and that current is the apparent power divided by the voltage, whatever share of it is real and whatever share reactive. For that reason the equipment that carries power is sized for the apparent power, and transformers are rated in volt-amperes, from a fraction of one to over a thousand megavolt-amperes.

A rating plate that gives both kilowatts and kilovolt-amperes therefore says two things: how much energy the load keeps, and how large a current the supply must be able to carry for it. At 230 V single phase a load of 7 kVA takes $7000/230 = 30.4$ A, however little of that is real power.

reveal.text: The cable carries 7,000 ÷ 230 = 30.4 A. The real power alone would suggest 5,000 ÷ 230 = 21.7 A, which a cable chosen for it could not safely carry.

The load takes 128.6 kVA while the transformer is rated 100 kVA, so a load that looks smaller in kilowatts is too large for the transformer. Choosing and changing such equipment is work for a licensed electrician and the supplier.

lessons.orientation: Use the power triangle to find the real, reactive and apparent power of a load from its voltage, current and phase angle, and say which of the three a cable, transformer or generator has to be sized for.
lessons.nextAction: Work out how a low power factor raises current and line loss, and choose and size a correction.

blocks.text: A resistor takes energy in one direction only. Its voltage and current change sign together, so their product, the instantaneous power, is never negative, and energy always flows into it. A coil is different, because its current lags the voltage, and the product of the two can then fall below zero.

A heater and a motor can take the same current at the same voltage and still differ in how much of that current does work, while the wires, transformers and generators between them and the power station have to carry all of it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the real, reactive and apparent power of a load from its voltage, current and phase angle, and say which one a cable or transformer is sized for.
intro.whyItMatters: The rating that limits a cable, a transformer or a generator is not the power the load uses, and reading the three powers tells you which figure to trust.

recap.keyIdea: A load's real power $P$ is the energy it keeps, its reactive power $Q$ is energy that goes back and forth, and the apparent power $S$, with $S^2 = P^2 + Q^2$, is what the supply has to carry.

blocks.text: Averaging voltage times current over a cycle gives the real power, $P = VI\cos\varphi$ in watts, while the energy that goes out and returns is the reactive power, $Q = VI\sin\varphi$ in var, and the product of the RMS values is the apparent power in volt-amperes. The three are the sides of a right triangle, so S is found with a square root and comes out smaller than the sum of P and Q.

Because the current that carries reactive power heats a conductor like any other, cables, transformers and generators are sized for the apparent power, and a load of 90 kW at a power factor of 0.70 asks for 129 kVA, which is more than its kilowatts suggest.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes the ratio of real to apparent power, the power factor, and shows how a low one raises current and line loss and how it is corrected.

lessons.title: Power factor and its correction

lead.text: The **power factor** of a load is the ratio of its real power to its apparent power, which is the cosine of the angle by which its current and voltage are out of step, and rating plates often abbreviate it to cos φ.

It has no unit and lies between 0 and 1 for a load that keeps energy. It is 1 when the current and voltage are in phase and falls to 0 when they are 90 degrees apart. A load that takes 700 W at an angle of 45.6 degrees has a power factor of $\cos 45.6^\circ = 0.700$, so its apparent power is $700/0.700 = 1000$ VA.

When the current lags the voltage the power factor is said to be **lagging**, and the load is inductive. Heaters and filament lamps are close to 1, while loads built from coils, such as motors, transformers and fluorescent lamp ballasts, can sit well below it.
At a fixed voltage the real power is $P = VI \times \text{power factor}$, so the current needed to deliver a given real power is

and it rises in proportion to 1 divided by the power factor. The loss in a line is $I^2R$, so it rises in proportion to 1 divided by the *square* of the power factor. At a power factor of 0.7 the current is $1/0.7 = 1.43$ times its value at a power factor of 1, and the loss is $1/0.7^2 = 2.04$ times as large, roughly double.

steps.headline: A 6 kW load on a 230 V single-phase supply has a power factor of 0.6. Compare its current and line loss with those at a power factor of 1.

workedSteps.text: At a power factor of 1 the current is the real power divided by the voltage.
At a power factor of 0.6 the supply has to provide more apparent power, so the current is larger.
The ratio of the two currents is 1 divided by the power factor.
The line loss follows the square of the current.

lead.text: The real power and the voltage are the same in both cases, so the only change is the power factor.

Where a load draws lagging reactive power, a capacitor connected close to it can supply that power, and the reactive current then passes between the capacitor and the load without travelling along the supply from the generator. In the power triangle the capacitor's reactive power points against the load's, so it subtracts from Q, leaves P as it was and shortens S. Bringing a load to a target power factor is called **power factor correction**, and its size follows from the reactive power before and after.

lead.latex: Q = P\tan(\arccos \text{power factor}) \qquad Q_{\text{capacitor}} = Q_{\text{load}} - Q_{\text{target}}

afterFigure.text: In the figure a load of 60 kW at a power factor of 0.75 has $Q = 52.9$ kvar and $S = 80.0$ kVA. A capacitor of 33.2 kvar leaves 19.7 kvar and brings S down to 63.2 kVA, which is a power factor of 0.95 and a current 21% smaller. The last view fits a capacitor that is too large: with 80 kvar it supplies more than the load needs, the reactive power turns round to leave a leading power factor, and S rises again to 65.8 kVA.

lead.text: For loads that change slowly, an automatic unit uses capacitors in several steps, switched by contactors that a controller operates after it measures the power factor. The steps keep the power factor near its target as the load rises and falls. A fixed capacitor has no such control and supplies its reactive power whether or not the load is running, which adds loss when the load is light and can leave the plant with a leading power factor.

An unloaded synchronous motor can do the same work, and is then called a **synchronous condenser**. The reactive power it supplies depends on its field current, so it behaves like a capacitor that can be adjusted smoothly, and Wikipedia lists steel mills among the large industrial users of synchronous condensers, along with high-voltage direct-current transmission projects. Reactive elements cannot simply be added to an installation without engineering analysis, and fitting them is work for a licensed electrician.

Contactors take time to switch, so a large load that changes rapidly is handled with a power electronic device, the static VAR compensator or the STATCOM, which responds much faster than a switched capacitor bank and needs less maintenance than a synchronous condenser.

Electronic power supplies are a different case, since they distort the current they draw, and capacitors alone cannot undo that. They are corrected by active or passive circuits built into the equipment, and the Energy Star guidelines for computers ask for a power factor of at least 0.9 at full output. Correction can therefore sit at a substation, be spread along a distribution system, or be part of the equipment that causes the problem.

blocks.text: A load that takes 1 kW of real power needs 1 kVA from its supply when its power factor is 1, and 5 kVA when its power factor is 0.2. The difference is extra current, which does no work at the load and still flows through every wire, transformer and generator between the load and the power station.
Whether it is worth removing that current depends on what it costs the supply and on what kind of load causes it, and both can be read from the power triangle of 'Real, reactive and apparent power'.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out how a low power factor raises current and line loss, size a capacitor that corrects it, and choose the kind of correction that suits a load.
intro.whyItMatters: A low power factor makes the same useful power cost more current, and the supply pays for that current in heat even though the load keeps none of it.

recap.keyIdea: Power factor is real power over apparent power, and a low one raises current by 1 divided by the power factor and line loss by its square, which a capacitor near the load reduces.

blocks.text: For the same real power at the same voltage, the current rises as 1 divided by the power factor and the loss in the lines as 1 divided by its square, so a power factor of 0.5 means four times the loss of a power factor of 1. The extra loss arises in the lines, transformers and generators that carry the current.

To correct a lagging load, find its reactive power with $Q = P\tan(\arccos \text{power factor})$ at the present and the target power factors and supply the difference with capacitors, taking care that fixed capacitors supply it even when the load is off. Switched capacitors suit slow changes, a static compensator suits fast ones, a synchronous condenser gives smooth adjustment, and electronic loads are corrected inside the equipment.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to three-phase supply, in which three waves a third of a cycle apart carry the power and a balanced load needs no return current at all.

lessons.title: Three-phase supply

lead.text: The three live conductors of a three-phase supply carry sine waves of the same frequency and size, each delayed by one third of a cycle, which is 120 degrees, from the one before. Each of them is called a **phase**, and the first view of the figure draws them as phase A, phase B and phase C.

A load that takes the same current from each phase is called a **balanced load**, and for it the three currents add up to zero at every instant. The second view marks the instant at 60 degrees, where two of the currents are equal and opposite and the third is zero. Each conductor's current is therefore equal and opposite to the sum of the other two, so that the other two act as its return path.

afterFigure.text: Cables inside buildings usually carry a fourth conductor, the neutral, as a return for any difference between the currents, and for a balanced load that difference is zero. The third view shows what happens when it is not: with phase A carrying more than the others, the three no longer cancel, and the neutral has to carry what is left.

diagram.alt: Three sine waves of equal size, each one third of a cycle behind the last, shown alone, with their values marked at 60 degrees where they add to zero, and with one wave made larger so that their sum is no longer zero.
diagram.caption: The three phase currents of a load. Use the buttons to see the three waves, their sum at one angle, and a load that is out of balance.

lead.text: The voltage from any one live conductor to the neutral is the **phase voltage**, and the voltage between two live conductors is the **line voltage**. The two live conductors reach their peaks one third of a cycle apart, so the line voltage is the difference of two phase voltages that are 120 degrees apart, and the first view of the figure shows that difference to be $2\sin 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}$ times as long as one phase voltage.

A balanced load can be joined to the three lines in two ways. In a **star** connection its three parts meet at a common star point, and in a **delta** connection they form a closed loop with a line joined to each corner. The factor $\sqrt{3}$, about 1.73, falls on a different quantity in each. In a star, $V_L = \sqrt{3}\,V_\varphi$ and $I_L = I_\varphi$, and in a delta, $V_L = V_\varphi$ and $I_L = \sqrt{3}\,I_\varphi$.

afterFigure.text: A supply is written with both its voltages, the phase voltage over the line voltage, so a supply with 120 V from each line to the star point has 120 × 1.732 = 208 V between lines and is written 120/208 V. A line current in a delta is a difference of two phase currents in the same way that a line voltage in a star is a difference of two phase voltages.

diagram.alt: A phasor diagram in which the voltage between two lines is the difference of two phase voltages 120 degrees apart and is 1.73 times as long, then a star connection of three loads with a common star point, then a delta connection of three loads in a closed loop, each with its line and phase quantities described.

lead.text: A balanced load has the same impedance in each phase, so each phase takes the same real power, $V_\varphi I_\varphi\cos\varphi$, and the total is three times that. Written with line quantities, a star gives $3 \times (V_L/\sqrt{3}) \times I_L$ and a delta gives $3 \times V_L \times (I_L/\sqrt{3})$, and both reduce to the same result, with $\varphi$ the angle between a phase voltage and its own current.

lead.latex: P = \sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L \cos\varphi \qquad S = \sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L \qquad Q = \sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L \sin\varphi

lead.text: In a single-phase load the power pulses through each cycle, as the figures of 'Real, reactive and apparent power' showed, and in a balanced three-phase load the three pulses are timed so that they add up to a constant. That steady power is one reason why three-phase machines run with less vibration.

Each phase takes the same real power, and the total is three times that.

lead.text: For the same voltage between conductors, a three-phase supply with no neutral can carry the same power as a single-phase supply using only 0.75 times as much conductor material. A balanced load takes constant power, and three phases at 120 degrees produce a rotating magnetic field of constant size, which simplifies the design of motors because no separate starting circuit is needed.

Most loads are single-phase, so the best use of the conductors and transformers comes from spreading them over the three phases to keep the load as nearly balanced as possible. Currents that are unequal or not exactly 120 degrees apart cause more loss than balanced ones, and an unbalanced load uses a transformer's capacity less well. How the loads of a building are shared among its phases is part of its design and wiring, which a licensed electrician carries out.

reveal.text: The neutral is the return for the loaded phase, so it carries that phase's whole current, and the losses rise because the currents no longer cancel.

blocks.text: A three-phase supply has three live conductors, each carrying a sine wave of the same frequency and size, and each wave reaches its peak one third of a cycle after the one before it. Of all the forms of alternating current, this is the one most widely used for generation, transmission and distribution, and it is commonly used to run large motors.
It might seem that three waves need three pairs of wires, one pair for each, and yet a three-phase line needs three conductors, or four where a neutral is run. The timing of the waves is the reason.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the line and phase voltages and currents of a balanced star or delta load, work out the power it takes, and say why supplies are built this way.
intro.whyItMatters: Large motors and the networks that feed them are three-phase, and their ratings are quoted in line quantities that differ from the phase values by a factor of 1.73.

recap.keyIdea: A balanced three-phase load takes $P = \sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L\cos\varphi$, and the factor $\sqrt{3}$ falls on the voltage in a star and on the current in a delta.

blocks.text: Three sine waves 120 degrees apart add to zero at every instant, so a balanced load needs no return current, and the voltage between two lines is $\sqrt{3}$, about 1.73, times the voltage from a line to the star point. A supply whose phase voltage is 230 V therefore has a line voltage of about 400 V, and both numbers describe the same supply.

In a star the line current equals the phase current, and in a delta it is 1.73 times larger while the voltages match, and for either connection the total real power is three times that of one phase, $\sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L\cos\varphi$. The same power needs 0.75 times the conductor of a single-phase supply, and spreading single-phase loads over the phases keeps the load balanced and the losses low.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks inside the transformers that connect these supplies, where a kVA rating and two kinds of loss decide how much of the power gets through.

lessons.title: Real transformers: ratings and losses

lead.text: In the physics course a transformer passed on all the power it received, with the voltage fixed by the [[turns ratio|The ratio of the turns on the two coils, which is also the ratio of the voltages for an ideal transformer. Met in 'Changing fields make voltage' in Physics II: Waves, Electricity and Magnetism, and Heat.]]. A real transformer has two kinds of loss, and the handbook notes that every transformer has both. **Copper loss** is the power lost in the resistance of the primary and secondary windings. It is $I^2R$ in each, so it follows the square of the current, and the current follows the load.

**Core loss** arises in the iron core, in two ways: hysteresis, the energy spent in reversing the magnetic field as the alternating flux rises and falls, and eddy currents, which the changing flux drives round in the core itself. Core loss is the same at every load and dominates when the transformer is idle, so a transformer that supplies nothing still draws power from the supply.

afterFigure.text: The figure draws both losses for an invented 500 kVA unit, with a core loss of 1.2 kW and a copper loss of 6.0 kW at full load. The core loss is a flat line. The copper loss is a curve that rises with the square of the load, so it stays small over the lower part of the range and climbs steeply towards full load.

diagram.alt: A graph of loss in kilowatts against the fraction of full load for an invented 500 kVA transformer. The core loss is a flat line at 1.2 kilowatts. The copper loss, shown in the second view, is a curve that starts at zero, stays small at light load and rises to 6.0 kilowatts at full load.

lead.text: The efficiency of a transformer is its output power divided by its input power, and since the input is the output plus the losses, it can be found from the output and the two losses alone.

The output of a loaded transformer is its apparent power at that load multiplied by the power factor of the load. Typical distribution transformers reach between about 98 and 99 percent, and larger ones do better than small ones. Because the core loss stays fixed while the output falls with the load, a lightly loaded transformer wastes a larger share of what it takes in, and a few percent of a large power is still a large amount of heat.

steps.headline: A 10 kVA transformer has a copper loss of 100 W and a core loss of 70 W. Find its efficiency at full load, with a load of power factor 0.90.

workedSteps.text: At full load the output is the rating multiplied by the power factor.
The losses are the copper loss and the core loss together.
The input is the output plus the losses.
The efficiency is the output divided by the input.

lead.text: The two losses are the ones the handbook finds for this transformer, from a short-circuit test and an open-circuit test.

steps.headline: The invented 500 kVA unit has a core loss of 1.2 kW and a copper loss of 6.0 kW at full load. Find its efficiency at half load, with a load of power factor 0.8.

workedSteps.text: At half load the output is half the rating multiplied by the power factor.
The core loss stays at 1.2 kW, but the copper loss changes. Find it.
Add the losses to the output and find the efficiency.

lead.text: A transformer's windings heat with the current they carry, and the current that counts is the whole current, whatever share of it does useful work. Equipment that carries power has to be sized for that total current, and for this reason transformers are rated in volt-amperes, from a fraction of one to over a thousand megavolt-amperes.

The **rated current** on either side follows from the rating and the voltage on that side. For a single-phase unit it is $I = S/V$, and for a three-phase unit it is $I = S/(\sqrt{3}\,V_L)$. A 500 kVA three-phase transformer that steps 11 kV down to 400 V carries $500{,}000/(1.732 \times 400) = 722$ A on the 400 V side and $500{,}000/(1.732 \times 11{,}000) = 26.2$ A on the 11 kV side. The same apparent power is carried at both voltages, with the larger current at the lower voltage. Voltages of 11 kV and 33 kV are common for distribution in Australia, and the last step down is to 230/400 V.

A three-phase transformer has three windings on each side, and each side may be joined in star or in delta, or one of each. The voltage across a winding then follows the relations of 'Three-phase supply'. If the line voltage on the primary is 440 V, a delta winding has the whole 440 V across it and a star winding has $440/1.73 = 254$ V, as in the handbook's example.

The turns ratio $a$ then applies to each winding, and the line voltage on the secondary depends on how the secondary is joined: it equals the winding voltage for a delta, and 1.73 times the winding voltage for a star. A star secondary has a star point from which the neutral can be taken, which gives the phase voltage as well as the line voltage.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows three of the combinations, in each of which the primary has the line voltage $V$ across its windings. Delta to delta and star to star both leave the secondary line voltage at $V/a$, while delta to star adds the factor 1.73, so the connection is a second way, beside the turns ratio, of choosing the voltage that comes out.

reveal.text: Below the point where the losses are equal the core loss is the larger part of the heat, and above it the copper loss is, which is why a transformer that is oversized for its load loses most of its energy to the core.

lessons.orientation: Rate a transformer for a load, find its currents and efficiency from its losses, and say which losses change with load and which do not.
lessons.nextAction: Trace the path from the power station to the socket, and say why each voltage step is there.

blocks.text: The ideal transformer of the physics course passes on all the power it receives. A real distribution transformer is between about 98 and 99 percent efficient, so for every 100 kW that goes in, 1 to 2 kW is left behind as heat in the transformer itself.

Part of that heat is produced even when the transformer is supplying nothing, and the rest grows with how hard it works. The two parts follow different rules, and which of them matters depends on how the transformer is used.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a transformer's rated current from its kVA rating, work out its efficiency from its losses, and say which losses change with the load.
intro.whyItMatters: The rating says what a transformer can carry, and its two losses decide how much of the energy through it becomes heat at each load.

recap.keyIdea: A transformer is rated in kVA because voltage and current set its limits, and its efficiency follows from its output and two losses, one fixed and one that grows with the square of the load.

blocks.text: The copper loss is $I^2R$ in the windings and falls with the square of the load, while the core loss, from hysteresis and eddy currents, is the same at every load, so a lightly loaded transformer is less efficient than one near its rating. The efficiency is the output divided by the output plus both losses, and typical distribution transformers reach 98 to 99 percent.

The rated current on either side is the kVA rating divided by the voltage, with the factor 1.73 for a three-phase unit, so the same rating means a large current at 400 V and a small one at 11 kV. Delta and star windings change the voltage across each winding by a factor of 1.73, which is one more way of setting the voltage that comes out.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows the power from the station to the socket and uses the same $I^2R$ loss to show why each step up in voltage cuts the loss in the lines.

lessons.title: Why transmission uses high voltage

lead.text: A power station's generator produces its power at a voltage that suits the machine, and a step-up transformer then raises it to the voltage of the **transmission** network. Transmission lines carry bulk power from large generators to the load centres, and long-distance overhead lines typically run at between 115 and 1,200 kV. In South Australia, for example, the Heywood interconnector to Victoria, which was upgraded before the 2016 blackout to carry 650 MW at 275 kV.

At a **substation** the transmission voltage is stepped down to **distribution** voltage, and the electricity is injected into the distribution networks. In Australia 11 kV and 33 kV are common distribution voltages. Feeders carry the power along the streets to street transformers, and the last step down, to 230/400 V, supplies houses and small businesses.

afterFigure.text: Power passes from stage to stage almost undiminished, since in the United States transmission and distribution losses were estimated at 5% from 2013 to 2019. Each step down in voltage is therefore matched by a step up in current, while the long run between the power station and the first substation is made at the highest voltage in the path.

reveal.text: The loss falls to a quarter. For the same power, twice the voltage means half the current, and the heat in a conductor goes with the square of the current.

lead.text: Suppose a line of resistance $R$ delivers a power $P$ at a voltage $V$. The current in the line is $I = P/V$, so the power lost as heat in the line is $I^2 R = P^2 R / V^2$, and as a share of the power sent it is $PR/V^2$. For a fixed power and a fixed line, the share lost therefore varies as $1/V^2$.

The physics course met the same result when it raised a line from 230 V to 23,000 V and found that the loss fell to a ten-thousandth. Stated as a scaling rule, **the loss falls with the square of the voltage**: twice the voltage gives a quarter of the loss and ten times the voltage gives a hundredth, provided the conductors stay the same.

afterFigure.text: To compare two voltages for the same power over the same line, multiply the old loss by the square of the old voltage divided by the new one, so that $\text{new loss} = \text{old loss} \times (V_{old}/V_{new})^2$. The rule holds only while the power and the line stay the same, and a line that carries a different power or has a different conductor needs a fresh calculation.

diagram.alt: Four bars of relative line loss for the same power and line: 100% at voltage V, 25% at 2V, 6.25% at 4V and 1% at 10V, with the current falling to a half, a quarter and a tenth.
diagram.caption: Raising the voltage cuts the current in proportion and the loss with its square.

steps.headline: A line loses 6% of the power it carries at 66 kV. Find its loss for the same power over the same line at 132 kV.

workedSteps.text: Only the voltage changes, so start with the ratio of the old voltage to the new one.
The share lost varies as one over the voltage squared, so the old loss is multiplied by this ratio squared.
Multiply the old loss by that factor.
A check in words agrees: doubling the voltage halves the current, halving the current divides the heat by four, and 6% divided by 4 is 1.5%.

steps.headline: A 345 kV line carrying 1000 MW over 160 km loses 4.2% of the power. Estimate the loss on the same line at 765 kV.

workedSteps.text: The power, the line and the distance stay the same, so the loss is multiplied by the old voltage over the new one, squared.
Work out the factor for 345 kV and 765 kV.
Apply it to the 4.2%.

The source quotes 0.5% to 1.1% for a 765 kV line carrying 1000 MW over 160 km, so the estimate falls inside the range. The rule leaves out everything except voltage, which is why it lands near the middle and not exactly on a figure.

lead.text: A thicker conductor lowers the loss too, but *only* in proportion: doubling its cross-section halves its resistance and so halves the loss, whereas doubling the voltage quarters it. Larger conductors are also heavier and more expensive. Even when the conductor is made ten times smaller in cross-section to suit a current ten times lower, the loss at ten times the voltage is still ten times smaller, so **the voltage does most of the work**.

The voltage cannot rise without limit. Once the voltage between a conductor and the ground goes above 2,000 kV, **corona discharge** from the conductor causes losses large enough to cancel the saving in resistive loss, and the measures against it include larger conductor diameters, hollow conductors and bundles of conductors. The 115 to 1,200 kV of long-distance overhead lines sits below that point.

An AC line has inductance and capacitance of its own, and the currents that flow only in reaction to them transmit no power to the load. They still heat the conductors, so they add to the loss, and the more of them a line carries the lower its [[power factor|The ratio of real power to apparent power. Met in 'Power factor and its correction'.]]. A direct current has no such reactive part.

**High-voltage direct current** (HVDC) needs costly equipment to convert the power from AC and back again, so it pays only where the saving is large. That happens on very long, high-capacity lines, where the lower loss and the cheaper line can offset the converter stations at each end, and on long submarine cables, where cable capacitance rules AC out. HVDC is also necessary between two grids that are not synchronised, which means that their frequencies are not locked together.

Australia has examples of both kinds. Four of the National Electricity Market's networks form one synchronous grid, and Tasmania is linked to it by HVDC. Murraylink, which joins Berri in South Australia to Red Cliffs in Victoria, is an HVDC link rated at 220 MW at 150 kV, and submarine HVDC connections of up to 600 km have been built elsewhere.

reveal.text: The cable runs under the sea and joins grids that are out of step, so it meets two of the three conditions for HVDC at once, and either one alone would be enough to rule AC out.

lessons.orientation: Trace the path from a power station to a socket, say why each voltage step is there, and estimate how a change of line voltage changes the loss.
lessons.nextAction: Relate the poles, speed and frequency of a generator.

blocks.text: The National Electricity Market stretches from Port Douglas in Queensland to Port Lincoln in South Australia, more than 5,000 kilometres end to end, and it holds about 40,000 kilometres of high-voltage transmission line. The power point that gives you 230 V sits at the far end of that system, supplied by large generators that are usually located away from the towns they serve.

Between the generator and the socket the voltage is changed several times, and each change has a job to do. The order of the stages follows from one result of the physics course: a transformer that raises the voltage lowers the current by the same factor, and the heat a line loses depends on its current.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place the stages between a power station and a socket in order, estimate how a change of line voltage changes the loss, and say when HVDC is the better choice.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you estimate what a change of line voltage saves, and say why a link is built as AC or as HVDC.

recap.keyIdea: For the same power, the heat lost in a line falls with the square of the voltage, and HVDC takes over where AC cannot be used.

blocks.text: For a fixed power the current in a line is the power divided by the voltage, and the heat lost depends on the square of that current, so the share of power lost varies as one over the voltage squared. Doubling the voltage gives a quarter of the loss, and the 345 kV and 765 kV figures from the sources agree with the rule.

A bigger conductor helps only in proportion to its area, corona sets a limit above the voltages in use, and an AC line adds reactive current to its loss. HVDC accepts the cost of converter stations where a line is very long, runs under the sea, or joins grids that are not in step.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves to the start of the path and relates the poles, speed and frequency of the generators that feed it.

lessons.title: Speed, poles and frequency

lead.text: A generator makes one cycle of alternating voltage whenever a north pole and a south pole of its rotor have both passed a given point on the stationary winding. A machine with two poles therefore makes one cycle per turn, which is the single coil of the physics course, and a machine with four poles makes two cycles per turn, since two north and two south poles pass the winding in each revolution.

With $P$ poles there are $P/2$ pairs, so a machine turning at $N$ revolutions per minute makes $(P/2) \times (N/60)$ cycles every second. Setting that equal to the frequency $f$ gives $f = PN/120$, and solving for the speed gives the **synchronous speed**, $N = 120f/P$.

afterFigure.text: At 50 Hz a 2-pole machine therefore turns at $120 \times 50 / 2 = 3000$ rpm and a 4-pole machine at $120 \times 50 / 4 = 1500$ rpm. More poles mean a *slower* machine for the same frequency, because each turn then delivers more cycles.

diagram.alt: A rotor seen end-on with a stationary winding at the top, beside a graph of the winding voltage over one turn. Two poles give one cycle per turn and four poles give two, so at 50 Hz the rotors turn at 3000 and 1500 revolutions per minute.
diagram.caption: The same winding and the same 50 Hz, with two and four poles. Use the buttons to count the cycles in one turn.

reveal.text: At 1000 rpm a 6-pole machine turns a third as fast as a 2-pole machine, and each of its turns delivers three cycles to make up the difference.

lead.text: A synchronous generator connected to the grid has its frequency *fixed* by the grid, because its own output is small beside the load of a large grid, and its frequency is proportional to its speed. Each machine therefore turns at the synchronous speed for its own number of poles. A 2-pole generator at 3000 rpm and a 6-pole generator at 1000 rpm deliver the same 50 Hz, and both are **locked in step with every other machine on the grid**.

A governor that asks for more power from such a machine raises its fuel flow and its output, and the speed stays where the grid holds it. Because its speed follows from the grid's frequency and its own poles, dividing 120 times the frequency by the speed of a machine gives its number of poles.

reveal.text: A generator with one pair of poles turns at 3000 rpm to give 50 Hz, which is the fastest of the synchronous speeds at that frequency.

A voltage regulator adjusts the field current to hold the output voltage, and in a central power station the field current also regulates the [[reactive power|The part of the power that moves back and forth between source and load with no net transfer. Met in 'Real, reactive and apparent power'.]] that the machine exchanges with the grid. The frequency stays at the grid's value, and so does the speed.

lead.text: In a three-phase motor the stator carries three windings whose currents are 120 degrees apart in phase, so their magnetic fields combine into one field that rotates. The field turns at the synchronous speed $N_s = 120f/P$ for the supply frequency and the number of poles, which is the speed at which a generator with that number of poles would turn on the same frequency.

An **induction motor** has a rotor that follows this field without any connection to the supply. The rotating field cuts the rotor's conductors and induces a current in them, and the rotor's own magnetic field is then pulled round by the stator's. If the rotor ever reached the field's speed there would be no relative motion, no induced emf and so no torque, which means that the rotor always turns more slowly than the field. The percentage by which it falls short is the **slip**, $(N_s - N_r)/N_s \times 100\%$, where $N_r$ is the speed of the rotor.

afterFigure.text: The handbook works a case at 60 Hz: a 2-pole motor with a full-load speed of 3554 rpm has a field speed of 3600 rpm, so its slip is $46/3600 = 1.3\%$. A heavier load needs more rotor current and so more slip, up to about 10% in the range where the torque rises steadily with the slip, and the figure shows a 4-pole motor at two loads.

diagram.alt: A vertical speed scale from 1450 to 1500 revolutions per minute for a 4-pole induction motor on 50 Hz. The field sits at 1500. The rotor sits at 1485 with a slip of 1 percent on light load, and at 1455 with a slip of 3 percent on heavy load.
diagram.caption: An illustrative 4-pole motor. A heavier load pulls the rotor further below the field, which raises the slip.

lead.text: A **synchronous motor** has a stator like that of an induction motor, and so the same rotating field, but its rotor is supplied with direct current from an outside source and locks into step with the field. It turns at exactly the synchronous speed at every load. As the load grows the rotor pole shifts back a little behind the pole of the field and the speed does not change, and if the load grows until the rotor is pulled out of step the motor develops no torque and stops.

A synchronous motor also cannot start itself, because it develops torque only at synchronous speed. It is more often started as an induction motor by means of a winding in the faces of its rotor poles, and the direct current is applied once it has reached about 95% of synchronous speed.

The direct current in the rotor, called the field excitation, has a second effect that links back to [[power factor|The ratio of real power to apparent power. Met in 'Power factor and its correction'.]]. At a constant load, raising the excitation moves a synchronous motor toward a leading power factor and lowering it moves the motor toward a lagging one, and the speed does not change. Synchronous motors are used to drive large loads, and large industrial plants also use them to correct their power factor.

reveal.text: A speed of exactly 1500 rpm at every load means that the slip is zero, which only a synchronous motor can manage, and a rotor that is pulled out of step with the field produces no torque, so the motor stops.

lessons.orientation: Relate the poles, speed and frequency of generators and motors, and use slip to tell an induction motor from a synchronous machine.
lessons.nextAction: Predict which way grid frequency moves when supply and demand differ.

blocks.text: Every synchronous generator on the grid delivers alternating current at the same frequency, 50 hertz in Australia, yet the machines do not all turn at the same speed. A coil turning in a magnetic field gives one cycle of alternating voltage for each turn, as the physics course showed, so a single coil would have to turn 50 times a second to give 50 Hz.

Real generators are built with more than one pair of magnetic poles, and the number of poles decides how fast a machine has to turn to hold the grid's frequency. The same relation fixes how fast the rotating magnetic field of a three-phase motor turns, and it explains why such a motor always turns a little more slowly than that field.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the synchronous speed of a machine from its poles, work out the slip of an induction motor, and tell it from a synchronous motor.
intro.whyItMatters: It connects the speed of a machine to the frequency it delivers or draws, and shows what a generator's field current can and cannot change.

recap.keyIdea: A machine's synchronous speed is 120 times the frequency divided by its poles, an induction motor turns below it by the slip, and a synchronous machine locks to it exactly.

blocks.text: A machine with $P$ poles on a supply of frequency $f$ has a rotating field, or a rotor, that turns at $N = 120f/P$ revolutions per minute, so on a 50 Hz grid a 2-pole generator turns at 3000 rpm, a 4-pole one at 1500 rpm and a 6-pole one at 1000 rpm. The grid fixes the frequency of every connected synchronous machine, and the field current of a generator sets its voltage and reactive power.

An induction motor must turn more slowly than its field, and the slip is the shortfall as a percentage of the field's speed. A synchronous motor locks to the field at every load, stops if it is pulled out of step, cannot start itself, and uses its excitation to move its power factor between leading and lagging.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows what happens to the grid's frequency when the power supplied and the power demanded stop matching.

lessons.title: Grid frequency and inertia

lead.text: In a synchronous grid every generator must run at the same frequency and stay very nearly in step with the others. Each synchronous generator is a large spinning machine whose speed is tied to the frequency, as 'Speed, poles and frequency' showed, so there is an electromechanical link between the energy of its rotor and the frequency of the whole system.

That link makes **frequency a measure of the balance of the whole grid**. When the load is greater than the power put in, the excess load draws rotational energy from *every* rotor at once and the frequency falls, and when more power is put in than is drawn, the excess adds rotational energy and the frequency rises. Control systems read the frequency to decide whether generators should produce more or less, because it is the one number that the whole grid shares.

A synchronous generator and its turbine store a large amount of energy in their rotation, and that energy is available at once. When the load exceeds the power supplied, the rotors of all the synchronous machines slow down and give up some of it, and when there is a surplus they speed up and absorb it. The response is built into the machines, it needs no measurement and no signal, and it gives the grid operator a few seconds in which to rebalance the system.

The property that makes this store large is called **inertia**. For the same shortfall of power, a grid with more rotating mass has more energy to draw on, so its rotors slow more gradually and its frequency falls more slowly. Generators that connect through an inverter, such as solar plants and many wind farms, are not coupled to the grid by a rotating mass in this way, so replacing synchronous machines with them lowers the inertia of the grid.

afterFigure.text: Inertia does not stop the frequency from falling. It *slows* the fall, and the time it buys is what lets governors and other controls respond and restore the balance. The sketch shows two grids after the same loss, with the normal band marked around 50 Hz.

diagram.alt: A sketch of grid frequency against time after the same loss of generation on two grids, with a normal band marked around 50 hertz. The grid with more inertia falls slowly and takes longer to leave the band, and the grid with less inertia falls fast and leaves it sooner. The sketch is not to scale.

reveal.text: Grid B has less stored rotational energy to give up, so the same 500 MW shortfall moves its frequency faster. Its controls have less time to act before the frequency reaches the edge of its band.

lead.text: How fast the frequency moves is the **rate of change of frequency**, written ROCOF and measured in hertz per second. It is the change in frequency divided by the time that the change takes, and for a given loss it is larger when the grid has less inertia. A system with a high share of inverter-based generation can therefore show large rates, which stress the remaining synchronous generators and can trigger protection devices and load shedding.

Using the rate to tell harmless noise from a dangerous excursion is difficult, and a poor choice can cause false disconnections. As of 2017 the regulations of some grids required power plants to tolerate rates of 1 to 4 Hz per second, and the upper end of that range is an order of magnitude beyond what older gas turbines were designed to tolerate.

The loss of one unit in December 2017 gives a record from which a rate can be read. Unit A3 of the Loy Yang Power Station tripped at 1:58:59 am and its 560 MW was lost to the grid. The generators spun down over the next seconds, and twenty seconds after the trip, at 1:59:19, the frequency stood at 49.8 Hz.

A source on the Hornsdale Power Reserve reports that the fall brought in the battery, which injected 7.3 MW, and that the Gladstone Power Station responded at 1:59:27, eight seconds after the reading of 49.8 Hz.

afterFigure.text: The record gives two readings, the trip at 1:58:59 and 49.8 Hz at 1:59:19, and it does not give the frequency at the instant of the trip. A rate worked out over those 20 seconds is therefore an **average**, and it says nothing about how fast the frequency moved in the *first* second, when the inertia was doing the work.

reveal.text: The average fall was 0.01 Hz each second, much gentler than the 1 to 4 Hz per second that some grids required plants to tolerate. The start frequency of 50.00 Hz is an assumption of the question, since the record does not give it, and the rate in the first second could have been larger.

lead.text: The same failure is not the same size of event on every grid. In the United States a single failure can remove a power equal to 6.4% of the average load of the Texas grid, ERCOT, against 2.6% for the Western Interconnection and 1.3% for the Eastern Interconnection. Texas is relatively small and has a high share of wind power, and it took the lead in the United States in looking for alternatives to the traditional inertia.

A loss that is **a larger share of the load is a larger imbalance**, so other things equal it moves the frequency further. Smaller power systems that are not widely interconnected, with fewer generators and loads, also hold their frequency less accurately than large ones.

reveal.text: The comparison is between the loss and the grid, not between megawatts. A loss of the same number of megawatts is a larger event on a grid with a smaller load.

lead.text: A grid that is losing synchronous machines has several remedies. **Synchronous condensers** bring rotating mass onto the grid, so they add inertia *directly*. Large loads that can tolerate a brief interruption, such as industrial cooling plants, can be fitted with relays that disconnect them at a set frequency, which can remove the demand within about half a second including the measurement. Operators can also allow a wider swing of the frequency, or oblige some synchronous generators to keep running, which the source describes as a temporary measure on economic grounds.

Batteries are another route, because their inverters can be set to behave like a machine. In 2021 the Hornsdale battery reported a successful real-life test of a virtual machine mode, in which a small selection of trial inverters gave an inertial response, and Wikipedia says that after an upgrade in 2022 the battery had 2,000 megawatt-seconds of grid inertia, about 15 percent of the state's total requirement. A response that starts only after the frequency has been measured is a different thing from the inertia of a spinning rotor, which needs no measurement at all.

reveal.text: Only the condensers add rotating mass. The relays and the wider band are ways of coping with a fall, and solar plant adds generation without adding inertia.

lessons.orientation: Predict which way grid frequency moves when supply and demand differ, and explain how inertia sets how fast it moves.
lessons.nextAction: Put the layers of frequency control in order of speed.

blocks.text: At 1:58:59 am on 14 December 2017, unit A3 of the Loy Yang Power Station tripped and took 560 MW out of the grid. Twenty seconds later the frequency had dropped to 49.8 Hz. The shortage of power showed up as a change in a number that every generator on the grid shares.

Frequency measures the balance between the power generated and the power drawn, and how fast it moves after a loss depends on how much spinning machinery is connected to the grid. The question below asks what the remaining generators do in the first seconds after such a trip.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict which way the frequency moves when supply and demand differ, compare grids by their inertia, and read a frequency event.
intro.whyItMatters: It shows why a grid with less rotating machinery needs faster controls, and how to size a loss against the grid that suffers it.

recap.keyIdea: Frequency is the balance signal of the whole grid, inertia sets how fast it moves after a loss, and the same loss moves it further where it is a larger share of the load.

blocks.text: Every synchronous generator is locked to the grid frequency, so a shortage of power slows all the rotors together and a surplus speeds them up. The rotors supply or absorb the imbalance at once, which is inertia, and it slows the first fall so that governors and reserves have time to act.

The rate of change of frequency is larger when inverter-based plant replaces synchronous machines, and a record of two readings gives only an average rate. The same loss moves the frequency further where it is a larger share of the load, and condensers, load shedding and batteries with suitable inverters are ways to put inertia or its effect back.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson puts the layers of frequency control in order of speed and follows how the market buys them.

lessons.title: Frequency control and reserves

lead.text: The first layer is the **inertia** of the synchronous rotors, which acts at once because it is built into the machines. Each running generator then changes its power through its **governor**, a controller that raises the fuel flow when the speed falls, and this response is automatic and needs no instruction from outside. Together they slow the fall in frequency and give the slower layers time to arrive.

**Automatic generation control**, or AGC, adjusts the output of generators at different power stations in response to the measured frequency, within several tens of seconds. Spinning reserve is extra output from generators that are already connected, so it is headroom on running machines and not idle plant, while non-spinning reserve is capacity that can start up and join the system after a short delay. Generators offering either should reach their promised output within about ten minutes. Replacement reserve comes from plant that needs thirty to sixty minutes to start, and it relieves the other reserves so that the system is ready for the next loss.

afterFigure.text: Operating reserve is the capacity that the operator can call on at short notice, and most power systems are designed to hold at least as much as their biggest single supplier together with a share of the peak load, so that the loss of any one unit can be covered. Batteries can act as reserve too, because they react within fractions of a second.

lead.text: A governor with **droop** lets a generator's output rise as the frequency falls and fall as it rises, in proportion to the change. The droop is stated as the percentage change in speed that would carry the machine from no load to full load. A turbine rated at 3000 rpm that slows to 2880 rpm between no load and full load has a droop of $(3000 - 2880)/3000 = 4\%$.

For a unit with 4% droop, every 1% change in speed changes the output by 25% of its rating, since 1% is a quarter of the 4% that covers the whole range. On a grid the speed of each synchronous machine follows the frequency, so every unit sees the same percentage change. Units with the same droop therefore share a change in load in proportion to their ratings.

steps.headline: A 600 MW unit has a droop of 4%, and the grid frequency falls from 50 Hz by 0.2 Hz. Find how much the unit raises its output.

workedSteps.text: Express the fall in frequency as a percentage of 50 Hz.
Each 1% change in speed moves a unit with 4% droop by 25% of its rating, so multiply the percentage by 25.
Take that percentage of the 600 MW rating.
The unit raises its output by 60 MW, and every unit with the same droop raises its own output by the same 10% of its rating.

steps.headline: A 300 MW unit has a droop of 4%, and the frequency falls from 50 Hz by 0.15 Hz. Find the extra power it supplies.

workedSteps.text: Express the fall in frequency as a percentage of 50 Hz.
At 4% droop each 1% moves the output by 25% of the rating, so multiply by 25.
Take that percentage of the 300 MW rating.

lead.text: Every 5 minutes the market operator, AEMO, decides which generators will run in the next interval. Power stations submit offers, each a quantity of power at a price, and AEMO dispatches the cheapest offers first and then progressively dearer ones until the demand is met. It sends each scheduled generator its target as an automatic generation control signal.

The highest-priced offer that is needed to meet the demand sets the price for that interval in the region, and **every dispatched generator is paid that price**, whatever it offered. The figure takes four invented offers and shows three levels of demand.

afterFigure.text: The price is set again for each 5-minute interval, so it moves whenever a change in demand brings a different offer to the edge of the dispatch.
