reveal.text: A and B supply 700 MW between them, and the other 150 MW has to come from C, so C is the last offer used and its $90 sets the price. D is not called on.

B offered $45 and so was called on early, and it is paid $90 like every other dispatched unit. An offer says the lowest price at which a generator will run, and the price that it receives is set by the market.

lead.text: Dispatch plans the energy for the next 5 minutes, and holding the frequency from second to second is a separate job that AEMO buys as frequency control ancillary services, or FCAS. Staying inside the band of 49.85 to 50.15 Hz for all but 1% of the time, which is 7.2 hours in 30 days, is the job these services do.

AEMO runs 10 FCAS markets, and each is for either a regulation service or a contingency service. **Regulation** services operate all the time and even out the small variations in frequency that arise from minor changes in demand or supply. **Contingency** services cover the large changes that follow a sudden, unexpected shift in supply or demand, so they are called on less often, and they are bought as raise or lower services.

AEMO buys FCAS through a market that is co-optimised with energy, which means that it considers the offers in both markets together to keep the overall cost down. Batteries, virtual power plants and demand response are among the newer providers of FCAS, and in some cases they have displaced coal, gas and hydro. From 8 June 2025 frequency performance payments have rewarded units that help stabilise the frequency and charged those that make deviations worse. The first stage of the Hornsdale battery shows the two roles side by side: 70 MW for 10 minutes was contracted to the government for grid services, and 30 MW for 3 hours was used to buy energy when prices were low and sell it when demand was high.

reveal.text: Regulation follows the small continuous wander of supply and demand, contingency covers the large sudden losses, and dispatch plans the energy for each interval ahead.

lessons.orientation: Put the layers of frequency control in order of speed, match each disturbance to the layer that handles it, and say how the NEM dispatches generators and buys frequency services.
lessons.nextAction: Say which device clears a fault, and why it has a short-circuit rating.

blocks.text: The operator of the National Electricity Market must keep the system frequency between 49.85 and 50.15 hertz, and the frequency may leave that range for at most 1% of any 30 days. When a large unit trips, the frequency begins to fall at once, and no single control can stop the fall on its own. A series of controls, each slower to arrive than the one before, takes over in turn.
Knowing which layer acts when tells the operator how much reserve to hold and tells the market which services to buy.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to put the layers of frequency control in order of speed, find a droop response, read a dispatch price, and match a disturbance to the service that handles it.
intro.whyItMatters: It shows what the grid holds in reserve against a loss, and how a market turns offers into one price and a set of frequency services.

recap.keyIdea: A trip is met by inertia and droop at once, AGC within tens of seconds, reserves within minutes and replacement reserve later, and the NEM buys frequency services apart from the energy it dispatches at one price.

blocks.text: After a large trip the layers act in order of speed: the inertia of the rotors, the droop of each governor, automatic generation control, the spinning and non-spinning reserves, and the replacement reserve. A unit with 4% droop changes its output by 25% of its rating for each 1% change in speed, so units with the same droop share a change in proportion to their ratings.

Every 5 minutes AEMO dispatches the cheapest offers first, and the highest offer needed sets the price that every dispatched generator receives. Regulation services follow the small continuous variations of normal operation, contingency services answer large sudden losses, and both are bought together with energy to hold the frequency between 49.85 and 50.15 Hz.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from the machines to the protection that disconnects a faulty part of the network.

lessons.title: Protecting against overcurrent

lead.text: A short circuit can draw many times the normal rated current of its circuit, and the largest current that a fault could draw at a given point is called the **prospective short-circuit current**. Ohm's law gives the fault of the opening question a current of $230 / 0.05 = 4600$ A, which is 230 times the 20 A that its circuit normally carries, so a protective device has to be able to interrupt a current far greater than any load it serves.

When a device opens against such a current an arc tends to form between its contacts, and the arc can keep the current flowing, ionise the gases around it and melt or vaporise metal. Circuit breakers therefore carry two ratings, the normal current they are expected to carry and the largest short-circuit current they can safely interrupt, which is their **interrupting capacity**. Typical domestic panel breakers are rated to interrupt 10 kA, which is 10,000 A.

The interrupting capacity has to be at least the prospective current at the point where the breaker is used. A breaker applied where the prospective current is higher may fail to interrupt the fault safely, and the arc can then damage the breaker and the equipment around it.

reveal.text: The interrupting capacity is the rating that matters for a fault, and it is below the current that a fault could draw at that point, so the breaker is under-rated for its position whatever its current rating says.

lead.text: A **fuse** is the simplest of the devices. It holds a fusible link sized so that the heat from the normal current does not melt it, and when an overcurrent or a short-circuit current flows through it the link melts and opens the circuit. A fuse protects against overcurrent only, and since it clears a fault by melting it needs no mechanical operation and so no mechanical maintenance. A fuse that has operated has been destroyed by the fault and has to be replaced.

Fuses act quickly. A fuse can clear a fault inside a quarter of a cycle, where a circuit breaker needs about half a cycle to a whole one. At 50 Hz one cycle lasts 20 ms, so by those cycle counts the fuse clears the fault in about 5 ms and the breaker in about 10 to 20 ms. Current-limiting fuses open in less than one cycle, which limits the energy let through into the circuit, and where the fault level is very high some moulded-case breakers are preceded by one.

A fuse senses overcurrent and nothing else. In a three-phase circuit, if one fuse opens the other phases carry more than their normal currents and the voltages become unbalanced, which can damage motors, and a fuse cannot detect an earth fault on its own.

A **circuit breaker** has to detect a fault and then open. In small low-voltage breakers the detection happens inside the device, through the heating or the magnetic effect of the current, and a mechanism that stores energy, such as a spring, then separates the contacts against the arc that forms. Unlike a fuse, a breaker can be reset after the fault has been cleared, although some types need regular maintenance to keep their mechanism working. Miniature circuit breakers for domestic circuits are made in ratings from 6 A to 125 A.

A breaker for large currents or high voltages is usually paired with a **protective relay**, which senses the fault and operates the opening mechanism, so that the relay does the sensing and the breaker does the opening. Relays are not limited to overcurrent. They can be designed to guard generating equipment and circuits against conditions such as undervoltage and underfrequency, and the breakers that they work with disconnect the part that is at fault.

reveal.text: The three devices share a job and divide it differently: a fuse senses and opens by melting, a breaker senses small faults itself and opens by moving contacts, and a relay senses and leaves the opening to a breaker.

lead.text: Protective devices at different levels of a network are in series, so a fault on a branch circuit sends the same current through the branch device, the feeder device and the main device. If all of them operated, a fault in one small circuit would cut off everything that the feeder and the main supply. **Coordination** is the design that makes only the device closest to the fault clear it, so that the branch device disconnects its circuit well before the feeder device begins to act, and the other circuits fed from the same supply are disturbed as little as possible. The same idea holds for breakers and for a mixture of fuses and breakers.

reveal.text: The branch device is chosen to act before the devices behind it begin to, so a fault in one branch takes only that branch out of supply.

lead.text: On a large network the same idea is applied to the equipment itself. A separate **zone of protection** is drawn around each element of the system, such as a generator, a bus, a transformer or a feeder, and a fault anywhere in a zone makes all the circuit breakers of that zone open. The figure shows a generator, a bus, a transformer and two feeders, with each zone bounded by its breakers.

afterFigure.text: The zones overlap at the breakers, because each breaker belongs to the zones on both sides of it. A fault inside one element opens only the breakers around that element. A fault that falls in the overlap, at a breaker, opens the breakers of both zones, which is more breakers than the fault strictly needs.

reveal.text: If two zones met along a line with no overlap, a fault on that line would belong to neither zone and no breaker would open. Overlapping the zones puts every point in at least one of them, at the cost of opening a few more breakers than a fault needs.
The fault lies in one zone, so the breakers of that zone open and nothing else does. Motor 1 and the bus stay in supply.

lessons.orientation: For a described fault, say which device clears it (fuse, circuit breaker or relay with a breaker), which should operate first, and why a breaker has a short-circuit rating as well as a current rating.
lessons.nextAction: Say which protection acts for a household fault, and when to call a licensed electrician.

blocks.text: A circuit in a house may normally carry 20 A, and a breaker rated at 20 A protects it. If a fault joins the conductors of the supply through a path of very low resistance, the current is limited only by that resistance, and Ohm's law shows how large it can become.

Protective devices have to open against a current of that size, and where several of them stand in series the right one has to act first. Nothing here is a guide to working on them, because inspecting and installing household wiring is work for an A grade electrician, as Energy Safe Victoria says.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which device clears a fault, which should act first, and why a breaker has a short-circuit rating as well as a current rating.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you read a protection arrangement and judge whether a device suits its position and acts in the right order.

recap.keyIdea: A fault can draw many times the rated current, so a breaker's interrupting capacity has to exceed the prospective current, and the device or zone closest to the fault should clear it.

blocks.text: A fault can draw a current many times the rated current of its circuit, so a breaker carries an interrupting capacity as well as a current rating, and it is suitable only where that capacity exceeds the prospective short-circuit current. A fuse melts and has to be replaced, a breaker opens its contacts and can be reset, and a protective relay senses a condition and tells a breaker to open.

Devices in series are coordinated so that the one closest to the fault clears it and the other circuits stay on. On a larger network each element has a protective zone, the zones overlap at the breakers, and a fault in the overlap opens a few more breakers than it needs, which is accepted because a gap between zones would leave a fault with no protection.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the protection of people, and what a safety switch does that a breaker or a fuse does not.

lessons.title: Earthing and safety switches

lead.text: A breaker or a fuse acts only when the current in the circuit as a whole is excessive, and Wikipedia's article on residual-current devices says that this level can be thousands of times the leakage that matters to a person. A leak through a person can still be a very serious fault, but it adds too little to the total for a fuse or an overload breaker to isolate the circuit. The device that does respond is the safety switch, which the standards call a **residual-current device**, or RCD.

It works by comparison. A differential current transformer, which both conductors pass through, measures the difference between the current going out on the line and the current coming back on the neutral. In a healthy circuit the two are equal, because everything that leaves by the line returns by the neutral. If some of the current takes another way back, for instance through a person to earth, the neutral carries less than the line, and the difference is the leak. When it reaches the device's rating, which is 30 mA on a household safety switch, the device opens, and ESV says it does so within 0.03 of a second.

afterFigure.text: The switch does not need to know where the leak goes. Wikipedia notes that the trip works just as well when the current returns through plumbing, or through contact with the ground, or by any other route, so it still gives some protection when the earth wiring is damaged or incomplete. The figure shows the same circuit twice, with nothing wrong and then with a leak through a person, and the reading on the neutral is the first thing that changes.

diagram.alt: A household circuit with line and neutral conductors from the supply, through a safety switch, to an appliance. Healthy: both carry 5.000 A, the difference is zero and the switch stays closed. Leaking: 50 mA passes from the appliance through a person to earth, the neutral carries 4.950 A, the difference is above 30 mA and the switch opens.
diagram.caption: The safety switch compares the two currents that pass through it. Use the buttons to see a healthy circuit and a leak through a person.

reveal.text: The leak is the only thing the switch measures. A line current of 8 A says nothing about whether the circuit is safe, while a neutral that is 60 mA short of it shows a leak.

lead.text: Because the switch reads only the difference between line and neutral, that difference also marks the limit of what it can protect. Current that goes out along the line and returns along the neutral gives no difference, whether it passes through a heater or through a person who is touching both conductors, and Wikipedia says that a device cannot tell current through an intended load from current through a person. An RCD alone also does not detect an overload or a short circuit between line and neutral, which is why the breaker or fuse stays on the circuit and why some units, called RCBOs, combine the two.

ESV puts the same limits from the householder's side: a safety switch adds protection alongside breakers and fuses, it may leave some wiring and appliances unprotected, and it cannot prevent every shock. A [[safety switch|Compares the current out on the line with the current back on the neutral, and opens when the difference reaches its rating. Met earlier in this lesson.]] also acts only on the circuit it is connected to, and only while it is working correctly.

reveal.text: Wikipedia adds one qualification: the switch may still trip if the person is also in contact with the ground, because some current then passes through the finger and body to earth. It is not something to rely on.

lead.text: A leak is one way for a shock to arise. The other is a fault that makes metal which was never meant to carry current live, for example when a loose live conductor touches the casing of an appliance. Wikipedia describes a second kind of protection, which relies on earthing. Exposed metal parts are connected to the earthing system, so that if one of them becomes live a circuit is completed and current flows, and the aim is for that current to be large enough to open the breaker or fuse. Wikipedia counts this method, called **automatic disconnection of supply**, among the most widely used protections against electric shock.

It works only if the path back to the supply is easy for the current to take. Wikipedia explains that when the fault path has a sufficiently low impedance, the fault current makes the overcurrent device open and clear the fault, and that if the impedance is too high the current may not open it quickly enough. The earth conductor is not part of the circuit that powers the appliance, and it exists to give a fault a path. Wikipedia adds that an earthing system, together with its protective devices, must ultimately stop a person touching metal whose voltage relative to the person exceeds a safe threshold, typically about 50 V AC.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the same fault is drawn with and without the earth connection. With it, the fault becomes a large current that the breaker clears, and the casing is not left live for anyone to touch. Without it nothing opens, and the casing stays live until a person provides the way back, which is the leak that the safety switch exists to catch. Australia and New Zealand use the multiple earthed neutral system, which section 5 of AS/NZS 3000 covers, and how it is wired is work for licensed electricians, so this lesson goes no further into it.

diagram.alt: A live wire inside an appliance touches its metal casing, drawn twice. With an earth connection a large fault current flows along the earth conductor, the breaker opens and the casing goes dead. Without one the breaker stays closed and the casing stays live until a person touching it gives the current a way to earth.

lead.text: An Australian switchboard can hold three kinds of protective device, and ESV asks householders to understand how they differ. A circuit breaker, or a fuse, protects against short circuits and overloads, for instance on an overloaded power point. A safety switch protects people from shock by a leak, and ESV says it always has a test button and 30 mA printed on it. A **surge diverter** guards the property against voltage surges, for example from a lightning strike, by capturing the spikes in the wiring that would otherwise pass on to the equipment inside.

None of them replaces another. ESV is explicit that neither a surge diverter nor a circuit breaker stands in for a safety switch when a person has to be protected from shock, and that a safety switch is an extra layer to use alongside breakers and fuses. According to Wikipedia, Australia has required safety switches on power circuits since 1991 and on lighting circuits since 2000, and ESV says one is now compulsory on new residential installations. ESV also lists an old switchboard, particularly one without a safety switch, among the signs that wiring may be faulty.

reveal.text: Each device answers to one measurement, so a hazard that none of the three measures, such as the finger across line and neutral, is left uncovered.

lead.text: A safety switch has a test button, which creates a small leak on purpose. ESV's household pages describe a householder pressing it, checking that the lights and appliances on that circuit have lost power, and resetting the switch. Wikipedia explains why the test matters: a safety switch is built to trip on a very small current, which gives it too little force to free a stuck mechanism, so a switch that has not operated for a long time can fail without anyone knowing. If the lights and appliances stay on, ESV says the safety switch may have failed and a licensed electrician should be called immediately to investigate. ESV's own pages give different intervals for testing, so this lesson gives none, and the regulator's current advice is the one to follow.

Everything beyond the test button is licensed work. ESV says that household wiring may be inspected and installed only by an A grade electrician. For a house built before the 1980s it wants the wiring checked, before anyone moves in, by a licensed electrical inspector or a registered electrical contractor. Each year, fire brigades are called to more than 300 domestic electrical fires, and ESV says that many come from old wiring that has degraded or cannot cope with modern equipment. ESV calls the safety switch an additional protection, and its advice on old wiring is an inspection by a licensed electrician.

reveal.text: The devices on the board act when a fault occurs, and an inspection finds the conditions that lead to one, which is why ESV asks for both.

lessons.orientation: For a described household fault, say which protection acts, what it does and does not protect against, and when the answer is to call a licensed electrician.
lessons.nextAction: Read the 2016 South Australian blackout as a timeline, and separate its trigger, the weaknesses that let it spread and the protection that acted.

blocks.text: A kettle rated at 2.3 kW on a 230 V supply draws 10 A, and the breaker on its circuit is built to let that current flow and to open only when the current climbs well above what the wiring can carry. A shock is a different kind of fault, because the current that matters is a few hundredths of an ampere passing through a person to earth. A breaker has no means of telling that this has happened, and the device that does notice it is the safety switch.

Energy Safe Victoria (ESV), the Victorian electrical safety regulator, tells householders to understand how the protective devices on a switchboard differ, and it leaves any work on household wiring to licensed electricians. How much the leak changes the circuit's current is the place to begin.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which protective device deals with a described household fault, what it does and does not protect against, and when the right step is to call a licensed electrician.
intro.whyItMatters: Devices on a switchboard look alike, and knowing which one senses what tells you what a given fault leaves unprotected.

recap.keyIdea: A breaker senses total current, a safety switch senses the difference between line and neutral, and earthing gives a fault a path that opens the breaker, so each covers a different hazard and a failed test or old wiring is a job for a licensed electrician.

blocks.text: A breaker or fuse responds to the total current in a circuit, which a leak through a person barely changes, so a safety switch compares the line and neutral currents and opens within about 0.03 of a second when the difference reaches its 30 mA rating. It cannot see current that returns on the neutral through a person, or an overload, and a surge diverter protects equipment and not people.

Earthing connects exposed metal to the supply so that a fault to it becomes a large current for the breaker or fuse to clear. When the test button leaves the lights on, or when wiring is old, ESV's answer is the same: call a licensed electrician.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows a real blackout, South Australia in 2016, in which protection that acted as designed still left most of a state without power.

lessons.title: How a grid trips: South Australia, 2016

lead.text: South Australia's grid is run by ElectraNet and connected to the rest of the National Electricity Market by two interconnectors to Victoria. The Heywood interconnector had been upgraded shortly before to carry 650 MW at 275 kV, and Murraylink is a 220 MW link at 150 kV that uses HVDC. On 28 September 2016 the state was hit by a violent storm, reported as a once-in-50-years event, with at least seven tornadoes and at least 80,000 lightning strikes. The wind damaged 23 pylons on transmission lines, and the grid operator, which had not foreseen a significant lightning risk to its transmission system, had taken no protective action against one.

The Heywood interconnector had been out of service for an upgrade earlier in the year, and it was blamed for the outage at first. Wikipedia's account of the sequence gives that upgrade no part. The next screen asks you to put five events in order, using what you know about how protection, interconnectors and wind generation behave.

reveal.text: The next screen puts times to the first four of these events, which all fall inside a minute and a half.

lead.text: Wikipedia's summary of the preliminary report from AEMO, the market operator, puts the start of the trouble 90 seconds before the state went dark. The figure lays the main events along that minute and a half in two views, and the second magnifies the last ten seconds. Each event is a line or a plant that tripped or cut its output. The first line to trip was reset automatically, and so was the Davenport to Belalie line, which then tripped a second time nine seconds later and was isolated for manual inspection.

afterFigure.text: These times are as Wikipedia gives them from the preliminary report. AEMO's own reports are not among this course's sources, so treat the details as that summary's. Two features stand out. For more than a minute the early faults came one at a time and the state stayed connected, and the final events came within a few seconds of each other, with the wind farm reductions arriving just before the flow on the Heywood interconnector rose above 850 MW and its two circuits tripped. Wikipedia attributes that trip to imminent loss of synchronism between South Australia and the eastern states.

In the last 10 seconds a second 275 kV line trips again, the Hallett wind farm cuts 123 MW, a third 275 kV line faults, and within one second after that two more wind farms cut output and both Heywood circuits trip.

lead.text: Wikipedia's account singles out the wind farms. The damaged lines caused several voltage glitches, which strained the ride-through ability of most of the state's wind farms. **Ride-through** is a plant's ability to stay connected while a voltage or frequency disturbance passes. According to AEMO, settings in the wind farms' software stopped turbines from restarting again and again once such disturbances came too close together. One group of turbines tolerated nine ride-throughs in 120 seconds and remained connected for much of the event, while a larger group could not accept that many and dropped out, which shut down the interconnector and so cut the state's supply.

AEMO recommended that the wind farms improve their fault ride-through. In 2019 the Australian Energy Regulator started proceedings in the Federal Court against the operators of four wind farms, alleging that they had not complied with the performance requirements for riding through major disruptions and disturbances. Wikipedia records the filing and gives no outcome, so this lesson says nothing about how it ended.

Three kinds of event can be told apart in a blackout timeline. The **trigger** is the event that starts the chain, which here is the storm and its damage to the lines. A **weakness** is a condition already in place that decides how far the chain can run, such as the wind farm settings, or the fact that the grid operator had not foreseen a significant lightning risk and so took no protective action against one. A **protective response** is automatic action that isolates plant or lines, and Wikipedia's account describes two: early on, the network's automatic safety features isolated generators to protect both the plant and consumers' equipment, and at the end both circuits of the Heywood interconnector tripped out because synchronism with the eastern states was about to be lost.

A chain in which each failure loads or disturbs the next is a **cascade**, and reading one means asking of each link whether it began the chain, let it widen or acted on it. The three kinds do not compete for blame. A protective response is protection doing what it is built to do, as the devices of 'Protecting against overcurrent' and 'Earthing and safety switches' do, and it can still end in a blackout when the weaknesses have left too little of the network to run on.

reveal.text: Wikipedia's account does not rank the three, and a claim that gives one of them the whole blame goes further than the evidence.

lead.text: Restoring a grid takes longer than losing one, because a power station cannot start without power. A steam plant needs station service power, up to about 10 percent of its capacity, for boiler feedwater pumps, combustion air blowers and fuel preparation. Normally it draws that from its own generators, or from the grid through its transmission line when the generators are shut down, and in a wide-area outage the grid has none to give. A **black start** brings a station, or part of a grid, back into operation with no help from the outside transmission network, and it needs a source that does not depend on the grid, such as a small diesel generator that can start larger generators.

South Australia in 2016 shows how hard that is. AEMO had restart contracts with two providers of System Restart Ancillary Services. The Quarantine Power Station could not start its larger Unit 5, which was needed to restart any of the Torrens Island units, and Torrens Island therefore had to wait for power from the Victorian interconnector. Wikipedia gives the reason as a circuit breaker in the Quarantine switchyard that tripped repeatedly on in-rush current and used up its stored energy before Unit 5 could start. Restoration began with the Victorian interconnectors establishing a stable frequency, and South Australia's generators were added gradually. Adelaide's suburbs began to get power back within about three hours, and the city was largely restored by 10 p.m., while large areas of the Mid North and the Eyre Peninsula were still without power 24 hours after the failure.

The AER's State of the energy market 2025 sets out the vocabulary of these problems. Power system security is the technical stability of frequency, voltage, inertia and similar characteristics, and system strength is the ability of the power system to keep network protection operating correctly and voltage waveforms stable. The AER notes that synchronous generators, meaning coal, gas and hydro, have traditionally supplied these services, and that other technologies can replicate them with the right market settings, including synchronous condensers and grid-forming inverter-based resources such as batteries.

AEMO may direct market participants to act to maintain or restore security, as a last resort when the market has not delivered what is needed, and in May 2025 it published plans to cut the number of synchronous generators that must be running in South Australia from 2 to 1, if certain criteria are met. The report does not link those plans to the events of 2016, and this lesson does not either.
The AER's report also records that South Australia was cut off from Victoria again in early 2020. Islanded means separated from the rest of the grid and left to run on its own.

reveal.text: The note ties the cost to the islanding and names the bushfires as a separate driver, which is the same kind of separation that the 2016 timeline asks for.

blocks.text: On 28 September 2016 a storm damaged electricity transmission infrastructure in South Australia, and at about 3:50 p.m. almost the entire state grid had been cut out. About 850,000 customers lost supply, and only Kangaroo Island kept its power, because its own power station had been built for the case in which the cable under Backstairs Passage failed.

The sequence below comes from Wikipedia's summary of the market operator's preliminary report, because AEMO's own reports are not among this course's sources, so its details are that summary's. Before the details, make a guess about how fast it happened.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a blackout timeline, separate the trigger, the weaknesses and the protection that acted, and judge which statements about the cause the evidence supports.
intro.whyItMatters: The 2016 blackout was a chain of events, and sorting them shows why protection that works can still end in lost supply.

recap.keyIdea: Reading a blackout means asking of each event whether it started the chain, decided how far it spread, or was protection acting, and in 2016 the storm began it, wind farm settings let it spread and protection separated the state.

blocks.text: The 2016 blackout took about 90 seconds from the first line trip to the loss of almost the whole state. A storm damaged the lines, wind farm settings left many turbines unable to ride through repeated faults, and protection isolated generators and then tripped both circuits of the Heywood interconnector. The account does not rank these, so a claim about the cause has to be checked against all three.

Restoring a grid starts with a source that needs no grid, since a power station needs its own power to start, which is why South Australia relied on restart contracts and on the Victorian interconnectors. The details come from Wikipedia's summary of AEMO's preliminary report, and AEMO's own reports are the next source to read.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the inverters on millions of Australian roofs, which follow the grid and do not hold it up the way a spinning generator does.

lessons.title: Inverters and rooftop solar

lead.text: Solar panels produce direct current, and a **grid-tie inverter** converts it to alternating current at the voltage and frequency of the grid. To feed power into the grid efficiently and safely, the inverter has to line up with the grid's sine wave in voltage, frequency and phase. According to Wikipedia an internal computer senses the grid's waveform and sets its own output voltage to track it, holding that voltage slightly above the grid's at each instant so that current flows out to the grid. A grid-tie inverter therefore follows the grid and does not set it.

That has consequences. A grid-tie inverter is built to disconnect quickly when the grid goes down, and it will not run at all unless it can detect the grid, which avoids islanding, a condition Wikipedia says can cause safety problems. Wikipedia notes that a requirement in the United States exists so that an inverter's output cannot harm people repairing the lines, and this course's sources give no Australian rule on the subject, so the lesson does not say what Australian standards require. A house with a plain grid-tie system therefore has no supply from its panels during a blackout.

An inverter also has no rotating mass tied to the grid. Wikipedia explains that a generator connected through an inverter cannot contribute inertia in the way a synchronous generator does, so any inertial response has to be added by design. In 2021 the Hornsdale battery in South Australia reported a successful real-life test of a virtual machine mode, in which a small selection of trial inverters gave an inertial response, and Wikipedia says that after an upgrade in 2022 the battery had 2,000 megawatt-seconds of grid inertia, about 15 percent of the state's total requirement.

On an ordinary street a transformer steps the distribution voltage down to the 230 V that the houses use, and a feeder carries the power along the street, so that power flows from the transformer outwards. The AER describes what rooftop solar changes: small generators are now embedded within distribution networks, and the result is two-way flows. At midday a house with solar uses what its panels make and sends the surplus back along the feeder, and if enough houses do so at once, the transformer carries the sum of their exports.

A transformer is rated in kVA for the current it can carry without overheating, and that rating gives a way to judge how large the exports are. A modern grid-tie inverter holds a fixed unity power factor, according to Wikipedia, and at unity power factor a kilowatt and a kilovolt-ampere are equal, so the exports of the houses can be added up and compared directly with the rating. The next screen does that for an invented street.

steps.headline: Thirty houses on an invented street each export 5 kW at midday onto a 100 kVA transformer. How large is the flow back, compared with the rating?

workedSteps.text: Add up the exports of the houses.
At unity power factor a kilowatt equals a kilovolt-ampere, so the flow can be set beside the rating directly.
Divide the flow by the rating.
The flow back through the transformer is 1.5 times its rating, so on this street the transformer is the first limit on how much solar the houses can export.

steps.headline: Twenty houses on a second invented street each export 6 kW at midday onto a 150 kVA transformer. Is the transformer the first limit?

workedSteps.text: Add up the exports, and treat them as kVA at unity power factor.
Divide the flow by the rating to see what fraction of the rating it reaches.
Decide whether the transformer is the first limit on this street.

lead.text: A transformer is not the only limit. The AER names a second, called **voltage rise**, in which a network limits exports indirectly, by not managing voltages on its network well enough, so that the inverter trips itself off or down. The AER does not explain why exports raise the voltage, so the explanation here is this lesson's own and rests on Ohm's law. A feeder has resistance, and when current flows along it from the transformer to the houses, the voltage falls along the way by the current times the resistance, so that in the evening the houses at the far end of a long street see the lowest voltage.

afterFigure.text: At midday the current runs the other way. Houses that export push current back along the feeder towards the transformer, and the drop of current times resistance now lifts the voltage above its value at the transformer, with the largest lift at the far end, where the exports of every house along the street have to pass. If the voltage at an inverter rises past what the inverter is set to accept, it reduces its output or disconnects, which is the behaviour the AER describes as tripping itself off or down. The figure shows the shape of the voltage on an invented street, with the numbers left off because only the shape matters.

diagram.alt: An invented street with a transformer, a feeder and six houses, with the voltage along the feeder drawn beneath it. In the evening power flows to the houses and the voltage falls along the street. At midday with solar on half the houses the voltage rises but stays under an upper limit. With solar on every house it rises past the limit at the far end, where inverters switch down.
diagram.caption: An invented street with no real voltages, drawn to show the shape. Use the buttons to change which houses export.

reveal.text: The transformer was not the problem. Nothing about it changes from one end of the street to the other, and the voltage does.

lead.text: The AER lists three forms of export curtailment. A **static limit** sets a fixed maximum on the electricity that a solar system can export. Voltage rise, described above, limits exports indirectly. A **flexible export limit** is a connection under which the network can cut solar exports at the moments it must, to protect supply in the area, and which otherwise lets customers export more than the static limit. The AER's example is Endeavour Energy in New South Wales, which announced a flexible exports service that lets eligible customers increase the amount they can export from 5 kW up to 10 kW for 95 percent of the year, and which will limit exports only if grid stability is at risk.

A fixed limit has to be low enough for the worst case on the street, which is a midday with every house exporting, so it also holds back exports in the many hours when the street has room. A flexible limit watches the network and acts only when it must. The AER's note does not say how low a flexible limit goes on the days it applies, so the comparison here is about when each limit applies, and it says nothing about how much a customer exports over a year.

Rooftop solar is not traded through the NEM unless it is offered as a demand response service, but it still lowers the demand that the market's generators have to meet. The AER reports that between 2019 and 2024 the NEM saw a noticeable decline in demand in the middle of the day, driven by the growth in rooftop solar, while grid demand rose in the early morning and the early evening, when solar generation is minimal or nonexistent. It adds that on a sunny day rooftop solar can now meet more than half of the underlying demand across the NEM at midday, and that in the first quarter of 2025 it made up 14.7 percent of everything the NEM generated, ahead of utility-scale solar at 9.3 percent. The midday that strains a street is also the time when the market needs least from its generators, and the next lesson follows what that means for storage.

Energy Safe Victoria's solar pages report house fires every year that start in rooftop systems never serviced, older ones above all. They say servicing has to be done by a licensed A grade electrician working for a Registered Electrical Contractor, and that a service is needed at least once every two years. A service is more than cleaning the panels: the electrician checks for deteriorated or corroded parts, defective switches and damaged wiring, confirms that fittings and cables are secure, reviews the inverter display for recorded faults, and checks that access to the isolator switches is clear and that the emergency shutdown instructions are displayed.

ESV adds that some firms claiming to service solar panels only clean them, and it asks owners to keep the space around inverters and batteries clear, naming wood piles and paint as things not to store against them. The lesson describes what a service covers, and the work itself belongs to the licensed electrician.

Two invented streets each have 16 houses with 5 kW of solar and a 200 kVA transformer, so midday exports at unity power factor reach 80 kVA on each. Street P is short, with every house close to the transformer. Street Q has a much longer and thinner feeder, so its resistance is several times larger.

reveal.text: Both streets have the same exports and the same room in the transformer, so any difference between them has to come from the feeder.

lessons.orientation: Say what an inverter gives and does not give a grid, and judge what limits rooftop solar on a given street.
lessons.nextAction: Tell power from energy when sizing a battery, and match a variability problem to storage, curtailment, a transmission upgrade or demand shifting.

blocks.text: According to the Australian Energy Regulator's State of the energy market 2025 report, no country has invested more per person in rooftop solar than Australia. Each system is a set of panels on a roof and an inverter, and each is joined to the street wiring that carries power from the street transformer to the houses, a network in which power flowed in one direction before rooftop solar arrived.
On a single roof the system is small, so the first thing to settle is how large the total has become. Make a guess before the evidence.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what an inverter gives and does not give a grid, and judge which limit applies to rooftop solar on a given street.
intro.whyItMatters: Millions of inverters now sit on the grid, and their behaviour decides how much solar a street can carry and what a blackout does to it.

recap.keyIdea: A grid-tie inverter follows the grid and adds no inertia, and the amount of rooftop solar a street can carry is limited by its transformer rating, by voltage rise along the feeder and by the export limits that the network sets.

blocks.text: A grid-tie inverter converts direct current to alternating current matched to the grid's voltage, frequency and phase, disconnects quickly when the grid goes down, and has no rotating mass, so any inertia has to be designed in. On a street the midday exports run back along the feeder, so the sum of the exports is compared with the transformer's kVA rating and the voltage along the feeder is watched.

Voltage rises towards the far end because the drop of current times resistance acts the opposite way at midday, and inverters there reduce their output or trip. Networks limit exports with a static limit or a flexible limit, and ESV says a solar system is serviced by a licensed A grade electrician.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at what a surplus at midday and a peak in the evening ask of storage, and at how a battery's power rating differs from its energy rating.

lessons.title: Storage, variability and curtailment

lead.text: A power rating is a rate. Megawatts say how much energy a battery can deliver each second, and megawatt-hours say how much it can deliver in all. Dividing the energy by the power gives the **duration**, the time the battery can run at full power before it is empty. Wikipedia notes that grid batteries are usually built to run at full power for 1 to 4 hours, and Hornsdale follows that pattern: its original 2017 installation was 100 MW and 129 MWh, and the 2020 expansion took it to 150 MW and 194 MWh. Two batteries with the same power rating can hold very different amounts of energy, so neither rating can stand in for the other, and an invented battery of 100 MW that held only 10 MWh would be empty in six minutes.

The same distinction holds across whole technologies. Wikipedia reports that by 2025 global grid battery capacity was 267 GW of power and 610 GWh of energy, against 200 GW and 9,000 GWh for pumped storage hydroelectricity, the other major form of grid storage. Batteries had overtaken pumped hydro in power, and they remained far smaller in energy.

steps.headline: The Victorian Big Battery began operations in December 2021 at 300 MW and 450 MWh. For how long can it deliver its full power?

workedSteps.text: The duration is the energy divided by the power.
Divide the energy by the power.
That is an hour and a half, which lies inside the 1 to 4 hours that grid batteries are generally designed for.

lead.text: Hornsdale's first 129 MWh of storage was divided by contract into several parts, and two of them show how differently a battery can be used. 70 MW for 10 minutes was contracted to the government for grid stability, so that blackouts from load shedding are avoided while other generators start up after a sudden fall in wind or another network problem. Neoen uses the other part, 30 MW for 3 hours or 90 MWh, to trade: it charges the battery when prices are low and sells the energy when demand is high. The first job asks for a lot of power for a short time, and the second asks for less than half as much power for far longer, so the second job uses much more of the battery's energy.

Batteries suit the first job because they have no moving parts and can respond or start in as little as 10 ms, and Wikipedia calls battery storage the quickest dispatchable source of power on electric grids. It also reports that this stability service cut AEMO's cost of grid services by 90 percent in the first four months. The second job depends on how much energy the battery holds, and speed matters less to it.

steps.headline: How much energy does Hornsdale's stability job of 70 MW for 10 minutes use?

workedSteps.text: Energy is power multiplied by time, with the time in hours. The trading job shows the pattern.
Work out the energy of the stability job, taking care over the units of time.
Set the two jobs side by side. The job with more than twice the power uses far less energy, because it lasts only minutes.

lead.text: Variable generation turns the problem into one about the clock. Wikipedia defines the **duck curve** as a graph of the electricity demand remaining after the electricity supplied by variable renewable sources, mainly solar, is subtracted, over the course of a day. With a lot of solar the remaining demand sinks at midday and then climbs steeply as the sun sets, and the other generators have to supply the climb. The name comes from the shape of the graph, and the California system operator coined it in 2012. The AER reports a version in Australia: between 2019 and 2024 demand on the grid fell around the middle of the day, driven by rooftop solar, while demand in the early morning and early evening rose.

afterFigure.text: The figure draws an invented day, with two batteries of the same power beneath it. A battery's power sets how much of the climb it can take at once, and its energy sets how long it can keep that up, so the 1-hour battery is empty by 6 pm and the 4-hour battery lasts until 9 pm. Wikipedia notes that storing surplus solar by day and using it in the evening can narrow the gap in price between cheap midday energy and expensive evening energy.

diagram.alt: An invented, simplified day of demand minus solar. It is highest at the early morning, falls to a deep belly at midday and climbs steeply from mid-afternoon to an evening peak. Beneath it a battery of the same power is drawn as a band: a 1-hour battery covers an hour of the evening climb and is empty by 6 pm, and a 4-hour battery covers four hours and is empty by 9 pm.
diagram.caption: An invented day, drawn to show the shape. Both batteries have the same power, and the width of the band is how long each lasts. Use the buttons to compare them.

lead.text: Wikipedia names three key ways to replace the flexibility that fossil fuels gave the grid. **Storage** keeps energy from one hour for use in another. **Demand response** changes when or how much consumers use electricity, for example through cheaper night tariffs, and industry and commercial customers can change their demand to meet supply. **Interconnection** links regions, so that when there is little wind in one place another may have a surplus, although expanding transmission lines usually takes a long time.

Storage comes in several forms. Pumped storage hydroelectricity was the largest form of grid storage in 2023, with 181 GW installed worldwide, and Wikipedia gives it an efficiency of 75 to 85 percent, which means that for every 100 MWh used to fill it, 75 to 85 MWh come back. Storage therefore moves energy in time and does not create any, and a store returns less than it takes in.

Curtailment is the deliberate cutting of a generator's output, also called dispatch down, to keep the grid stable, as when balancing supply and demand. Load shedding is a different action, because it cuts demand to keep the grid stable. Curtailment is a long-standing technique, but this century it has become an economic problem for the owners of wind and solar plants, because those plants have no fuel to save and very low marginal costs, so curtailment weighs on their projects much more than on conventional units. Australia curtailed 4.5 TWh of solar and wind in 2024.

Curtailment wastes energy that could have been useful, but Wikipedia points out that putting every bit of available energy to use can call for expensive measures, such as new power lines or storage, that cost more than letting the surplus go. It lists four ways to reduce or avoid curtailment: transmission upgrades, demand response, more energy storage and better forecasting. Its Texas example is the clearest evidence in this course's sources: in 2013 ERCOT built a new transmission line linking West Texas, home of the Competitive Renewable Energy Zone, with the central cities, and curtailment fell from 8 to 16 percent to near zero. The sources give no comparison of what the fixes cost, so the judgement here is about which fix addresses the constraint that limits the output.

reveal.text: Power and energy are separate needs, and a battery that meets one of them can still fail the other.

lessons.orientation: Match a variability problem to storage, curtailment, a transmission upgrade or demand shifting, and tell power from energy when sizing a battery.
lessons.nextAction: You can now read a battery's power and energy ratings, size one for a job, and match a variability problem to storage, a new line, demand shifting or curtailment.

blocks.text: The Hornsdale Power Reserve in South Australia is described as a 150 MW (194 MWh) battery, and the two figures answer different questions. The megawatts say how fast the battery can deliver energy, and the megawatt-hours say how much it holds, so only the two together say how long it can keep going.
A battery chosen on one of the two figures alone can be the wrong size for its job, and Hornsdale's figures are the place to see why. The first question asks for a guess at how long it can run.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell power from energy when sizing a battery, and match a variability problem to storage, curtailment, a transmission upgrade or demand shifting.
intro.whyItMatters: The ratings on a battery, and the choice between storage, a new line and curtailment, decide what a grid can do with a midday surplus.

recap.keyIdea: A battery's MW rating is how fast it can deliver and its MWh rating is how much it holds, so its duration is the energy divided by the power, and a variability problem is matched to the fix that addresses what limits the output.

blocks.text: Power and energy answer different questions, which is why Hornsdale's two jobs, 70 MW for 10 minutes and 30 MW for 3 hours, use very different amounts of energy even though the first has more than twice the power. A store also returns less than it takes in, as the 75 to 85 percent efficiency of pumped hydro shows.

Variability can be met by storage, demand response, interconnection or curtailment, and the choice depends on what limits the output. A full line is a transmission problem, a midday surplus with an evening peak calls for storage, and some curtailment is cheaper than the fix. The sources give no costs for these options, so the lesson judges which one fits the problem and leaves price aside.

questions.prompt: A heater gives the same heat on a 230 V AC supply as on a 230 V DC supply. The AC voltage passes through zero twice in every cycle. What does that say about the highest voltage the AC supply reaches?
hints: Heating follows how large the voltage is at each instant.
A wave that spends time near zero delivers little heat then, so it must deliver more at other times.

acceptedIdeas: It is above 230 V, to make up for the time spent near zero
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is above 230 V, to make up for the time spent near zero

choices.label: It is exactly 230 V, because the two supplies heat equally
It is above 230 V, to make up for the time spent near zero
It is below 230 V, because the voltage averages to zero over a cycle

questions.onCorrect: The wave spends time below 230 V, so it has to rise above 230 V to match the steady supply. The next screens find how far above.

misconceptions.feedback: A wave that touched the steady supply's value only at its highest point would spend the rest of the cycle below it and would heat less. To match the steady supply, the highest voltage has to be larger.

The average of the voltage over a cycle is zero, but heating follows the square of the voltage, and a square is positive in both halves of the cycle. A wave whose highest value was below the steady supply's voltage would heat less than it.

questions.prompt: An oscilloscope shows a sine wave with a peak of 340 V and a period of 20 ms. What is its RMS value, in volts?
hints: The RMS value of a sine wave is a fixed fraction of its peak.
The fraction is $1/\sqrt{2}$, about 0.707.
The period is not needed for the RMS value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: RMS = peak × 0.707 = 340 × 0.707 = 240 V, a supply close to the Australian nominal value.

questions.onCorrect: Multiplying the peak by 0.707 gives 240 V, a little above the nominal Australian supply of 230 V.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the peak by 1.414, which converts the other way, from RMS up to peak. The RMS value must be smaller than the peak.
That halves the peak. The factor for a sine wave is $1/\sqrt{2}$, about 0.707, because the wave is squared before it is averaged.
That uses 0.637, the average over a half cycle. Heating follows the square of the voltage, so the factor is 0.707.

questions.prompt: A heater is rated 230 V RMS. Why does its rating use the RMS value and not the average of the voltage?
hints: Ask what a rating has to tell you about a heater.
A heater cares about the heat it gets, which depends on the square of the voltage.

acceptedIdeas: The RMS value gives the heating that a DC supply of that voltage would give
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The RMS value gives the heating that a DC supply of that voltage would give

choices.label: The RMS value gives the heating that a DC supply of that voltage would give
The RMS value is the voltage level that the wave spends the most time at
The average voltage is larger than the RMS value, so it would overrate the heater
The RMS value is half of the peak, so it is easy to find from a trace

questions.onCorrect: The rating says what steady voltage would heat the element equally, so it can be compared with a DC supply directly.

misconceptions.feedback: RMS is defined by heating, and nothing in its definition says how often the voltage takes that value. It describes what the supply does to a heater.
Over a whole cycle the average is zero, and over one half cycle it is 0.637 of the peak, which is smaller than the 0.707 that gives RMS. An average understates the heating.
Half of the peak would be 0.5 of it. The RMS value of a sine wave is 0.707 of the peak, which comes from squaring, averaging and taking the root.

questions.prompt: A voltmeter at a point of supply on a nominal 230 V system reads 212 V. Which statement about that reading is right?
hints: Work out the lowest voltage each rule allows, as a percentage below 230 V.
A fall of 6 percent and a fall of 10 percent give different lower limits.

acceptedIdeas: It is inside the 2022 range and outside the range of 2000
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is inside the 2022 range and outside the range of 2000

choices.label: It is outside both the 2000 range and the 2022 range
It is inside both the 2000 range and the 2022 range
It is inside the 2022 range and outside the range of 2000
It cannot be judged, because the meter might be showing a peak

extracts.text: In 2000, Australia converted to 230 V as the nominal standard with a tolerance of +10%/−6%, this superseding the old 240 V standard, AS 2926-1987. The tolerance was increased in 2022 to ± 10% with the release of AS IEC 60038:2022. The utilization voltage available at an appliance may be below this range, due to voltage drops within the customer installation.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: The 2000 rule stops at 216.2 V and the 2022 rule at 207 V, so 212 V falls in between.

misconceptions.feedback: The older lower limit, 216.2 V, does exclude 212 V, but the 2022 lower limit is 207 V and 212 V clears it.
The older tolerance allowed a fall of only 6 percent, which puts its lower limit at 216.2 V. A reading of 212 V is below that.

Supply voltages are quoted as RMS values, so a reading is compared with the limits directly. A meter that showed a peak would read 325 V on a 230 V supply, and 212 V as a peak would mean about 150 V RMS, far below either range.

questions.prompt: Why is the 3 ms delay divided by the 20 ms period before it is converted to degrees?
hints: The delay and the period are both times, so the ratio has no unit.
A ratio of 1 would mean a delay of a whole cycle.

acceptedIdeas: The ratio is the fraction of a cycle, and a cycle is 360 degrees
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ratio is the fraction of a cycle, and a cycle is 360 degrees

choices.label: The period is the angle that the wave turns through in each millisecond
Dividing by the period turns the frequency into hertz
The ratio is the fraction of a cycle, and a cycle is 360 degrees

questions.onCorrect: Because the ratio is a fraction of a cycle, multiplying by 360 degrees gives the angle.

misconceptions.feedback: The period is a time. The wave turns through 360 degrees in one period, which makes the rate 18 degrees every millisecond.
Hertz are cycles per second, and the frequency is found by dividing 1 by the period. The ratio of the two times has no unit and says what fraction of a cycle the delay is.

questions.prompt: A delay of 0.2 of a cycle is how many degrees?
hints: A full cycle is 360 degrees.
The delay is a fraction of a whole cycle.
Take that fraction of the full cycle.
questions.onCorrect: A fifth of a cycle is a fifth of 360 degrees.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction of a cycle. Multiply it by 360 to turn it into degrees.
That is the delay in milliseconds. The angle is the fraction of a cycle multiplied by 360.

questions.prompt: The current crosses zero 4 ms before the voltage does. Which statement describes the two waves?
hints: Decide which wave reaches zero first.
The wave that arrives first is ahead of the other.

acceptedIdeas: The current leads the voltage by 72 degrees
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The current leads the voltage by 72 degrees

choices.label: The current leads the voltage by 72 degrees
The current lags the voltage by 72 degrees
The current leads the voltage by 4 degrees

questions.onCorrect: The current reaches each zero 4 ms early, which is 72 degrees ahead.

misconceptions.feedback: The wave that crosses zero first is the one that leads. Here that is the current, so it is ahead of the voltage.
The 4 is a time in milliseconds. At 50 Hz each millisecond is 18 degrees, so the delay has to be converted.

questions.prompt: At 50 Hz, a load current crosses zero 5 ms after the voltage does. By how many degrees does the current lag the voltage?
hints: Find the period at 50 Hz.
Write 5 ms as a fraction of that period.
Take that fraction of 360 degrees.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The period is 20 ms and 5/20 = 0.25 of a cycle, which is 0.25 × 360 = 90 degrees.

questions.onCorrect: A delay of a quarter of a cycle is a lag of 90 degrees, the largest that an ideal coil or capacitor produces.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction of a cycle. Multiply it by 360 to get degrees.
That is the delay in milliseconds. At 50 Hz each millisecond is 18 degrees, so the delay still has to be converted.
That multiplies the delay by 360 directly. The delay first has to be divided by the 20 ms period.

questions.prompt: On a 50 Hz supply a motor's current lags its voltage by 27 degrees. How long after the voltage crosses zero does the current cross zero, in milliseconds?
hints: Work out what fraction of a cycle 27 degrees is.
The whole cycle takes 20 ms at 50 Hz.
Take that fraction of the 20 ms period.
questions.onCorrect: Each degree is 20/360 ms, about 0.056 ms, so 27 degrees is 1.5 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the angle. To turn it into a time, take the fraction 27/360 of the 20 ms period.
That multiplies 27 by 18, which converts milliseconds into degrees. Here the conversion goes the other way.

questions.prompt: The 2022 tolerance lets a 230 V supply reach 253 V RMS. What is the peak voltage of a sine wave at that limit, in volts?
hints: The peak of a sine wave is larger than its RMS value.
The factor between them for a sine wave is the square root of 2.
Multiply the RMS value by 1.414.
questions.onCorrect: At the upper limit the wave peaks at about 358 V, 33 V above the 325 V peak of the nominal supply.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 0.707, which goes from peak to RMS. Here the RMS value is given and the peak is wanted.
That doubles the RMS value. The factor from RMS to peak for a sine wave is 1.414.

questions.prompt: A student measures the full height of the trace in the extract, from its lowest point to its highest. Which value does that give?
hints: The trace runs from -170 V to 170 V.
The distance between those two levels is the whole height.

acceptedIdeas: The peak-to-peak value, 340 V, which is the same wave as 120 V RMS
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The peak-to-peak value, 340 V, which is the same wave as 120 V RMS

choices.label: The RMS value, 340 V, because the trace covers both polarities
The peak-to-peak value, 340 V, which is the same wave as 120 V RMS
The peak value, 340 V, because the trace reaches both extremes
The average value, 340 V, because the two halves are added

extracts.text: Seen with an oscilloscope, the domestic power supply in North America would look like a sine wave, oscillating between −170 volts and 170 volts, giving an effective voltage of 120 volts RMS.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: The full height is 2 × 170 = 340 V peak-to-peak, and 170 × 0.707 gives the 120 V RMS value in the extract.

misconceptions.feedback: The extract itself gives the RMS value of this supply, and it is far smaller. The full height of the trace is twice the peak.
The peak is measured from zero to the highest point, which is half of the full height.
The average over a whole cycle of a sine wave is zero, since the halves cancel. The full height of the trace is a different quantity, the peak-to-peak value.

questions.prompt: At 50 Hz a motor's current crosses zero 2 ms after its voltage does. A technician says the load must be faulty because the two waves do not line up. What is the right reply?
hints: Convert the 2 ms delay to an angle first.
Think about which kinds of load make the current lag the voltage.

acceptedIdeas: The current lags by 36 degrees, which any load built from coils produces
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The current lags by 36 degrees, which any load built from coils produces

choices.label: The current lags by 36 degrees, so that part of the energy is wasted as heat
The current leads by 36 degrees, which only a faulty load produces
The waves cannot be out of step, because both are at 50 Hz
The current lags by 36 degrees, which any load built from coils produces

questions.onCorrect: A delay of 2 ms is 2/20 of a cycle, 36 degrees, and a lag of this kind is normal for a load with coils.

misconceptions.feedback: The angle describes timing. A coil stores energy in its magnetic field and returns it later in the cycle, and that exchange is what shifts the current.
The current crosses zero second, so it follows the voltage and lags. A current that leads belongs to a capacitive load, and that is no fault either.
Two waves can share a frequency and still cross zero at different times. The phase difference measures that gap.

questions.prompt: At one instant the voltage across a coil is +100 V and the current through it is −2 A. What is happening to energy at that instant?
hints: Multiply the voltage by the current at that instant, keeping the sign.
A positive power means that energy flows into the load. What would a negative power mean?

acceptedIdeas: The coil is returning energy to the supply at 200 W
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The coil is returning energy to the supply at 200 W

choices.label: The coil is taking energy from the supply at 200 W
The coil is returning energy to the supply at 200 W
No energy moves, because a negative current delivers none

questions.onCorrect: The product is negative, so energy is flowing back out of the coil to the supply, as it does for half of every cycle in an ideal coil.

misconceptions.feedback: The product of voltage and current has a negative sign here, because the current is negative while the voltage is positive. A positive product means that energy flows into the load, and a negative one means that it flows back out.
A negative current still flows. It runs against the voltage, and the product of the two is a negative power, which is energy returning to the source.

questions.prompt: A pump motor on a 230 V supply draws 12 A, and its current lags the voltage so that cos φ = 0.75. What real power does it take, in watts?
hints: Real power is the product of voltage, current and the cosine of the angle.
Voltage times current is the apparent power, and the cosine scales it down.
Multiply 230, 12 and 0.75.
questions.onCorrect: The apparent power is 2,760 VA, and the cosine of 0.75 leaves 2,070 W of real power.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the apparent power, voltage times current. The real power is smaller by the factor cos φ.
That divides by cos φ where the formula multiplies by it, so the result is larger than the apparent power.

questions.prompt: A load draws 1.5 kVA of apparent power and takes 1.2 kW of real power. How much reactive power does it draw, in var?
hints: Real, reactive and apparent power are the sides of a right triangle.
S is the longest side, so $Q^2 = S^2 - P^2$.
Work in kilowatts and kilovolt-amperes, then convert the result to var.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Q = √(S² − P²) = √(1.5² − 1.2²) = √0.81 = 0.9 kvar, which is 900 var.

questions.onCorrect: The sides of the triangle are 1.2, 0.9 and 1.5, so Q is 0.9 kvar.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the two figures as plain numbers. P, Q and S are the sides of a right triangle, so the square of S is the sum of the squares of P and Q.
That is the right size in kvar. The question asks for var, which are a thousand times smaller.
That adds P and S. Q is a side of the triangle, found from the other two sides by Pythagoras.

questions.prompt: Why is S found from the square root of $P^2 + Q^2$ and not from the plain sum $P + Q$?
hints: Look at how the triangle in the figure is drawn.
In a right triangle the slope is shorter than the sum of the other two sides.

acceptedIdeas: P and Q are at right angles on the triangle, so S is its longest side
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: P and Q are at right angles on the triangle, so S is its longest side

choices.label: P and Q are both energy, so they add like any two energies do
A plain sum would give S in watts when it must be in volt-amperes
P and Q are at right angles on the triangle, so S is its longest side

questions.onCorrect: The two powers meet at a right angle, so Pythagoras gives the apparent power.

misconceptions.feedback: Real power is energy that the load keeps and reactive power is energy that moves back and forth, so they are different in kind and sit at right angles in the triangle.
A unit is only a label that follows from the quantity. The sum would be wrong in size as well, because the sides of a right triangle do not add up to its slope.

questions.prompt: A load draws 10 A from a 230 V supply with cos φ = 0.8, so S = 2,300 VA. What is its real power, in watts?
hints: Real power is the part of the apparent power along the base of the triangle.
P = S cos φ.
Multiply 2,300 by the cosine.
questions.onCorrect: The base of the triangle is 0.8 of the apparent power.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the upright side of the triangle, which is the reactive power. The real power uses the cosine.
That is the apparent power. The real power is smaller by the factor cos φ.

questions.prompt: For the same load, with S = 2,300 VA and cos φ = 0.8, what is the reactive power, in var?
hints: Reactive power is the part of S along the upright side: Q = S sin φ.
Find sin φ from the cosine, since $\sin^2\varphi + \cos^2\varphi = 1$.
The sine is 0.6, because $0.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 1$.
questions.onCorrect: A cosine of 0.8 goes with a sine of 0.6, so the upright side is 0.6 of the apparent power.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the real power, found with the cosine. The reactive power uses the sine.
That multiplies 2,300 by 1 minus 0.8, which is not the sine. The sine follows from $\sin^2\varphi + \cos^2\varphi = 1$.

questions.prompt: A load on a 230 V single-phase supply has a rating plate of 5 kW and 7 kVA (an invented plate). Which figure decides the current that its cable must carry?
hints: The cable heats with the current that flows through it.
Apparent power is voltage times current, so it carries the whole current.

acceptedIdeas: The 7 kVA, because the cable carries the whole current
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 7 kVA, because the cable carries the whole current

choices.label: The 7 kVA, because the cable carries the whole current
The 5 kW, because that is the power the load uses
The mean of the two, because the load uses a mixture of both
Neither, because the current depends only on the voltage

questions.onCorrect: The current follows from the apparent power divided by the voltage.

misconceptions.feedback: Real power leaves out the extra current that carries the reactive power, and that current heats the cable like any other.
The two ratings are different kinds of quantity, and an average of them describes nothing about the current.
At a fixed voltage the current is set by the load, and the apparent power is the voltage multiplied by that current.

questions.prompt: A workshop draws 90 kW at a power factor of 0.70 from a supply transformer rated 100 kVA. Can the transformer supply it?
hints: A transformer is limited by the current it carries, so compare its rating with the load's apparent power.
The power factor is $P/S$, so $S = P/\text{power factor}$.

acceptedIdeas: No, because the load needs about 129 kVA
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because the load needs about 129 kVA

choices.label: Yes, because 90 kW is less than 100 kVA
Yes, because reactive power does not load a transformer
No, because the load needs 90 kW plus 92 kvar, which is 182 kVA
No, because the load needs about 129 kVA

questions.onCorrect: The apparent power is 90 ÷ 0.70 = 128.6 kVA, which is 29% over the 100 kVA rating.

misconceptions.feedback: This compares watts with volt-amperes. The rating limits the apparent power, which is larger than the real power whenever the power factor is below 1.
The current that carries the reactive power flows through the windings and heats them, so it counts towards the rating.
This adds P and Q as plain numbers. They meet at a right angle, so they combine as the sides of a right triangle.

questions.prompt: A bakery's oven fans and motors together take 48 kW of real power and 36 kvar of reactive power (invented figures). What apparent power must its supply carry, in kVA?
hints: The two powers are at right angles, so they do not add as plain numbers.
Square both, add them, and take the root.
Check whether 48 and 36 are multiples of a familiar right triangle.
questions.onCorrect: The sides 48 and 36 are twelve times 4 and 3, so the slope is twelve times 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two figures. Real and reactive power are at right angles, so S is the square root of the sum of their squares.
That subtracts the two figures. S is the slope of the triangle and is longer than either side.

questions.prompt: Sort each item by whether the real power or the apparent power of the load sets it.
hints: Ask whether the item depends on the energy a load keeps or on the current that flows.
A cable, a generator and a transformer are all limited by current.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Real power sets the heat of a heating element, the average of voltage times current and the net energy over an hour. Apparent power sets the cable current, the generator rating and the heat in a transformer's windings.

items.label: The heat given out by a heating element
items.explanation: An element is resistive, so its current is in phase with the voltage and all of its power is real power.

items.label: The current that a supply cable must carry
items.explanation: A cable heats with the whole current, whatever part of it does work, and apparent power is voltage times that current.

items.label: The average of voltage times current over one cycle
items.explanation: That average is the definition of real power.

items.label: The rating that a generator needs
items.explanation: A generator has to supply the whole current, including the part that does no work.

items.label: The net energy a load takes from the supply in an hour
items.explanation: Reactive energy goes out and comes back each cycle, so only the real power adds to the net energy.

items.label: The heat in a transformer's windings
items.explanation: The windings heat with the current that flows through them, and apparent power measures that current.

questions.onCorrect: Items that depend on the whole current follow the apparent power, and items that depend on the energy a load keeps follow the real power.

questions.prompt: A supply cable feeds a load that draws 4.6 kVA at 230 V. What current does the cable carry, in amperes?
hints: Apparent power is voltage multiplied by current.
Convert the kilovolt-amperes to volt-amperes first.
Divide the apparent power by the voltage.
questions.onCorrect: The apparent power divided by the voltage is the whole current, 20 A.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 4.6 by 230 without converting the kilovolt-amperes to volt-amperes.
That multiplies the apparent power by the voltage. The current is the apparent power divided by the voltage.

questions.prompt: A load takes 3 kW of real power at a power factor of 0.5. What apparent power must the supply provide, in kVA?
hints: The power factor is the real power divided by the apparent power.
Rearrange that to find the apparent power.
A power factor of 0.5 means the real power is half of the apparent power.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: S = P ÷ power factor = 3 ÷ 0.5 = 6 kVA.

questions.onCorrect: A power factor of 0.5 means that the supply provides twice as many kilovolt-amperes as the load keeps in kilowatts.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the real power by the power factor. The apparent power is larger than the real power, so it is found by dividing.
That is the real power. At a power factor below 1 the apparent power is larger.

questions.prompt: A motor's rating plate gives 4.2 kW and 5.6 kVA (an invented plate). What is its power factor?
hints: The power factor compares the real power with the apparent power.
Put the real power on top.
The ratio cannot be more than 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Power factor = P ÷ S = 4.2 ÷ 5.6 = 0.75.

questions.onCorrect: Three quarters of the apparent power is real power, so the power factor is 0.75.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the apparent power by the real power, which is the reciprocal. The power factor cannot be more than 1.
That subtracts the two figures. The power factor is their ratio.

questions.prompt: A load takes the same real power on the same voltage at a power factor of 0.8 as at 1.0. By what percentage is its current higher at 0.8?
hints: At a fixed voltage and real power, the current is proportional to 1 divided by the power factor.
Compare 1 ÷ 0.8 with 1 ÷ 1.0.
Turn the ratio into a percentage increase.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The current ratio is 1 ÷ 0.8 = 1.25, so the current is 25% higher.

questions.onCorrect: A power factor of 0.8 needs one quarter more current than a power factor of 1 for the same real power.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes the shortfall of 0.8 from 1 as the rise. The current rises by the ratio 1 ÷ 0.8, and the ratio is not the shortfall.
That is the ratio as a percentage of the original. The increase is the part above 100%.

questions.prompt: A feeder carries 100 kW. By what factor do its losses rise if the load's power factor falls from 1.0 to 0.5 at the same voltage?
hints: First find how much the current rises when the power factor halves.
