Line loss is $I^2R$, so it follows the square of the current.
Square the change in the current to get the change in the loss.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The current doubles, because it is proportional to 1 ÷ power factor, and the loss follows the square of the current, so it rises by $2^2$ = 4.

questions.onCorrect: Halving the power factor doubles the current, and the loss in the lines goes up by the square of that.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rise in current. The loss follows the square of the current, so it rises by more.
That is the power factor itself. The loss rises as the power factor falls.
That cubes the change. The loss follows the square of the current and no more.

questions.prompt: Why does the loss rise by the square of the current ratio and not by the ratio itself?
hints: Recall the form of power in a resistor that uses the current and the resistance.
Doubling the current doubles the voltage drop along a line as well.

acceptedIdeas: Heating in a conductor is $I^2R$, so it follows the current squared
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Heating in a conductor is $I^2R$, so it follows the current squared

choices.label: Heating in a conductor is $I^2R$, so it follows the current squared
The loss is current times voltage, and the voltage also rises with the current
A lower power factor adds a second loss on top of the first

questions.onCorrect: The line's resistance stays the same, so its heating follows $I^2$.

misconceptions.feedback: The supply voltage is held fixed throughout the comparison. The loss in a line is its resistance times the square of the current that flows through it.
No second loss appears. The current is larger, and the one loss that a line has, the heating of its resistance, grows with the square of it.

questions.prompt: A site draws 100 kW at a power factor of 0.70 lagging. What reactive power does the load draw, in kvar?
hints: Use $Q = P\tan(\arccos \text{power factor})$.
The angle whose cosine is 0.70 is about 45.6 degrees.
Multiply the real power by the tangent of that angle.
questions.onCorrect: A real power of 100 kW at this angle goes with 102 kvar of reactive power.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the power factor times the real power. The reactive power uses the tangent of the angle, which is larger than 1 here.
That uses the sine of the angle with the real power as the hypotenuse. The real power is the base of the triangle, so the reactive power is $P\tan\varphi$.

questions.prompt: The load draws 102 kvar, and at a power factor of 0.95 it may draw 32.9 kvar. How many kvar of capacitors bring it to 0.95, to the nearest kvar?
hints: The capacitors supply reactive power, so they take away from what the load draws.
Subtract the reactive power that is allowed from the reactive power that is drawn.
Round the difference to the nearest kvar.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Q_C = 102.0 − 32.9 = 69.2 kvar, about 69 kvar.

questions.onCorrect: The capacitors supply the difference between what the load draws and what the target allows.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two reactive powers. The capacitor works against the load's reactive power, so the figures are subtracted.
That is the reactive power left after correction. The capacitor supplies the part that is removed.

questions.prompt: Why are the two reactive powers subtracted to size the capacitor, and not the two apparent powers?
hints: Look at which sides of the triangle the capacitor acts on.
Compare the base of the triangle before and after the capacitor.

acceptedIdeas: The real power is unchanged, so only the reactive side of the triangle moves
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The real power is unchanged, so only the reactive side of the triangle moves

choices.label: Apparent power cannot be subtracted because its unit is the volt-ampere
The real power is unchanged, so only the reactive side of the triangle moves
The capacitor takes away real power as well as reactive power

questions.onCorrect: The base of the triangle, the real power, stays fixed, and the capacitor shortens only the upright side.

misconceptions.feedback: Apparent powers can be compared and subtracted as numbers of volt-amperes. The reason they do not give the capacitor is that the capacitor acts on the reactive side alone.
A capacitor stores and returns energy and keeps none, so the real power is the same before and after.

questions.prompt: A factory's power factor is 0.70 lagging because dozens of induction motors run steadily all shift. Which correction fits?
hints: The motors are inductive, so their current lags the voltage.
Ask which device supplies reactive power rather than absorbing it.

acceptedIdeas: Capacitors connected near the motors
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Capacitors connected near the motors

choices.label: A bank of inductors connected in parallel
A thicker cable to carry the supply to the factory
Capacitors connected near the motors
Fewer motors of a larger size, doing the same work

questions.onCorrect: Capacitors supply the motors' reactive power locally, so it no longer has to be carried from the generator.

misconceptions.feedback: Inductors absorb reactive power in the way the motors do, so they add to the lagging reactive power and make the power factor worse.
A thicker cable lets the extra current flow with less heating, but the extra current is still there. It treats the loss and leaves its cause.
A motor of any size is an inductive load that draws reactive power to build its magnetic field, so the lag remains.

questions.prompt: Each of these sites has a low power factor. Sort each by the correction that suits it best.
hints: Ask first how quickly the load changes, and then whether it is a motor or an electronic supply.
A condenser is chosen for smooth adjustment, and a compensator for speed.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The workshop and the pumping station suit switched capacitors, the rapidly swinging load suits a static compensator, the computer power supply is corrected inside the equipment, and the steelworks suits a synchronous condenser.

items.label: A workshop of induction motors whose load rises and falls slowly through the day
items.explanation: A controller can switch capacitors in steps to follow a slow change in the load.

items.label: A large industrial load that swings between light and heavy several times a second
items.explanation: Power electronic compensators respond much faster than capacitors switched by contactors.

items.label: A computer power supply that distorts the current it draws
items.explanation: A load that distorts the current is corrected by active or passive circuits built into the equipment.

items.label: A steelworks that wants reactive power it can adjust smoothly, like a variable capacitor
items.explanation: An unloaded synchronous motor supplies reactive power set by its field current, and large industrial plants use them.

items.label: A pumping station whose motors start and stop in groups through the day
items.explanation: Capacitor steps can be switched in and out as groups of motors come on and go off.

questions.onCorrect: Slow, motor-like changes suit switched capacitors, fast ones a compensator, distorted electronic loads a correction built in, and adjustable supply a synchronous condenser.

questions.prompt: A plant draws 160 kW at a power factor of 0.85 lagging and wants 0.95. How many kvar of capacitors does it need, to the nearest kvar?
hints: Find the reactive power at each power factor with $Q = P\tan(\arccos \text{power factor})$.
At 0.85 the angle is 31.8 degrees, and at 0.95 it is 18.2 degrees.
Subtract the smaller reactive power from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Q at 0.85 is 160 × 0.6197 = 99.2 kvar and at 0.95 it is 160 × 0.3287 = 52.6 kvar, so the capacitors supply 99.2 − 52.6 = 46.6 kvar, about 47 kvar.

questions.onCorrect: The load's reactive power falls from 99.2 kvar to 52.6 kvar, and the 46.6 kvar difference comes from the capacitors.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reactive power of the load before correction. The capacitors supply only the part that has to be removed.
That subtracts the two power factors and multiplies by the real power. Reactive power follows the tangent of the angle, which the power factor does not give directly.

questions.prompt: A plant fits fixed capacitors sized to bring its full load to a power factor of 0.95. At night only a few motors run. What happens?
hints: Fixed capacitors have no controller.
Compare what the few running motors need with what the capacitors supply.

acceptedIdeas: The capacitors still supply all their reactive power, so the power factor may lead
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The capacitors still supply all their reactive power, so the power factor may lead

choices.label: The capacitors reduce their output with the load, so the power factor stays at 0.95
The power factor rises to 1, because the motors draw less current
Nothing changes for the supply, because the load is smaller
The capacitors still supply all their reactive power, so the power factor may lead

questions.onCorrect: Fixed capacitors supply reactive power whether or not a load is running, so a controller that switches steps is used where the load varies.

misconceptions.feedback: A fixed capacitor has no way to change its reactive power. It supplies the same amount whether or not the motors are running.
The motors' reactive demand falls, but the capacitors' supply does not, so the supply exceeds the demand and the net reactive power turns round.
The capacitors add no-load loss and a net leading reactive power of their own, which the supply has to carry whatever the real load.

questions.prompt: A feeder's loss is 9 kW when its load has a power factor of 0.9. The real power and voltage stay the same, and the power factor falls to 0.6. What is the loss now, in kW?
hints: Find the ratio of the currents at the two power factors.
The loss follows the square of the current.
Multiply the old loss by the square of that ratio.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The current ratio is 0.9 ÷ 0.6 = 1.5, so the loss is multiplied by $1.5^2$ = 2.25, which gives 9 × 2.25 = 20.25 kW.

questions.onCorrect: The current rises by half and the loss by 2.25 times, from 9 kW to 20.25 kW.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the loss by the current ratio only. The loss follows the square of the current.
That divides by the ratio. A lower power factor means more current and more loss.

questions.prompt: On a 50 Hz three-phase supply, phase B reaches its peak one third of a cycle after phase A does. How long after phase A's peak is that, in milliseconds?
hints: Find the length of one cycle at 50 Hz.
Take one third of it.
A cycle at 50 Hz lasts 1/50 of a second, which is 20 ms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One cycle takes 20 ms, and a third of 20 ms is 6.7 ms.

questions.onCorrect: A third of the 20 ms cycle is 6.7 ms, which is 120 degrees of the wave.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a whole cycle. The delay between phases is one third of it.
That is one sixth of the cycle, which is 60 degrees. The delay here is one third.
That is an angle in degrees. The question asks for a time in milliseconds.

questions.prompt: A balanced three-phase load takes equal currents of the same size from each of three line conductors. At one instant the currents in two of them are +6 A and +2 A. What is the current in the third, in amperes? Give its sign, with positive meaning the same direction as the other two.
hints: For a balanced load the three currents add up to zero at every instant.
The third current must cancel the sum of the other two.
Add the two known currents and change the sign of the result.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The three currents sum to zero, so the third is −(6 + 2) = −8 A.

questions.onCorrect: The third current is 8 A in the opposite direction, so the other two conductors act as its return path.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the sign matters: the third current flows the opposite way to the other two.
That is the mean of the two. The three currents add up to zero, so the third has to cancel both.
A current of zero in the third would leave the sum at 8 A. The three must add up to zero.

questions.prompt: A balanced three-phase supply measures 230 V from each line to the star point. What is the voltage between two lines, in volts?
hints: The voltage between two lines is the difference of two phase voltages 120 degrees apart.
In a star connection the line voltage is 1.73 times the phase voltage.
Multiply the phase voltage by 1.73.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: In a star connection the line voltage is $\sqrt{3}$ times the phase voltage: 230 × 1.732 = 398 V.

questions.onCorrect: The line voltage is 1.73 times 230 V, which the usual way of writing this supply rounds to 400 V.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the phase voltage, which would be the difference of two voltages in opposite directions. Voltages 120 degrees apart differ by a smaller amount.
That multiplies by 3. The factor is the square root of 3, about 1.73.
That divides by 1.73, which goes from line voltage down to phase voltage. Here the line voltage is wanted.

questions.prompt: Three 20 Ω resistors are connected in delta across a three-phase supply with 400 V between its lines. What current flows in each line?
hints: Find the voltage across one resistor, and then its current.
In a delta each resistor is connected between two lines.
Apply the delta relation between line current and phase current.

acceptedIdeas: 34.6 A, since the line current is 1.73 times the resistor current
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 34.6 A, since the line current is 1.73 times the resistor current

choices.label: 20 A, since the line current is the current in each resistor
34.6 A, since the line current is 1.73 times the resistor current
60 A, since the three resistor currents add to give the line current
11.5 A, since each resistor has the phase voltage across it

questions.onCorrect: Each resistor carries 400 ÷ 20 = 20 A, and the line current is 1.73 times that.

misconceptions.feedback: That makes the line current equal to the phase current, which holds in a star connection. In a delta each line splits between two resistors.
That adds the three phase currents as plain numbers. They are 120 degrees apart, and each line carries the difference of two of them.
That treats the resistors as a star, where each would see about 231 V. In a delta each resistor is connected between two lines and has the full line voltage across it.

questions.prompt: Why is the total power of a balanced three-phase load three times the power of one phase?
hints: A balanced load has the same impedance in each phase.
Each phase has the same voltage across it and the same current through it.

acceptedIdeas: The phases take equal power, so the total is three equal parts added
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The phases take equal power, so the total is three equal parts added

choices.label: The phases take equal power, so the total is three equal parts added
The three phases add their voltages, so the voltage and the power triple
The line current is three times the phase current in a balanced load

questions.onCorrect: Each phase takes $V_\varphi I_\varphi \cos\varphi$, and three equal phases give three times that.

misconceptions.feedback: The voltages do not add up that way. The line voltage is 1.73 times the phase voltage, and the power of each phase is found from its own voltage and current.
The line current equals the phase current in a star and is 1.73 times it in a delta, and neither is three times.

questions.prompt: Each phase of a delta-connected load takes 200 A. What is the current in each line, in amperes?
hints: In a delta connection the line current is larger than the phase current.
The factor is the square root of 3.
Multiply the phase current by 1.73.
questions.onCorrect: In a delta the line current is 1.73 times the phase current.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the phase current. In a delta the line current is larger by the factor 1.73.
That adds the three phase currents as plain numbers. The line current is the difference of two of them.
That divides by 1.73, which is the relation for the other direction. In a delta the line current is the larger.

questions.prompt: The load has 440 V between its lines, takes 346.4 A in each line, and has a power factor of 0.6 lagging. What real power does it take, in kW?
hints: The total power of a balanced load is 1.73 times the line voltage times the line current times the power factor.
Work in volts and amperes, then convert to kilowatts.
questions.onCorrect: The product 1.732 × 440 × 346.4 is 264 kVA, and 0.6 of that is 158.4 kW.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the apparent power in kVA, found without the power factor. The real power is smaller by the factor 0.6.
That leaves out the 1.73. The power of the three phases together carries it.

questions.prompt: A balanced three-phase motor takes 15 kW at a power factor of 0.85 from a 400 V supply. What is the current in each line, in amperes?
hints: Rearrange $P = \sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L \cos\varphi$ for the line current.
Work in watts, so 15 kW is 15,000 W.
Divide by 1.73, by the voltage and by the power factor.
questions.onCorrect: The apparent power is 15 ÷ 0.85 = 17.6 kVA, and dividing by 1.73 times 400 V gives 25.5 A in each line.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 400 and the power factor but leaves out the 1.73, as for a single-phase supply.
That divides the power by the voltage only. The 1.73 and the power factor are both needed.
That leaves out the power factor. The motor takes more current than its real power alone would suggest.

questions.prompt: Three identical heaters are connected one to each line and the neutral of a four-wire three-phase supply. What current flows in the neutral?
hints: The heaters are equal, so the currents are equal in size.
Think about the sum of three waves that are 120 degrees apart.

acceptedIdeas: Almost none, because the three currents cancel each other
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Almost none, because the three currents cancel each other

choices.label: The same as in one heater, because the neutral is shared
Three times the current of one heater, because they add
About 1.73 times the current of one heater, the line factor
Almost none, because the three currents cancel each other

questions.onCorrect: In a balanced load the neutral carries almost no current, which is why a long line can do without one.

misconceptions.feedback: The three currents are 120 degrees apart, so at every instant they add to zero. The neutral is not left with one heater's current.
That adds the three currents as plain numbers. Currents 120 degrees apart cancel one another.
The factor 1.73 relates line and phase quantities. It does not apply to the sum of three equal currents that cancel.

questions.prompt: All of a building's single-phase loads are connected to one phase of a four-wire supply, and the other two phases carry almost nothing. What follows?
hints: Think about what happens to the three currents when two of them nearly vanish.
An unbalanced load gives more loss than a balanced one.

acceptedIdeas: The neutral carries a large current and the losses rise
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The neutral carries a large current and the losses rise

choices.label: The neutral carries a large current and the losses rise
Nothing changes, because the supply is three-phase whatever the loads
The neutral carries no current, because the other phases carry none
The line voltage rises to 1.73 times its normal value

questions.onCorrect: Spreading single-phase loads across the three phases keeps the load balanced, so the neutral stays nearly free of current and the losses stay low.

misconceptions.feedback: The cancellation depends on the loads being balanced. With one phase loaded and two idle there is nothing to cancel the loaded phase's current.
The neutral is the return path for the loaded phase, and with no other currents to cancel it, it carries the same current as that phase.
Placing loads on one phase does not change the line voltage, which comes from the supply. What changes is the current in the neutral and the loss.

questions.prompt: A balanced three-phase load takes 20 A in each line from a 400 V supply, at a power factor of 0.8. What real power does it take, in kW?
hints: Use $P = \sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L \cos\varphi$ with the line values.
The 400 V is the voltage between lines, and the 20 A is the current in a line.
Multiply 1.73, 400, 20 and 0.8, then convert to kilowatts.
questions.onCorrect: The apparent power is 13.9 kVA, and 0.8 of it is 11.1 kW.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the factor 1.73, as for a single-phase load.
That multiplies by 3 where the line quantities need the square root of 3.
That is the apparent power, without the power factor.

questions.prompt: Three 30 Ω resistors are connected in star across a three-phase supply with 400 V between its lines. What current flows in each line?
hints: Find the voltage across one resistor first.
In a star each resistor is connected between a line and the star point.

acceptedIdeas: 7.7 A, since each resistor has about 231 V across it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 7.7 A, since each resistor has about 231 V across it

choices.label: 13.3 A, since each resistor has the full 400 V across it
23.1 A, since the line current is 1.73 times the resistor current
7.7 A, since each resistor has about 231 V across it
4.4 A, since the current is shared among the three resistors

questions.onCorrect: Each resistor has 400 ÷ 1.73 = 231 V across it, so the current is 231 ÷ 30 = 7.7 A, and the line carries the same.

misconceptions.feedback: In a star each resistor is connected between a line and the star point, so it sees the phase voltage, which is the line voltage divided by 1.73.
That is the relation for a delta. In a star the line carries the same current as the resistor.
The resistors sit in three separate legs, and the current in a line is the current in one leg. Nothing is shared.

questions.prompt: Sort each statement by whether it holds for a balanced star load, a balanced delta load, or both.
hints: In a star the loads share a point; in a delta they form a loop.
Ask which of the voltage and the current changes by the factor 1.73 in each connection.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Star only: the line voltage is 1.73 times the load voltage and the line current equals the load current. Delta only: the load voltage equals the line voltage and the line current is 1.73 times the load current. Both: the power formula and the zero sum of the line currents.

items.label: The line voltage is 1.73 times the voltage across one load
items.explanation: Each load sits between a line and the star point, so the voltage between lines is the larger.

items.label: The line current is 1.73 times the current in one load
items.explanation: Each line splits into two loads, and its current is the difference of two phase currents.

items.label: The total power is 1.73 times the line voltage times the line current times the power factor
items.explanation: Three equal phases give this total for either connection.

items.label: The line current is the same as the current in one load
items.explanation: The line conductor runs straight to one load, so it carries that load's current.

items.label: The voltage across each load is the same as the voltage between lines
items.explanation: Each load is connected directly between two lines.

items.label: The three line currents add up to zero at every instant
items.explanation: A balanced load has currents of equal size 120 degrees apart, whichever way it is connected.

questions.onCorrect: The factor 1.73 falls on the voltage in a star and on the current in a delta, and the total power has the same form in both.

questions.prompt: A distribution transformer is 98.5 percent efficient, which means that its output power is 98.5 percent of its input power. It takes in 200 kW. How much power does it lose as heat, in kW?
hints: The power that does not come out as output is lost.
Find what percentage of the input is lost.
Take that percentage of 200 kW.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The loss is 100 − 98.5 = 1.5 percent of the input, and 1.5 percent of 200 kW is 3 kW.

questions.onCorrect: Only 1.5 percent of the input is lost, and in a transformer taking 200 kW that is 3 kW of heat.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the output power. The question asks for the power that is lost.
That is the percentage lost. Take that percentage of the 200 kW that goes in.

questions.prompt: The load on a transformer falls until the current in its windings is one third of what it was. The winding resistance is unchanged. The copper loss falls to what fraction of its old value?
hints: Copper loss is $I^2R$, and $R$ does not change.
Square the factor by which the current has changed.
A third squared is one over a number you can find.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The loss follows the square of the current, so it falls to $(1/3)^2$ = 1/9 of its old value, which is 0.111.

questions.onCorrect: A third of the current gives a ninth of the copper loss, since the loss follows $I^2$.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction of the current. The loss follows its square.
That takes away a third of the loss. The loss follows the square of the current, so it falls by much more.
That cubes the fraction. The loss follows the square of the current.

questions.prompt: A transformer's copper loss is 6.0 kW at full load. What is its copper loss at half load, in kW?
hints: Half the load means half the current.
The copper loss follows the square of the current.
Multiply 6.0 kW by the square of one half.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The current is half, so the loss is $(1/2)^2$ = 1/4 of 6.0 kW, which is 1.5 kW.

questions.onCorrect: Half the current gives a quarter of the copper loss.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves the loss. It follows the square of the current, so it falls by more than half.
That is the core loss, which does not change with load.

questions.prompt: At half load the unit delivers 200 kW, with a copper loss of 1.5 kW and a core loss of 1.2 kW. What is its efficiency, in percent?
hints: The input power is the output plus both losses.
Efficiency is the output divided by the input.
Write the answer as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The input is 200 + 1.5 + 1.2 = 202.7 kW, so the efficiency is 200 ÷ 202.7 = 0.9867, or 98.7%.

questions.onCorrect: The two losses together are 2.7 kW of an input of 202.7 kW, so 98.7 percent comes out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the percentage lost. The efficiency is the percentage that comes out.
That leaves out the core loss, which is present at every load and has to be added to the output.

questions.prompt: Why is the input power found by adding the losses to the output power?
hints: Energy is conserved, so what goes in has to be accounted for.
Ask where the power that does not reach the load goes.

acceptedIdeas: Everything that goes in either comes out or is lost as heat
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Everything that goes in either comes out or is lost as heat

choices.label: Everything that goes in either comes out or is lost as heat
The losses are a second output that the transformer delivers to the load
Efficiency is defined as the output plus the losses

questions.onCorrect: The input is the output plus the losses, so adding them gives the denominator of the efficiency.

misconceptions.feedback: The losses stay in the transformer as heat and are not delivered to the load. They are counted so that the input can be found.
Efficiency is the output divided by the input. The losses are added to find the input, since the input is not measured here.

questions.prompt: The invented 500 kVA unit runs at one tenth of full load. It delivers 40 kW, its core loss is 1.2 kW, and its copper loss at that load is 0.06 kW. What is its efficiency, in percent?
hints: Add both losses to the output to find the input.
Divide the output by that input.
Express the ratio as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The input is 40 + 1.2 + 0.06 = 41.26 kW, so the efficiency is 40 ÷ 41.26 = 0.9695, or 96.9%.

questions.onCorrect: The fixed core loss of 1.2 kW is now a large share of the 41.26 kW that goes in, so the efficiency is well below that at full load.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the efficiency at full load. At one tenth of the load the core loss takes a larger share of the input.
That counts the copper loss alone. The core loss of 1.2 kW is much larger at this load and has to be included.

questions.prompt: A 200 kVA three-phase transformer has a 400 V secondary. What is its rated line current, in amperes?
hints: For a three-phase unit the apparent power is 1.73 times the line voltage times the line current.
Work in volt-amperes, so 200 kVA is 200,000 VA.
Divide by 1.73 and by 400.
questions.onCorrect: The rating of 200 kVA at 400 V corresponds to 289 A in each secondary line.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the apparent power by the voltage, as for a single-phase unit. A three-phase unit has the factor 1.73 as well.
That multiplies by 1.73 where it should divide.
That leaves the apparent power in kilovolt-amperes while the voltage is in volts.

questions.prompt: A supplier rates a transformer 100 kVA and does not rate it in kW. Why?
hints: Think about what heats the windings, and what that depends on.
A load with a low power factor takes more current for the same real power.

acceptedIdeas: The limit is set by voltage and current, whatever the power factor
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The limit is set by voltage and current, whatever the power factor

choices.label: Kilowatts and kilovolt-amperes are two names for the same unit
A transformer makes no real power, so a kilowatt rating cannot apply
Heaters are the only loads that are rated in kilowatts
The limit is set by voltage and current, whatever the power factor

questions.onCorrect: The windings heat with the whole current, which the voltage and the volt-amperes fix, whatever the load's power factor.

misconceptions.feedback: The two differ by the power factor. A load of 100 kVA at a power factor of 0.7 takes only 70 kW, yet it carries the full current.
A transformer passes real power through, less its losses. The rating follows from the current the transformer can carry.
The rating follows from what limits the equipment, the current. It does not follow from the kind of load that the equipment feeds.

questions.prompt: A 100 kVA transformer has a core loss of 0.9 kW and a copper loss of 1.6 kW at full load. At what fraction of full load are the two losses equal?
hints: The copper loss at a fraction $x$ of full load is $1.6x^2$ kW.
Set that equal to the core loss, which does not change with load.
Solve for $x$ by taking a square root.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1.6$x^2$ = 0.9 gives $x^2$ = 0.5625, so $x$ = 0.75, which is three quarters of full load.

questions.onCorrect: Below three quarters of full load the core loss is the larger part of the heat, and above it the copper loss is.

misconceptions.feedback: That is $x^2$, the core loss divided by the copper loss. The fraction $x$ is its square root.
That divides 0.9 by 2.5, the sum of the two losses. The two losses are equal when the copper loss, $1.6x^2$, equals the core loss.

questions.prompt: A 300 kVA three-phase transformer steps 33 kV down to 400 V. What is its rated line current on the 33 kV side, in amperes?
hints: The rating is the same on both sides, and the line voltage differs.
Use the 33 kV line voltage with the factor 1.73.
Divide 300,000 VA by 1.73 times 33,000 V.
questions.onCorrect: On the 33 kV side the same 300 kVA is carried by 5.25 A, much less than the 433 A on the 400 V side.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the current on the 400 V side. The question asks for the 33 kV side, where the voltage is higher and the current smaller.
That leaves out the 1.73, as for a single-phase unit. A three-phase unit needs it.
That uses kilovolt-amperes with a voltage in volts. Convert the units first.

questions.prompt: A pole transformer rated 100 kVA serves four houses and rarely carries more than 10 kVA. Which loss accounts for most of its heat over a year?
hints: Compare the load with the rating to see how far below full load it runs.
Ask which of the two losses changes with the load and which does not.

acceptedIdeas: Core loss, because it is present all the time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Core loss, because it is present all the time

choices.label: Core loss, because it is present all the time
Copper loss, because it grows with the load
Neither, because it loses almost nothing at light load
Copper loss, because the current is small but steady

questions.onCorrect: The core loss goes on every hour of the year, whereas the copper loss is small at a tenth of full load.

misconceptions.feedback: At 10 kVA the current is a tenth of the rated current, so the copper loss is a hundredth of its full-load value. It is the small one.
Core loss does not depend on load, so even an idle transformer loses power.
A small current gives a small loss, since the loss follows the square of the current. A steady current does not make it larger.

questions.prompt: A lightly loaded transformer delivers 2,400 kW and is 97 percent efficient. How much heat does it produce, in kW?
hints: Efficiency is the output divided by the input, so the input is larger than 2,400 kW.
Find the input from the output and the efficiency.
The heat is the input minus the output.
questions.onCorrect: A few percent of a large power is still a lot of heat: 74.2 kW from this transformer.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes 3 percent of the output. The percentage applies to the input, since efficiency is the output over the input.
That is the input power. The heat is the part of the input that does not come out.
That is 97 percent of the output. The output is the 2,400 kW that is delivered, and the efficiency applies to the input.

questions.prompt: Power travels from a power station to a house through six stages. Put them in order, starting at the power station.
hints: Power is sent a long way at a high voltage, and the voltage is lowered in steps as it nears people.
Ask which stage covers the long distance between towns, and which covers the streets of one suburb.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The generator and step-up transformer come first, then the transmission line, a substation, a distribution feeder, a street transformer and the house, because the voltage is raised once for the long run and then lowered in steps.

items: The generator and its step-up transformer
A substation that steps the voltage down
A distribution feeder along the streets of a suburb
A street transformer that steps the voltage down again

questions.onCorrect: The voltage is raised once for the long run and lowered in steps near the customer, so the transmission line comes first.

questions.prompt: A line of fixed resistance delivers the same power as before, but at twice the voltage. What happens to the power lost as heat in the line?
hints: For the same power, what does doubling the voltage do to the current in the line?
The heat produced in a resistance depends on the square of the current, $I^2R$.

acceptedIdeas: It falls to a quarter, as the loss depends on current squared
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls to a quarter, as the loss depends on current squared

choices.label: It halves, because the current in the line is halved
It falls to a quarter, as the loss depends on current squared
It stays the same, because the delivered power is unchanged
It doubles, because the higher voltage drives the line harder

questions.onCorrect: Halving the current divides the heat by four, because the heat in the line depends on the square of the current.

misconceptions.feedback: The current does halve, but the heat in a conductor depends on the square of the current. Work out what halving a quantity does to its square.
The delivered power is unchanged, but the current that carries it is not. The loss depends on the current in the line, and that current has changed.
A higher voltage does not drive more current through the line. The load fixes the power, so the current is the power divided by the voltage and falls as the voltage rises.

questions.prompt: In this line, why is the ratio of the two voltages squared before it is applied to the loss?
hints: What does the heat in a resistance depend on, the voltage or the current?
For a fixed power, how does the current change when the voltage is doubled?

acceptedIdeas: The heat depends on the current squared, and the current falls as the voltage rises
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The heat depends on the current squared, and the current falls as the voltage rises

choices.label: The heat depends on the current squared, and the current falls as the voltage rises
Power is voltage times current, so the voltage enters the loss twice over, as $V^2$
A transformer changes a voltage by the square of its turns ratio, so the ratio is squared
The resistance of the line itself changes with the square of the voltage that it carries

questions.onCorrect: The current is the power divided by the voltage and the heat depends on its square, so the loss varies as 1/V squared.

misconceptions.feedback: The voltage that matters is not a drop across the line. The heat depends on the current in the line, which is the power divided by the line voltage.
A transformer changes the voltage in the ratio of its turns, not in the square of it. The square comes from the current in the line.
The resistance of a line is set by its conductor and its length, and it does not depend on the voltage it carries.

questions.prompt: A line carries the same power at 345 kV and at 765 kV. The loss is multiplied by the old voltage divided by the new one, squared. What is that factor?
hints: The loss depends on the current squared, and the current falls in proportion to the voltage rising.
Divide 345 by 765 first.
Square the result of that division.
questions.onCorrect: The factor is 0.203: the current falls to 0.451 of its old value and the loss to the square of that.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio of the voltages itself. The loss depends on the current squared, so the ratio has to be squared.
That ratio is upside down. A higher voltage lowers the loss, so the factor must be below 1.

questions.prompt: A 345 kV line carrying 1000 MW over 160 km loses 4.2% of the power. By the square law, what would the same line lose at 765 kV, in percent?
hints: Raising the voltage lowers the loss, so the answer must be below 4.2%.
Multiply the 4.2% by the factor from the line above.
The result should be a little under 1%.
questions.onCorrect: The rule gives 0.85%, which lies inside the 0.5% to 1.1% that the source quotes for a 765 kV line.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the unsquared ratio, 0.451. The loss depends on the square of the voltage ratio.
That applies the factor upside down. Raising the voltage lowers the loss, so the answer must be below 4.2.

questions.prompt: Two grids whose frequencies are not locked together are to be joined by a cable that runs 400 km under the sea. Which choice fits this link?
hints: Which of the two conditions, the sea or the frequencies, rules out an ordinary AC line?
Look back at the three situations in which direct current pays for its converter stations.

acceptedIdeas: HVDC, to suit a long cable under the sea and grids out of step
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: HVDC, to suit a long cable under the sea and grids out of step

choices.label: AC at the highest voltage available, to keep the current low
AC with a much thicker conductor, to cut the loss in proportion
HVDC, to suit a long cable under the sea and grids out of step
Three-phase AC at a lower voltage, to reduce the insulation needed

questions.onCorrect: HVDC suits a long submarine cable, where AC cannot be used, and it is necessary between grids that are not synchronised.

misconceptions.feedback: A high voltage does lower the current, but cable capacitance rules AC out on a long submarine run, and the two grids would still not be in step.
A thicker conductor lowers the loss only in proportion to its area, and it does nothing about the grids being out of step.
A lower voltage raises the current for the same power, and with it the loss, and an AC link would still need the grids to be in step.

questions.prompt: A line that carries a fixed power loses 1.2% of it at 275 kV. The same line has to carry the same power at 110 kV instead. What share of the power does it lose, in percent?
hints: Is the new voltage higher or lower than the old one, and so does the loss rise or fall?
Work out the ratio of the old voltage to the new one.
Square the ratio before you apply it to the 1.2%.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The loss is multiplied by (275/110)^2 = 6.25, so 1.2% x 6.25 = 7.5%.

questions.onCorrect: A lower voltage means a larger current, so the loss rises with the square of the ratio, 6.25 times, to 7.5%.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the ratio 2.5 without squaring it. The loss varies with the square of the voltage ratio.
That applies the ratio upside down. A lower voltage needs a larger current for the same power, so the loss rises.

questions.prompt: Five links are being planned. The cases are invented, and each is described only by what matters to the choice. Sort them by whether the link would be built as AC or as HVDC.
hints: Ask whether the link crosses the sea or joins grids that are not in step; if neither, the converter stations are hard to justify.
HVDC needs costly conversion equipment, so it appears only where AC cannot do the job or the distance is very large.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: HVDC for the undersea cable and for the link between unsynchronised grids. AC for the 60 km overhead line, the suburban feeder and the wind farm connection.

items.label: A 300 km cable laid under the sea to join an island grid to the mainland
items.explanation: AC cannot be used on a long submarine cable because of its capacitance, and HVDC is used for such cables.

items.label: A link between two grids whose frequencies are not locked together
items.explanation: Energy can only be sent between unsynchronised grids by HVDC.

items.label: A 60 km overhead line between two substations of one synchronous grid
items.explanation: Both ends share a frequency and the run is overhead, so an ordinary high-voltage AC line serves without converter stations.

items.label: A feeder that runs along the streets of one suburb
items.explanation: A feeder is a short AC line at distribution voltage, and converters would cost far more than they could save.

items.label: A line joining a new wind farm to a nearby substation of the same grid
items.explanation: A short overhead run inside one grid gives HVDC nothing to offset the cost of its converter stations.

questions.onCorrect: HVDC is used where AC cannot be, under the sea and between unsynchronised grids; short links inside one grid stay AC.

questions.prompt: An invented case: a wind farm 300 km from a city is to deliver 600 MW to it. A planner suggests joining the two at 33 kV, the voltage of an ordinary distribution feeder, so that no high-voltage line is needed. What is the main objection?
hints: For the same power, what happens to the current if the voltage is much lower?
Which stage of the voltage ladder is meant for the long distance, and which for the streets?

acceptedIdeas: The current for that power at 33 kV would be very large, and the line would lose far more as heat
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The current for that power at 33 kV would be very large, and the line would lose far more as heat

choices.label: At 33 kV the line cannot push 600 MW over 300 km, because the voltage is too low to drive it
A conductor thick enough would lower the loss as much as a higher voltage, so cost is the only issue
Nothing is wrong, since the same power arrives whatever the voltage and the loss is unaffected
The current for that power at 33 kV would be very large, and the line would lose far more as heat

questions.onCorrect: The voltage fixes the current for a given power, and the heat depends on its square, so a long run belongs at transmission voltage.

misconceptions.feedback: Voltage does not push power along a line. The load fixes the power, and what the voltage changes is the current needed to carry it.
A thicker conductor lowers the loss only in proportion to its area, while a higher voltage lowers it with the square. Matching the effect of the voltage would take an enormous conductor.
The power sent is the same, but the current is not, and the heat in the line depends on that current. At a low voltage the current is large.

questions.prompt: A single coil turning in a magnetic field gives one cycle of alternating voltage for every turn. How many turns per minute give a frequency of 50 Hz?
hints: A frequency of 50 Hz is 50 cycles in every second.
How many turns is that in one second, and how many seconds are there in a minute?
Multiply the turns per second by 60.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50 cycles per second needs 50 turns per second, and 50 x 60 = 3000 turns per minute.

questions.onCorrect: Fifty turns each second is 50 x 60 = 3000 turns each minute.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of turns each second. The question asks for turns each minute.

questions.prompt: A 6-pole machine is connected to a 50 Hz supply. What is its synchronous speed, in revolutions per minute?
hints: Use N = 120 f / P.
Put f = 50 Hz and P = 6 into the formula.
Multiply 120 by 50 before you divide.
questions.onCorrect: N = 120 x 50 / 6 = 1000 rpm, a third of the 2-pole speed, because each turn now delivers three cycles.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the speed of a 2-pole machine. More poles mean a slower machine, since each turn delivers more cycles.
That is the speed of a 4-pole machine. A 6-pole machine turns more slowly still.

questions.prompt: A generator on a 50 Hz grid is driven at 3000 rpm. How many poles does it have?
hints: Rearrange N = 120 f / P to give P in terms of f and N.
Put f = 50 Hz and N = 3000 rpm into P = 120 f / N.
questions.onCorrect: P = 120 x 50 / 3000 = 2, so the generator has one pair of poles.

misconceptions.feedback: A 4-pole machine turns at 1500 rpm on 50 Hz. At 3000 rpm there are fewer poles.
That is 3000 divided by 50, the number of rpm for each hertz. Use P = 120 f / N.

questions.prompt: The operator of a generator that is connected to a large grid raises its field current. What changes?
hints: Think about what a stronger rotor field does to the voltage induced in the stator winding.
Which quantity does the grid hold fixed for every connected synchronous generator?

acceptedIdeas: Its voltage and its reactive power, while its frequency stays at the grid's
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its voltage and its reactive power, while its frequency stays at the grid's

choices.label: Its voltage and its reactive power, while its frequency stays at the grid's
Its frequency, because a stronger field makes the rotor turn faster than before
Its speed, because the extra field current adds torque that accelerates the rotor
Nothing at all, because field current matters only to a machine that stands alone

questions.onCorrect: The field current sets the induced voltage and the reactive power, and the grid keeps the frequency, so the speed does not change.

misconceptions.feedback: The grid holds the frequency, and the rotor stays locked to it. A stronger field changes what the generator does electrically, and it does not change how fast the rotor turns.
Field current sets the strength of the rotor's magnetic field and adds no torque. The speed is fixed at the synchronous value by the grid.
A central-station generator uses its field current in the grid to regulate voltage and reactive power, so it matters a great deal to a connected machine.

questions.prompt: Why must the rotor of an induction motor turn more slowly than the rotating field?
hints: What does a conductor need, relative to a magnetic field, if a current is to be induced in it?
What would the rotor feel if it turned at exactly the speed of the field?

acceptedIdeas: Without relative motion no emf is induced, and so the rotor would have no torque
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Without relative motion no emf is induced, and so the rotor would have no torque

choices.label: Friction in the bearings holds the rotor back by a few percent whatever the load is
Without relative motion no emf is induced, and so the rotor would have no torque
The rotor has more poles than the stator, and that lowers its speed by the slip
A rotor turning at the field's speed would draw so much current that it overheated

questions.onCorrect: A conductor needs relative motion with the field to have an emf induced in it, so the rotor must lag the field.

misconceptions.feedback: Friction takes a share of the torque, but it does not set the slip. The slip is the speed difference that the rotor needs for its current to be induced at all.
The rotor of an induction motor follows the field of the stator and has no pole count of its own to subtract. The difference in speed comes from the need for induced current.
At the field's speed the trouble would be the opposite: the rotor would have no current at all, because nothing is induced without relative motion.

questions.prompt: A 4-pole motor is connected to a 60 Hz supply. What is the speed of its rotating field, in revolutions per minute?
hints: The frequency here is 60 Hz, not 50 Hz.
Use N = 120 f / P with f = 60 and P = 4.
Multiply 120 by 60 and divide by 4.
questions.onCorrect: N = 120 x 60 / 4 = 1800 rpm, the speed of the rotating field for this motor.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the speed on a 50 Hz supply. This supply is 60 Hz.

questions.prompt: The rotor of this motor turns at 1746 rpm under load, and the field turns at 1800 rpm. What is the slip, in percent?
hints: Slip is the shortfall of the rotor, as a percentage of the field's speed.
Find the difference between the two speeds.
Divide the difference by 1800 and multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: The shortfall is 54 rpm, which is 3% of the field's 1800 rpm.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the shortfall in rpm. Slip expresses it as a percentage of the field's speed.

questions.prompt: A motor on a 50 Hz supply drives a pump. A tachometer reads exactly 1500 rpm whether the pump is idling or working hard, and the motor stops dead when a blockage overloads the pump. Which kind of motor is it?
hints: Does the speed change at all as the load changes?
What would a rotor pulled out of step with the field produce?

acceptedIdeas: A synchronous motor, whose rotor stays locked in step with the field
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A synchronous motor, whose rotor stays locked in step with the field

choices.label: An induction motor, whose slip is very small but never quite zero at any load
An induction motor, whose slip changes sign as the load reaches its full value
A synchronous motor, whose rotor stays locked in step with the field

questions.onCorrect: A speed that does not change with load, and a rotor that stops when pulled out of step, are the marks of a synchronous motor.

misconceptions.feedback: A small slip is still a slip, so the speed would fall a little as the load rises. A reading of exactly 1500 rpm at every load means no slip at all.
The slip of an induction motor does not change sign when the load rises. Negative slip belongs to a machine that is driven faster than the field, which is generating.

questions.prompt: An 8-pole induction motor is connected to a 50 Hz supply and its rotor turns at 735 rpm under load. What is its slip, in percent?
hints: Find the speed of the field first, for 8 poles at 50 Hz.
The shortfall is the difference between that speed and 735 rpm.
Divide the shortfall by the field's speed and multiply by 100.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The field turns at 120 x 50 / 8 = 750 rpm, so the slip is (750 - 735) / 750 x 100% = 2%.

questions.onCorrect: The field turns at 750 rpm and the rotor is 15 rpm short of it, which is a slip of 2%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the shortfall in rpm. Slip is a percentage of the field's speed.
That is the rotor's speed. Slip compares the shortfall with the field's speed.

questions.prompt: Two three-phase motors with 6 poles run from a 50 Hz supply, so their rotating field turns at 1000 rpm. A tachometer reads motor X at 985 rpm when idling and 960 rpm at full load, and motor Y at 1000 rpm in both conditions. Which description fits?
hints: Work out how far each reading lies below 1000 rpm.
Which kind of motor keeps the same speed whatever the load?

acceptedIdeas: X is an induction motor, with slip rising from 1.5% to 4%, and Y is a synchronous motor
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: X is an induction motor, with slip rising from 1.5% to 4%, and Y is a synchronous motor

choices.label: Both are induction motors, and the slip of Y is too small for a tachometer to show
X is a synchronous motor that loses a little step as it loads, and Y is an induction motor
Both are synchronous motors, and X is only running below its rated load
X is an induction motor, with slip rising from 1.5% to 4%, and Y is a synchronous motor

questions.onCorrect: X slips further as it loads, as an induction motor does, and Y holds the field's speed at both loads, as a synchronous motor does.

misconceptions.feedback: A slip too small to show would still let the speed fall as the load rises. Y reads exactly the field's speed at both loads, which an induction motor cannot do.
A synchronous motor does not lose speed as it loads, since its rotor stays locked to the field. It stops if it is pulled out of step, and it never runs slowly.
A synchronous motor turns at exactly the field's speed at every load. X changes speed with load, so it is not synchronous.

questions.prompt: A synchronous motor drives a constant load from a 50 Hz supply, with its field excitation set for a power factor of 1. The excitation is then lowered a little. What follows?
hints: Recall what raising the excitation did to the power factor at a constant load.
Does the speed of a synchronous motor depend on its excitation?

acceptedIdeas: Its speed stays the same, and its power factor moves toward lagging
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its speed stays the same, and its power factor moves toward lagging

choices.label: Its speed falls a little, and its power factor stays at 1
Its speed stays the same, and its power factor moves toward lagging
Its speed stays the same, and its power factor moves toward leading
Its speed stays the same, and it stops at once because it loses step

questions.onCorrect: Lowering the excitation at a constant load moves a synchronous motor toward a lagging power factor, and the speed does not change.

misconceptions.feedback: A synchronous motor turns at synchronous speed whatever its excitation. The excitation changes the phase of the current, and the speed is untouched.
That is the effect of raising the excitation. Lowering it moves the current the other way relative to the voltage.
A synchronous motor stops when its load drags the rotor out of step. A small drop in excitation changes its power factor and leaves the lock in place.

questions.prompt: A 600 MW generator trips and nothing else changes yet. What do the rotors of the remaining generators do in the first seconds?
hints: The load still draws the same power but less is being generated. Where could the difference come from in the first moment?
Think of the energy stored in the spinning rotors.

acceptedIdeas: They slow down a little, so the grid frequency falls below 50 Hz
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They slow down a little, so the grid frequency falls below 50 Hz

choices.label: They slow down a little, so the grid frequency falls below 50 Hz
They speed up a little, so the grid frequency rises above 50 Hz
They hold their speed, because the governors respond at once
They hold their speed, and the voltage falls in place of the frequency

questions.onCorrect: The rotors supply the missing power from their rotation, so they slow and the frequency falls.

misconceptions.feedback: That has the sign reversed. With a generator lost the load is greater than the power supplied, and the extra power has to come from the machines' rotation, so they slow.
A governor reacts to a change in speed, so the speed has to change before it acts. The rotors have already given up some of their energy by then.
The balance between supply and demand shows in the speed of the machines, and speed sets frequency. The voltage is held by a different control.

questions.prompt: Two grids of the same size lose the same 500 MW unit. Grid A has mostly synchronous generation, while grid B has replaced half of its synchronous generation with inverter-based plant. What should you expect in the first seconds?
hints: Which grid has more rotating mass to give up energy?
Does a grid with less stored rotational energy move more or less for the same shortfall?

acceptedIdeas: The frequency falls faster in grid B, because less rotating mass is joined to it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The frequency falls faster in grid B, because less rotating mass is joined to it

choices.label: The frequency falls at the same rate in both, because the lost power is the same
The frequency falls faster in grid A, because it has more rotating mass to slow
The frequency does not fall in grid B, because inverters respond faster than rotors
The frequency falls faster in grid B, because less rotating mass is joined to it

questions.onCorrect: Inverter-based plant adds no rotating mass of this kind, so grid B has less inertia and its frequency falls faster.

misconceptions.feedback: The lost power is the same, but how fast it moves the frequency depends on how much rotating mass supplies the shortfall. Grid B has less of it.
That reverses the role of inertia. More rotating mass means more stored energy to draw on, so the frequency of grid A falls more slowly.
A fast response cannot act before there is a frequency change to respond to. Inertia is the response that needs no change to begin, and grid B has less of it.

questions.prompt: A 560 MW unit trips at 1:58:59 am, and by 1:59:19 am the frequency has fallen to 49.8 Hz. Suppose it was 50.00 Hz at the trip. What was the average rate of fall, in hertz per second?
hints: A rate is a change divided by the time taken.
The change in frequency is 50.00 minus 49.8 hertz, and the time is from 1:58:59 to 1:59:19.
Divide the fall in hertz by the number of seconds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The fall is 50.00 - 49.80 = 0.20 Hz over 20 s, an average of 0.20 / 20 = 0.01 Hz per second.

questions.onCorrect: The frequency fell 0.20 Hz in 20 s, an average of 0.01 Hz per second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fall in hertz. A rate in hertz per second needs the fall divided by the time taken.
That divides the time by the fall. A rate is the change in frequency divided by the time.

questions.prompt: One failure removes 4% of the average load of one grid and 1.5% of the average load of another. Other things equal, in which grid would you expect the frequency to move further?
hints: Compare the two losses as shares of each grid's load, not as megawatts.
Which loss leaves the larger imbalance for the grid to absorb?

acceptedIdeas: In the grid where it is 4%, since the same loss is a larger share of its load
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In the grid where it is 4%, since the same loss is a larger share of its load

choices.label: In the grid where it is 4%, since the same loss is a larger share of its load
In the grid where it is 1.5%, since a smaller percentage shifts it more
In neither, since frequency depends only on the size of the unit in megawatts
In both equally, since each grid's inertia grows with its load

questions.onCorrect: A loss that is a larger share of the load is a larger imbalance, so it moves the frequency further.

misconceptions.feedback: A smaller share of the load is a smaller imbalance for the grid to absorb, so the frequency moves less.
The size in megawatts matters only against the size of the grid. A unit that is a larger share of the load is a bigger imbalance.
Inertia grows with the size of the grid, but that is already in the shares. The loss that is a larger share of the load still moves the frequency further.

questions.prompt: At midday a grid has few synchronous machines online, and the operator wants to add inertia to it. Which of these actions does that directly?
hints: Inertia comes from rotating mass that is joined to the grid.
Which options need the frequency to change before they act?

acceptedIdeas: Connecting synchronous condensers, which bring rotating mass onto the grid
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Connecting synchronous condensers, which bring rotating mass onto the grid

choices.label: Fitting some large cooling plants with relays that disconnect them at a set frequency
Allowing the frequency to swing further before the controls are asked to act
Connecting synchronous condensers, which bring rotating mass onto the grid
Connecting more solar plant, whose output follows the grid frequency

questions.onCorrect: Synchronous condensers bring rotating mass onto the grid, so they add inertia, whereas the other actions respond to a frequency change or tolerate it.

misconceptions.feedback: Relays that shed load are a quick response to a frequency fall. They need the frequency to be measured first, and they add no rotating mass.
A wider allowed swing is a way of living with low inertia, and it adds none.
Solar plant connects through inverters and has no rotating mass joined to the grid, so adding more of it does not add inertia.

questions.prompt: Two grids lose the same 400 MW unit. The frequency of grid P falls from 50.00 Hz to 49.70 Hz in 15 s, and that of grid Q falls from 50.00 Hz to 49.90 Hz in 20 s. How many times faster was the average rate of fall in P than in Q?
hints: Find the average rate of fall in each grid first, in hertz per second.
Rate is the fall in hertz divided by the time in seconds.
Divide the rate in P by the rate in Q.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: P fell at 0.30 / 15 = 0.02 Hz per second and Q at 0.10 / 20 = 0.005 Hz per second, and 0.02 / 0.005 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: Grid P fell at 0.02 Hz per second and grid Q at 0.005, so P fell four times as fast, which points to less rotating mass joined to P.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the rate in Q by the rate in P. The question asks how many times faster P was.
That compares the two falls in hertz, 0.30 and 0.10. The times differ too, 15 s and 20 s, so compare rates.

questions.prompt: A region exports 300 MW to its neighbour over a single interconnector, and the link trips. In the first moments after the trip, what happens to the frequency in the exporting region?
hints: Before the trip, where did the 300 MW go?
After the trip, is there more or less load in the region than generation?

acceptedIdeas: It rises, because the region now generates more than it uses
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises, because the region now generates more than it uses

choices.label: It falls, because the region has lost its connection to the wider grid
It rises, because the region now generates more than it uses
It stays at 50 Hz, because every generator in the region is still running
It falls first and then rises, because the governors respond to the loss

questions.onCorrect: The exporting region keeps the 300 MW it was sending out, a surplus of generation, so its rotors speed up and the frequency rises.

misconceptions.feedback: Losing a connection does not by itself take power from the region. The 300 MW that was flowing out now stays in, so the region has a surplus.
The generators are still running, but 300 MW of what they produced has no load now. A surplus speeds the rotors up, so the frequency moves.
The governors act after the frequency has moved, and the first movement is set by the surplus. The surplus speeds the rotors from the start.

questions.prompt: Grid P has an average load of 10,000 MW and loses a 500 MW unit. Grid Q has an average load of 30,000 MW and loses a 750 MW unit. Other things equal, in which grid should the frequency move further?
hints: Work out each loss as a percentage of its grid's average load.
Which loss is the larger share?

acceptedIdeas: Grid P, where the loss is 5% of the average load, against 2.5% in grid Q
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Grid P, where the loss is 5% of the average load, against 2.5% in grid Q

choices.label: Grid Q, because 750 MW is the larger loss and so moves the frequency further
Grid Q, because a larger grid has less inertia to slow a fall in frequency
Grid P, where the loss is 5% of the average load, against 2.5% in grid Q
Both the same, since each is the loss of one unit and the units are alike

questions.onCorrect: The loss is 5% of the average load in grid P and 2.5% in grid Q, so the frequency of P moves further.

misconceptions.feedback: The megawatts have to be compared with the size of the grid. 750 MW is a smaller share of grid Q's load than 500 MW is of grid P's.
A larger grid usually has more rotating mass in total, not less, and the shares of the loss already allow for its size.
A single unit can be a large or a small share of a grid. The share of the load decides how far the frequency moves.

questions.prompt: A large generator trips. Put these five responses in the order in which they act, the fastest first.
hints: Inertia is built into the machines, so it needs nothing to be measured or started.
A response that has to be started up takes longer than one that only has to be adjusted.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inertia acts at once, governors respond as the frequency falls, automatic generation control acts within several tens of seconds, reserves reach their promised output within about ten minutes, and replacement reserve takes 30 to 60 minutes.

items: Rotor inertia of the synchronous generators
Governor droop response of each running generator
Automatic generation control from the system operator
Spinning and non-spinning reserve brought to full output

questions.onCorrect: Each layer is slower than the one before it, from inertia at once to replacement reserve in 30 to 60 minutes.

questions.prompt: Why does a 1% change in speed move the output of a unit with 4% droop by 25% of its rating?
hints: Droop is the percentage change in speed for the whole range of the output, from none to the full rating.
What fraction of 4% is 1%?

acceptedIdeas: 1% is a quarter of the 4% change in speed that takes it from no load to full load
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 1% is a quarter of the 4% change in speed that takes it from no load to full load

choices.label: 1% is a quarter of the 4% change in speed that takes it from no load to full load
The governor can only change the output in steps of a quarter of the unit's rating at a time
The output of a turbine falls by 25% of its rating for each 1% that the load on it rises
A droop of 4% means that the unit supplies 4% of the total power that the grid is carrying

questions.onCorrect: A 4% change in speed covers the whole output range, so a 1% change covers a quarter of it.

misconceptions.feedback: A governor under droop control changes the output in proportion to the change in speed, not in fixed steps. The quarter comes from how far a 1% change goes towards the 4%.
A turbine under droop control raises its output when the speed falls. It does not lose a quarter of its output for each percent of load.
Droop is a setting of the governor and says nothing about the unit's share of the grid. It is the change in speed that takes the unit from no load to full load.

questions.prompt: A 300 MW unit with a droop of 4% sees the frequency fall from 50 Hz by 0.15 Hz. What is that fall as a percentage of 50 Hz?
hints: Divide the fall in hertz by the starting frequency.
Express the result as a percentage by multiplying by 100.
The fall is a small fraction of a percent.
questions.onCorrect: A fall of 0.15 Hz is 0.3% of 50 Hz.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fall in hertz. The droop rule works with a percentage of the frequency.
That is a factor of ten too large. Check the division of 0.15 by 50, and then the conversion to a percentage.

questions.prompt: The unit of 300 MW has a droop of 4%, so its output rises by 25% of its rating for each 1% fall in speed. By how many megawatts does it raise its output for a fall of 0.3%?
hints: Multiply the 0.3% by 25 to find the change as a percentage of the rating.
Take that percentage of 300 MW.
The percentage of the rating is 7.5%.
questions.onCorrect: The output rises by 7.5% of 300 MW, which is 22.5 MW.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change as a percentage of the rating. Apply it to the 300 MW to find megawatts.
That takes 0.3 of the rating. The 0.3% has first to be multiplied by 25 to give the change as a percentage of the rating.

questions.prompt: Offers for one 5-minute interval are A 400 MW at $0, B 300 MW at $45, C 200 MW at $90 and D 100 MW at $350 per MWh. Demand is 850 MW. What price per MWh is set for the region?
hints: Dispatch the cheapest offers first and keep a running total.
A and B together supply 700 MW, which is short of 850 MW.
Which offer is the last one that is needed to reach 850 MW?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A and B supply 700 MW, and the other 150 MW comes from C, the last offer needed, so the price is C's $90.

questions.onCorrect: C is the last offer used, so its $90 sets the price for every dispatched unit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B's offer. A and B supply only 700 MW, so C is needed and its offer sets the price.
D is not needed, since A, B and part of C already reach 850 MW.

questions.prompt: Generator B offered $45 per MWh and was dispatched in an interval in which the price was $90. What does B receive for its energy?
hints: Who sets the price, the lowest offer or the highest offer that is needed?
What is paid to a unit whose offer was lower than that price?

acceptedIdeas: $90 per MWh, the price set for the interval
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: $90 per MWh, the price set for the interval

choices.label: $45 per MWh, the price in its own offer
Nothing, because its offer was below the price
$90 per MWh, the price set for the interval
$67.50 per MWh, the average of offer and price

questions.onCorrect: The highest offer needed sets the price, and every dispatched generator is paid it, whatever its own offer.

misconceptions.feedback: A generator is not paid its own offer. The highest offer needed sets one price, and every dispatched generator receives it.
A low offer is the way to be dispatched. Offers below the price are called on first, and they receive the price.
There is no averaging rule. The price set by the highest offer needed is paid to every dispatched unit as it stands.

questions.prompt: Put each disturbance with the service that handles it. The cases are invented.
hints: Ask whether the event is small and continuous, large and sudden, or planned ahead.
Dispatch decides which offers run in each 5-minute interval, and the frequency services deal with what happens between the plans.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Regulation FCAS: the afternoon drift and the passing cloud. Contingency FCAS: the largest generator's trip and the loss of an interconnector. Energy dispatch: the forecast evening rise and the change of cheapest stations.

items.label: A few megawatts of drift as demand and wind output wander through the afternoon
items.explanation: Regulation services work continuously on the small variations of normal operation.

items.label: The sudden trip of the largest generator on the system
items.explanation: A large, sudden, unexpected shift in supply is what contingency services are bought for.

items.label: The loss of a major interconnector
items.explanation: A sudden loss of that size is a large change in supply or demand, so a contingency service answers it.

items.label: A forecast two-hour rise in evening demand
items.explanation: A forecast rise is planned for in the 5-minute dispatch, with the cheapest offers called on in turn.

items.label: A cloud that cuts a solar farm's output by a small amount for a minute
items.explanation: A small change in supply in normal operation is a regulation matter.

items.label: A change in which power stations are cheapest from one 5-minute interval to the next
items.explanation: Choosing which offers run for each interval is dispatch, not a frequency service.

questions.onCorrect: Regulation follows small continuous variations, contingency covers large sudden losses, and dispatch plans the energy for each interval.

questions.prompt: Two units are both set with a droop of 4%. One is rated at 600 MW and the other at 200 MW. The grid frequency falls from 50 Hz by 0.3 Hz. By how many megawatts do the two units together raise their output?
hints: Express the fall in frequency as a percentage of 50 Hz.
At 4% droop, multiply that percentage by 25 to find the change as a percentage of each unit's rating.
Apply that percentage to each rating, and add the two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The fall is 0.3/50 = 0.6%, which moves each unit by 0.6 x 25 = 15% of its rating. That is 90 MW from the 600 MW unit and 30 MW from the 200 MW unit, 120 MW together.

questions.onCorrect: Each unit raises its output by 15% of its rating, 90 MW and 30 MW, so the pair add 120 MW.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 600 MW unit alone. The 200 MW unit also responds, and the question asks for both.
That is the 200 MW unit alone. The 600 MW unit also responds, and the question asks for both.

questions.prompt: Offers for one interval are P 300 MW at $0, Q 200 MW at $35, R 200 MW at $70 and S 100 MW at $200 per MWh. Demand is 480 MW. What does unit P receive, per MWh?
hints: Dispatch the cheapest offers first, with a running total, until 480 MW is reached.
Which offer is the last one that is needed?
Every dispatched unit is paid the price that the last offer sets.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: P's 300 MW and 180 MW of Q meet the demand, so Q's $35 sets the price, and P is paid the same $35 per MWh although it offered $0.

questions.onCorrect: Q is the last offer needed, so the price is $35, and P receives that price even though it offered $0.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P's own offer. Every dispatched unit is paid the price set by the highest offer needed.
R's offer is not needed, since P and Q already supply 500 MW and the demand is 480 MW.

questions.prompt: A grid's largest units are 700 MW, 500 MW and 400 MW, and the operator holds 600 MW of reserve that can reach full output within ten minutes. What does the usual design rule say about this reserve?
hints: Which single loss would the reserve have to cover?
Compare 600 MW with the size of the largest unit.

acceptedIdeas: It falls short, because it should be at least the largest unit plus a share of peak load
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls short, because it should be at least the largest unit plus a share of peak load

choices.label: It is enough, because 600 MW is larger than the second-largest unit on the system, 500 MW
It falls short, because it should be at least the largest unit plus a share of peak load
It falls short, because it should cover all three of the largest units failing at the same time
It is enough, because 600 MW is larger than the average size of the three largest units, 533 MW

questions.onCorrect: Reserve should at least equal the biggest unit plus a share of the peak load, so 600 MW falls short of 700 MW.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule is built on the loss of the largest single supplier, which here is 700 MW. A reserve that is larger than the second-largest unit still cannot cover that loss.
The usual design covers the loss of the largest single supplier, not all of the large units failing together, which would call for a much larger reserve.
An average of the units' sizes is not the test. The reserve has to cover the loss of the largest unit, which is 700 MW here.

questions.prompt: A circuit normally carries 20 A. A fault joins the two conductors of its 230 V supply through a path of 0.05 ohm in total, an invented figure. Compared with 20 A, how large is the fault current?
hints: Ohm's law gives the current from the voltage and the resistance.
Compare 230 V across 0.05 ohm with the 20 A that the circuit's load draws.

acceptedIdeas: Over a hundred times larger, because the fault path resistance sets it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Over a hundred times larger, because the fault path resistance sets it

questions.onCorrect: The current is 230 / 0.05 = 4600 A, which is 230 times the 20 A that the circuit normally carries.

misconceptions.feedback: A breaker does not hold a fault current down to its rating. It has to open against the current that the fault drives, which the voltage and the resistance of the path decide.
A fault is not one more load. Its path has far less resistance than any load, so 230 V across 0.05 ohm drives 4600 A, not a few times 20 A.
A fault gives the current a second path of very low resistance beside the load. It does not take current away, and the supply drives far more current through it.

choices.label: About the same, because the breaker holds the current at its rating
Over a hundred times larger, because the fault path resistance sets it
A few times larger, because the fault adds one more load to the circuit
Smaller, because the fault takes current away from the load

questions.prompt: A breaker on a switchboard is rated to interrupt 6 kA. The prospective short-circuit current at that point is 14 kA. What is the problem?
hints: A breaker has two ratings. Which one does the fault current test?
Compare 6 kA with 14 kA.

acceptedIdeas: It may fail to interrupt a fault current of that size safely
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It may fail to interrupt a fault current of that size safely

choices.label: None, because its current rating already covers the normal load
It may open too slowly when the circuit is only overloaded
It may fail to interrupt a fault current of that size safely
None, because a fuse upstream always protects the breaker

questions.onCorrect: The breaker's interrupting capacity of 6 kA is below the 14 kA that a fault at that point could draw.

misconceptions.feedback: The current rating covers the normal load, and the interrupting capacity is a separate rating for faults. It is the second one that is exceeded here.
Interrupting capacity is about faults, not overloads. The question is whether the breaker can open against a current of that size.
A device upstream may or may not limit the current, and the breaker's own rating still has to suit its position. Nothing makes the problem go away.

questions.prompt: Put each description with the device it describes.
hints: Ask which device melts, which opens its contacts, and which only senses and tells another device to act.
A breaker can be reset, and a fuse that has operated cannot.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fuse: the melting link and the fuse ahead of moulded-case breakers. Circuit breaker: the resettable device with an interrupting rating and the small heat or magnetic breaker.
