Protective relay: the sensor of undervoltage or underfrequency and the sensor on a high-voltage circuit.

items.label: Has a link that is melted by the current passing through it
items.explanation: The fusible link is heated and destroyed by an overcurrent, which opens the circuit.

items.label: Applied ahead of moulded-case breakers where the fault levels are very high
items.explanation: Current-limiting fuses are used in front of some breakers to protect them at high fault levels.

items.label: Can be reset once the fault has been cleared, and is rated for the largest fault current it can interrupt
items.explanation: A breaker opens its contacts and is rated both for its normal current and for the short-circuit current it can interrupt.

items.label: In a small low-voltage version, detects the fault by the heating or magnetic effect of the current
items.explanation: Small breakers sense the fault inside the device and then open their own contacts.

items.label: Senses undervoltage or underfrequency and signals a breaker to open
items.explanation: A relay does the sensing for a condition other than overcurrent, and a breaker does the opening.

items.label: Senses a fault on a high-voltage circuit and operates the opening mechanism of a large breaker
items.explanation: Large and high-voltage breakers are paired with relays that sense the fault and operate the opening mechanism.

questions.onCorrect: A fuse melts, a breaker opens its contacts and has a short-circuit rating, and a relay senses and tells a breaker to open.

questions.prompt: A fault occurs in a branch circuit that is fed from a feeder, which is fed from the main supply. Each level has its own protection. Which should clear the fault, and why?
hints: The three devices are in series, so the same fault current passes through all of them.
Which device would put the fewest other circuits out of supply?

acceptedIdeas: The device closest to the fault, so that the rest of the supply stays on
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The device closest to the fault, so that the rest of the supply stays on

choices.label: The main supply device, because it carries the most current of the three
The device closest to the fault, so that the rest of the supply stays on
All three together, because a fault should be cleared as fast as possible
The feeder device, because it sits in the middle and covers both sides

questions.onCorrect: Only the device closest to the fault needs to open, and the other circuits fed from the same supply then stay on.

misconceptions.feedback: The main device carries the most current, but opening it would put out every circuit it supplies. The device nearest the fault clears it so that the others stay on.
Opening all three would cut off every circuit that the feeder and the main supply, for a fault in only one branch. Coordination aims for the opposite.
There is no benefit in the middle position. The feeder would take the neighbouring branches off supply as well, and the branch device can clear the fault alone.

questions.prompt: A fault in the region where two protective zones overlap opens the breakers of both zones. Why is the overlap accepted?
hints: Imagine two zones that meet at a line with no overlap. Which zone does a fault on the line belong to?
What would protect a point that belongs to neither zone?

acceptedIdeas: It leaves no gap, so a fault between two zones still triggers protection
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It leaves no gap, so a fault between two zones still triggers protection

choices.label: It halves the time that the breakers take to clear a fault
It lets the relays of neighbouring zones share a single breaker between them
It is a design flaw that engineers usually correct once the fault has been found
It leaves no gap, so a fault between two zones still triggers protection

questions.onCorrect: A point outside every zone would have no protection, so the zones overlap and a few more breakers open than are strictly needed.

misconceptions.feedback: Overlap does not make anything quicker. Each zone's breakers act on their own, and a fault in the overlap simply opens both sets.
Each zone has its own breakers, and the overlap is not a way of sharing them. It exists so that no point lies outside a zone.
The overlap is a deliberate part of the design, kept because the alternative leaves a gap in the protection.

questions.prompt: In a small plant, a bus feeds two motors, each through its own breaker, and a zone of protection surrounds the bus and each motor. A fault develops inside the winding of motor 2 and nowhere else. Which breakers open?
hints: Which zone contains the fault, the bus zone or the zone of motor 2?
A fault in a zone opens the breakers that bound that zone.

acceptedIdeas: Only the breaker between motor 2 and the bus, which bounds the zone of the fault
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the breaker between motor 2 and the bus, which bounds the zone of the fault

choices.label: Only the breaker between motor 2 and the bus, which bounds the zone of the fault
Every breaker in the plant, so that no part of the faulty motor is left connected
The breakers of both motors, because the two motors are fed from the same bus
The breakers around the bus, because the fault current has to flow through the bus

questions.onCorrect: A fault inside a zone opens the breakers of that zone, so only motor 2's breaker opens and the bus and motor 1 stay on.

misconceptions.feedback: Opening every breaker would put out the whole plant for a fault in one motor. Only the breakers of the zone that holds the fault open.
Motor 1 is in a different zone from the fault, so its breaker stays closed. Sharing a bus does not put motor 1 in the zone of motor 2.
The fault is inside the zone of motor 2, not the bus zone, so the bus zone's breakers stay closed. The fault current passes through the bus on its way, but the fault is not in it.

questions.prompt: Six breakers are being checked against the prospective short-circuit current at their positions. The pairs are invented. Which have an interrupting rating that is enough, and which are too low?
hints: Compare each rating with the prospective current at its position, and ignore the load current.
The rating has to exceed the current that a fault could draw.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Enough: the 6 kA breaker at 4 kA, the 10 kA breaker at 3 kA and the 25 kA breaker at 18 kA. Too low: the 10 kA breaker at 12 kA, the 6 kA breaker at 9 kA and the 16 kA breaker at 20 kA.

items.label: A 6 kA breaker where the prospective current is 4 kA
items.explanation: The rating of 6 kA is above the 4 kA that a fault could draw.

items.label: A 10 kA breaker where the prospective current is 12 kA
items.explanation: A fault could draw 12 kA, which is more than the 10 kA the breaker can safely interrupt.

items.label: A 10 kA breaker where the prospective current is 3 kA
items.explanation: The rating of 10 kA is far above the 3 kA that a fault could draw.

items.label: A 6 kA breaker where the prospective current is 9 kA
items.explanation: A fault could draw 9 kA, above the 6 kA rating.

items.label: A 16 kA breaker where the prospective current is 20 kA
items.explanation: A fault could draw 20 kA, above the 16 kA rating, even though 16 kA is a high rating.

items.label: A 25 kA breaker where the prospective current is 18 kA
items.explanation: The rating of 25 kA is above the 18 kA that a fault could draw.

questions.onCorrect: A breaker is suitable only where its interrupting rating exceeds the prospective short-circuit current at its own position.

questions.prompt: In an invented workshop, a fault occurs on the 10 A circuit of one bench. The 10 A breaker, the 40 A breaker of the sub-board and the 100 A main breaker all open, and the whole workshop goes dark. What does this show?
hints: The three breakers carry the same fault current. Which one should have been the only one to open?
What happened to the circuits that had no fault?

acceptedIdeas: The devices were not coordinated, since only the closest breaker should have opened
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The devices were not coordinated, since only the closest breaker should have opened

choices.label: The devices worked as intended, since a fault should open every device that carries its current
The devices were not coordinated, since only the closest breaker should have opened
The fault lay in an overlap of protective zones, so more breakers opened than were needed
The 100 A main breaker is right to open first for any fault, since it has the largest rating

questions.onCorrect: All three opened together, so the branch device did not clear the fault before the others acted, which is a failure of coordination.

misconceptions.feedback: A fault does send its current through all three devices, since they are in series, but the design aims for only the closest one to open so that the rest of the workshop stays on.
Overlap is a feature of zone protection around elements such as a bus or a transformer. A fault on one bench circuit is a coordination matter between devices in series.
The largest device protects the whole supply, and opening it for a fault on one bench would put out every other circuit. The closest device should clear the fault.

questions.prompt: A plant wants a generator to be disconnected whenever the grid frequency falls too far for it to run safely. Using the passage, which arrangement would do this?
hints: Which device senses conditions other than overcurrent, according to the passage?
Which device actually disconnects the faulty part?

acceptedIdeas: A protective relay set for underfrequency, which has a breaker disconnect the generator
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A protective relay set for underfrequency, which has a breaker disconnect the generator

extracts.text: Protective relays are aided in this task by circuit breakers that are capable of disconnecting faulty components or subsystems. Protective relays can be used for types of protection other than short circuit or overcurrent. The relays can be designed to protect generating equipment and electrical circuits from any undesirable condition, such as undervoltage, underfrequency, or interlocking system lineups.
extracts.who: U.S. Department of Energy, DOE Fundamentals Handbook, Electrical Science, Vol. 4 (1992, public domain)
extracts.kind: A US government handbook of electrical science, written with nuclear facilities in mind

choices.label: A fuse in the generator's connection, which melts when the frequency falls below a set value
A circuit breaker alone, which senses the low frequency from the heating of its own contacts
A protective relay set for underfrequency, which has a breaker disconnect the generator
A relay alone, which opens the generator's circuit itself by melting a link inside the relay

questions.onCorrect: The relay senses underfrequency and the breaker disconnects the generator, as the passage describes for conditions other than overcurrent.

misconceptions.feedback: A fuse senses overcurrent only, so it cannot respond to a fall in frequency. The passage assigns other conditions to relays.
A breaker's own detection works from the heating or magnetic effect of current, which does not measure frequency. The passage gives a relay the job of sensing such conditions.
A relay senses the condition, and the passage says that it is aided by circuit breakers in disconnecting the faulty part. Melting a link is how a fuse works.

questions.prompt: A faulty kettle leaks 30 mA through a person to earth while the circuit is carrying its normal 10 A. By roughly how much does the current in the line conductor rise?
hints: Convert 30 mA to amperes first, remembering that a milliampere is a thousandth of an ampere.
Then compare that current with the 10 A already flowing, as a percentage of the 10 A.

acceptedIdeas: About 0.3 percent, taking the line from 10 A to 10.03 A
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 0.3 percent, taking the line from 10 A to 10.03 A

choices.label: About 3 percent, taking the line current from 10 A to 10.3 A
About 0.3 percent, taking the line from 10 A to 10.03 A
About 30 percent, taking the line current from 10 A to 13 A

questions.onCorrect: The line carries 10.03 A instead of 10 A, a rise far too small for an overload device to react to, which is why a different device has to watch for leaks.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads 30 mA as 0.3 A. A milliampere is a thousandth of an ampere, so the leak is ten times smaller than that.
That reads 30 mA as 3 A. A milliampere is a thousandth of an ampere, so the leak is a hundred times smaller than that.

questions.prompt: A safety switch rated 30 mA protects a circuit. At one moment the line current is 8.000 A and the neutral current is 7.940 A. What does the safety switch do?
hints: Subtract the neutral current from the line current, and write the result in milliamperes.
Compare that difference with the rating of the safety switch.

acceptedIdeas: It opens, because 60 mA is leaking by another route, which is twice its 30 mA rating
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It opens, because 60 mA is leaking by another route, which is twice its 30 mA rating

choices.label: It stays closed, because the line and neutral currents are within 1 percent of each other
It stays closed, because 8 A is far below the current at which a circuit breaker would open
It opens, because 60 mA is leaking by another route, which is twice its 30 mA rating
It opens only if the line current climbs above the rating of the circuit breaker beside it

questions.onCorrect: The difference is 0.060 A, which is 60 mA and twice the rating, so the switch opens however small the difference looks beside 8 A.

misconceptions.feedback: The switch responds to the difference, not to how large the currents are. A difference of 60 mA is twice the rating, even though it is under 1 percent of the line current.
That treats it as an overload device. A safety switch does not measure how close the current is to a limit, and reads only the difference between the line and the neutral.
That describes a breaker. A safety switch opens on the difference between line and neutral currents, whatever the size of the line current.

questions.prompt: A person on a dry floor puts a finger across the line and neutral contacts of a light fitting, so that current passes through the person from one contact to the other. Can the safety switch be relied on to open?
hints: Follow the current: where does it leave the supply, and where does it come back?
Then ask whether the line and neutral currents differ, since that is all the switch compares.

acceptedIdeas: No, because the current returns on the neutral, so the line and neutral currents stay equal
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because the current returns on the neutral, so the line and neutral currents stay equal

choices.label: No, because the current returns on the neutral, so the line and neutral currents stay equal
Yes, because every shock is detected within 30 milliseconds, whichever way the current flows
Yes, because the switch measures the current in the person's body and compares it with its rating
No, because safety switches work only on appliances that have an earth pin on their plug

questions.onCorrect: The current that leaves on the line returns on the neutral, so the switch sees a balanced circuit and stays closed. Wikipedia says an RCD cannot protect a person who touches both conductors.

misconceptions.feedback: A safety switch detects a difference between line and neutral. Current through a person from the line to the neutral gives no difference, so the 30 millisecond figure does not apply.
The switch has no sensor in the body. It reads only the line and neutral currents, and current through a person from one conductor to the other looks like load current.
The switch compares line and neutral currents and needs no earth pin. Its limit here is that nothing leaks away from the pair of conductors, so there is nothing for it to compare.

questions.prompt: A loose live wire inside a dishwasher touches the dishwasher's metal casing, and the dishwasher is correctly earthed. What does the earth connection do?
hints: Ask what has to happen to the supply to the casing for the fault to stop being a hazard.
A breaker or fuse opens on a large current. What would give a fault a path that carries one?

acceptedIdeas: It gives the fault a low-resistance path to the supply, so a large current opens the breaker or fuse
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It gives the fault a low-resistance path to the supply, so a large current opens the breaker or fuse

choices.label: It carries part of the dishwasher's running current in normal use, so the neutral carries less
It lets the safety switch sense the fault, because a safety switch cannot work without an earth wire
It gives the fault a low-resistance path to the supply, so a large current opens the breaker or fuse
It takes the fault current into the ground and absorbs it harmlessly, so no device needs to open

questions.onCorrect: The path back to the supply has low impedance, so the fault current is large enough to open the breaker or fuse, which is automatic disconnection of supply.

misconceptions.feedback: The earth conductor is not part of the circuit that powers the appliance. It exists to give a fault current a path, and in normal use it has no job.
A safety switch senses a difference between line and neutral, and Wikipedia notes it works just as well when the return is through plumbing or the ground. The earth connection has a different job.
The earth connection does not make the fault harmless. It makes the fault large and quick to clear, so that the breaker or fuse opens and the supply to the casing is removed.

questions.prompt: Which protective device is designed to deal with each of these hazards?
hints: For each hazard, ask which quantity changes: the total current, the difference between line and neutral, or the voltage.
Then ask whether the device that senses that quantity protects wiring, a person or equipment.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The heater short circuit and the overloaded circuit go to the breaker or fuse, the iron and the water pipe leaks go to the safety switch, and the storm spike goes to the surge diverter.

items.label: A heater element fails and joins the line conductor directly to the neutral
items.explanation: A short circuit sends a very large total current through the circuit, which is what a breaker or fuse senses.

items.label: Damaged insulation in an iron lets current run through the person holding it to earth
items.explanation: Current that returns through a person to earth makes the neutral carry less than the line, and the safety switch reads that difference.

items.label: A storm sends a voltage spike along the supply towards the television
items.explanation: A surge is a spike in voltage, and a surge diverter captures spikes before they reach equipment inside the property.

items.label: Too many appliances on one circuit draw more current than its cable can carry
items.explanation: An overload is a total current above what the circuit is rated for, which breakers and fuses are built to catch.

items.label: Worn insulation lets a small current leak to a metal water pipe
items.explanation: A leak by any route makes line and neutral differ, so a safety switch can open, while a breaker would not notice so small a current.

questions.onCorrect: Each device senses one thing: total current for the breaker, the line and neutral difference for the safety switch, and voltage spikes for the surge diverter.

questions.prompt: A householder presses the test button on a safety switch, as Energy Safe Victoria's household pages describe, and the lights on that circuit stay on. What does that show, and what should happen next?
hints: What is the test button supposed to do to the power on its circuit?
If that did not happen, ask who the regulator says should look into it.

acceptedIdeas: The switch may have failed, so a licensed electrician should be called to investigate it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The switch may have failed, so a licensed electrician should be called to investigate it

choices.label: The switch is working, because the test button is not meant to cut the power
The switch may have failed, so a licensed electrician should be called to investigate it
The fault is in the circuit breaker, so a breaker with a higher rating will cure it
The switch needs cleaning, so the switchboard should be opened and its connections checked

questions.onCorrect: A working safety switch cuts the power when its button is pressed, so lights that stay on mean it may have failed, and ESV says to call a licensed electrician immediately.

misconceptions.feedback: The test button creates a small leak on purpose, and a working switch opens and cuts the power to its circuit. Lights that stay on show that it did not.

The test button belongs to the safety switch and not the breaker. A breaker's rating is chosen for the wiring it protects, so raising it would remove that protection, and work on a switchboard is for a licensed electrician.
Opening a switchboard and handling its connections is electrical work. Energy Safe Victoria leaves that to licensed electricians, and a failed test is the cue to call one.

questions.prompt: An invented buyer reads that a house built in the 1970s has circuit breakers, a safety switch and a surge diverter on its switchboard. The buyer concludes that with three protective devices the wiring needs no inspection. What is the best reply, using ESV's advice?
hints: Does any of the three devices protect against degraded wiring itself, or do they all respond only to faults after they happen?
Look for what ESV says about a house built before the 1980s, and about who is qualified to inspect wiring.

acceptedIdeas: A licensed electrician should still check it, since safety switches do not stop every shock and old wiring degrades
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A licensed electrician should still check it, since safety switches do not stop every shock and old wiring degrades

choices.label: A licensed electrician should still check it, since safety switches do not stop every shock and old wiring degrades
No check is needed, because three protective devices between them cover every fault that old wiring can develop in a house
The buyer can inspect the wiring personally, as long as the main breaker is switched off before the work starts
Only the safety switch needs attention, so pressing its test button is all the check that the whole house requires

questions.onCorrect: ESV advises that a house built before the 1980s have its wiring checked by a licensed inspector or a registered contractor, since protective devices do not make degraded wiring safe.

misconceptions.feedback: ESV states that safety switches may not protect all wiring and will not prevent all shocks, and it says old wiring can degrade or fail to cope with modern demands. Devices on the board do not replace an inspection.

ESV says that inspecting and installing household wiring is work only for an A grade electrician, and it advises that a house built before the 1980s be checked by a licensed inspector or registered electrical contractor.

The test button shows whether the safety switch operates. It says nothing about the condition of the wiring behind the walls, which ESV says a licensed electrician should check in a house of this age.

questions.prompt: A homeowner says: 'My switchboard has a circuit breaker for every circuit, so we are protected from electric shock.' What does this ESV statement say about the claim?
hints: Read which two devices the sentence names, and what it says neither of them does.
Then ask which device in the lesson does protect a person from a leak shock.

acceptedIdeas: It contradicts the claim, because a breaker does not act as personal protection against shock
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It contradicts the claim, because a breaker does not act as personal protection against shock

choices.label: It supports the claim, because a breaker opens on any current that could harm a person in the home
It contradicts the claim, because a breaker does not act as personal protection against shock
It leaves the claim open, because it refers only to surge diverters and not to circuit breakers
It supports the claim for circuits that also have a surge diverter fitted on the switchboard

questions.onCorrect: ESV says that breakers and surge diverters do not act as safety switches, so a board of breakers alone leaves the leak hazard to a safety switch.

misconceptions.feedback: A breaker opens on a total current that is excessive for the circuit, which may be thousands of times the leak that matters to a person. The statement says it does not act as personal protection.
The statement names both devices: surge diverters and circuit breakers. Neither acts as a safety switch for personal protection.
The statement says that neither a surge diverter nor a circuit breaker stands in for a safety switch as protection for a person, and it makes no exception for a board that has both.

extracts.text: Surge diverters and circuit breakers do not act as safety switches for personal protection against electric shock.
extracts.who: Energy Safe Victoria, Household wiring (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: A state safety regulator's guidance for householders

questions.prompt: Each statement describes how one of three things in a household circuit works. Which of the three is it?
hints: For each statement, ask what the thing senses or does: a path, the total current, or the difference between two currents.
Remember that the earth conductor is not a sensing device at all.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The earth conductor gives the low-impedance path and is joined to exposed metal, the breaker or fuse responds to the total current and misses small leaks, and the safety switch responds to the line and neutral difference whatever the return route.

items.label: Gives a fault current a low-impedance path back to the supply
items.explanation: That path is what turns a fault to the casing into a current large enough for the breaker or fuse to clear.

items.label: Opens when the total current in the circuit is excessive
items.explanation: A breaker or fuse responds to the size of the total current, which is why it protects wiring from overload and short circuit.

items.label: Opens when the line and neutral currents differ by more than its rating
items.explanation: The difference between line and neutral is the leak, and the rating is the 30 mA of a household safety switch.

items.label: Is connected to exposed metal parts, such as the casing of an appliance
items.explanation: Connecting metal that was never meant to be live to the earthing system is how automatic disconnection of supply starts.

items.label: Cannot tell a small leak through a person from the circuit's normal current
items.explanation: A leak adds so little to the total current that a breaker or fuse does not respond to it.

items.label: Still opens when the leaked current returns by a route other than the neutral wire
items.explanation: It reads the imbalance and ignores the route, so the earth wire does not have to be the way back.

questions.onCorrect: The earth conductor gives a fault a path, the breaker or fuse responds to the total current, and the safety switch responds to the difference between line and neutral.

questions.prompt: Sparks appear at a power point whenever a plug is pushed in, and the switches nearby are old and cracked. The switchboard has a working safety switch. What is the right course?
hints: Look at what ESV lists as tell-tale signs that wiring may be faulty, and see whether sparks and broken switches are among them.
Then ask who ESV says may inspect and install household wiring.

acceptedIdeas: Have a licensed electrician check the wiring, since sparks and broken switches signal that it may be faulty
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Have a licensed electrician check the wiring, since sparks and broken switches signal that it may be faulty

choices.label: Rely on the safety switch, which will open if the wiring ever becomes dangerous to anyone nearby
Replace the power point with a new one, since a broken fitting is the usual cause of sparks
Open the switchboard and tighten the connections to that circuit, since a loose one is likely
Have a licensed electrician check the wiring, since sparks and broken switches signal that it may be faulty

questions.onCorrect: ESV lists sparks and old or broken switches among the signs of faulty wiring, and says to have it checked by a licensed electrician.

misconceptions.feedback: A safety switch does not cover all wiring and will not prevent all shocks, and it does not detect an overload. ESV lists sparks and broken switches as signs that the wiring needs a licensed electrician's check.
Replacing a fitting is wiring work, which ESV leaves to licensed electricians. The sparks are a sign of a wider problem that the electrician is there to find.
Opening a switchboard and handling its connections is electrical work, and ESV says that only an A grade electrician may inspect and install household wiring.

questions.prompt: Wikipedia's summary of AEMO's preliminary report says when the trouble that ended in the blackout began. Roughly how long passed between the first line tripping and almost the whole state losing supply?
hints: The storm lasted all day. Ask whether the final sequence of line trips would also have taken all day.
Think about how fast protection acts: it trips in a fraction of a second, and each trip loads the next part of the grid.

acceptedIdeas: About 90 seconds, a minute and a half in all
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 90 seconds, a minute and a half in all

choices.label: About 9 hours, spread across the day of the storm
About 90 seconds, a minute and a half in all
About 90 minutes, over the afternoon of the storm

questions.onCorrect: Problems started 90 seconds before the blackout, so the storm lasted all day but the cascade itself took a minute and a half.

misconceptions.feedback: The weather did cause local outages through the day, but the preliminary report places the start of the final sequence far later than that, 90 seconds before almost the whole state lost supply.
The storm brought local outages through the afternoon, but the preliminary report dates the start of the final sequence to 90 seconds before almost the whole state lost supply.

questions.prompt: Put these five events of 28 September 2016 in the order they happened.
hints: The storm damage is the start of every other event on the list, so it comes first.
Ask which events needed the one before them: the state could only go dark once its generation and its link to Victoria had gone.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The storm damage came first, the wind farms cut output or dropped out as the faults repeated, both Heywood circuits then tripped, almost the whole state lost supply, and restoration began from Victoria.

items: Storm damage leaves several transmission lines faulted
Wind farms cut their output or drop out as the faults repeat
Both circuits of the Heywood interconnector trip out
Almost the whole state loses supply
Restoration begins, with the Victorian interconnectors used to establish a stable frequency

questions.onCorrect: The storm damage started it, the wind farm drop-outs and the interconnector trip followed within seconds, and restoration began only after the state had lost supply.

questions.prompt: Sort each statement about the 2016 blackout by the kind of event it describes.
hints: Ask of each statement: did it start the chain, was it a condition already in place, or was it automatic action by protection?
A setting or a missing precaution is in place before the event, while a trip happens during it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The storm damage is the trigger, the unanticipated lightning risk and the wind farm settings are weaknesses, and the isolating of generators and the Heywood trip are protective responses.

items.label: A violent storm brings at least 80,000 lightning strikes, and its wind damages 23 pylons
items.explanation: It is the event that started the chain, since every later event followed from the damage to the lines.

items.label: The grid operator had not foreseen a significant lightning risk, so it took no protective action against one
items.explanation: It was a condition already in place before the storm, which left the transmission system exposed to what the storm brought.

items.label: Software settings in many wind turbines stop them riding through voltage or frequency events that come too often
items.explanation: The settings were in place beforehand, and they decided how many turbines would drop out once the faults repeated.

items.label: Automatic protection isolates generators from the damaged network to protect them
items.explanation: Wikipedia says the network's automatic safety features isolated generators to protect both the plant and consumers' equipment.

items.label: Both Heywood interconnector circuits trip out because synchronism with the eastern states is about to be lost
items.explanation: A trip is protection operating, and this one separated South Australia from the eastern states.

questions.onCorrect: The storm is the trigger, the missing lightning precautions and the wind farm settings are weaknesses, and the isolation of generators and the Heywood trip are protective responses.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the cause of the 2016 blackout is best supported by the sequence of events that Wikipedia summarises?
hints: Check each statement against the timeline: what began it, what let it spread, and what acted.
Be wary of any option that names a single cause, or that says something the sequence does not say.

acceptedIdeas: The storm began it, ride-through settings helped it spread, and protection then separated the state
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The storm began it, ride-through settings helped it spread, and protection then separated the state

choices.label: Wind farm settings caused it, so the storm and the protection played no real part in it
The Heywood upgrade caused it, because the line was weaker after being out of service for work
The storm began it, ride-through settings helped it spread, and protection then separated the state
The protection should not have operated, because tripping the interconnector turned a fault into a blackout

questions.onCorrect: Wikipedia's account gives the storm as the start, the wind farm settings as a reason the loss spread, and protection as what separated the state, without ranking them.

misconceptions.feedback: Wikipedia's account treats the wind farm settings as one factor in how far the loss spread. It also records the storm damage that started the sequence and the protection that acted, and it does not rank the three.

Wikipedia says the interconnector was blamed at first. Its account of the sequence runs from the storm damage through the wind farm drop-outs to the interconnector trip, and it gives the earlier upgrade no part.
Wikipedia describes the trip as a response to imminent loss of synchronism and does not call it a mistake. To show that it should not have operated would need evidence that Wikipedia does not give.

questions.prompt: After a whole grid has shut down, why can a large steam power station not simply reconnect to the grid and restart?
hints: Think about what a steam plant needs running before its generators can produce anything.
Ask where that power normally comes from, and whether that source exists in a total shutdown.

acceptedIdeas: Its pumps and fans need power before it can generate, and a dead grid has none to give
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its pumps and fans need power before it can generate, and a dead grid has none to give

choices.label: The grid refuses new connections until its frequency has been brought to exactly 50 Hz
Its generators cannot run until a large load has been connected to them once more
Its pumps and fans need power before it can generate, and a dead grid has none to give
Regulations forbid a station reconnecting until the operator has inspected every line

questions.onCorrect: A steam plant needs station service power, up to about 10 percent of its capacity, before it generates, and a dead grid cannot supply it.

misconceptions.feedback: Frequency does have to be established, and in 2016 the Victorian interconnectors were used for that. The obstacle for the station itself is power for its own equipment.
Wikipedia gives no such condition. It says a steam plant needs station service power for pumps, blowers and fuel preparation before it generates anything.
Wikipedia gives a technical reason, which is that with the grid dead, the station has no source for the power that its own equipment needs.

questions.prompt: South Australia was cut off from Victoria again in early 2020. A note beneath an AER chart explains the highest frequency-control cost the chart shows. Which statement does the note support?
hints: Read what the note says the costs were due to, and keep that apart from what it says about bushfires.
Ask whether 'islanded' means the same as having no supply.

acceptedIdeas: South Australia was separated from the market for weeks, and its own frequency control cost a lot
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: South Australia was separated from the market for weeks, and its own frequency control cost a lot

choices.label: South Australia lost all supply for several weeks, which is why its frequency control cost so much
South Australia was separated from the market for weeks, and its own frequency control cost a lot
Bushfires damaged the Heywood interconnector, and that loss is what drove the high costs that quarter
The 2016 storm damage is the reason that frequency control cost so much in the quarter described

questions.onCorrect: The note ties the costs to South Australia running islanded after losing Heywood, and it names bushfires only as a separate driver of prices across the market.

misconceptions.feedback: Islanded means separated and still running on its own generation. The note speaks of high local costs for a system that was operating, and says nothing about a loss of supply.
The note says bushfires drove high prices across the NEM in January 2020. It does not say that they damaged the interconnector, and it gives the loss of Heywood as a separate fact.
The note is about early 2020, more than three years after the 2016 storm, and it gives the loss of the Heywood interconnector as the reason.

extracts.text: FCAS costs in the January to March quarter 2020 were due to high local costs in South Australia when it was islanded for several weeks following the loss of the Heywood interconnector. In January 2020 bushfires also drove high prices across the NEM.
extracts.who: Australian Energy Regulator, State of the energy market 2025 (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: A regulator's annual report on the electricity and gas markets

questions.prompt: Marlow Island is an invented place. A bushfire destroys its only transmission line to the mainland, and the island loses supply. Sort each item by the kind of event it is, as the lesson did for 2016.
hints: Ask of each item whether it started the chain, was a condition in place beforehand, or was automatic action during the event.
A setting, a missing precaution or a neglected piece of equipment is in place before the event.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The bushfire is the trigger, the wind farm setting and the unrun diesel station are weaknesses, and the relay and the substation protection are protective responses.

items.label: A bushfire destroys the island's only transmission line to the mainland
items.explanation: The fire started the chain by taking out the line, and the later events followed from it.

items.label: The island's wind farm is set to ride through only one voltage disturbance
items.explanation: A setting in place beforehand, which decides how many turbines drop out once disturbances repeat.

items.label: The island's diesel station has not been run for years, and its starting batteries are flat
items.explanation: A standing condition, which decides whether the island can restart itself after it loses supply.

items.label: A relay opens the breakers at both ends of the damaged line
items.explanation: Automatic protection isolating a faulted line is a protective response, even though customers lose supply.

items.label: Protection at the island's substation disconnects its transformer from the fault to protect it
items.explanation: Isolating equipment from a fault to protect it is the same kind of response as the isolating of generators in 2016.

questions.onCorrect: The bushfire is the trigger, the wind farm setting and the unrun diesel station are weaknesses, and the relay and the substation protection are protective responses.

questions.prompt: A region's large stations are mostly steam plants, which need station service power before they can generate. This passage names a kind of plant that operators often designate as a black-start source. What makes that choice suit the problem?
hints: Compare what the passage says a hydro station needs to start with what the steam plant in the question needs.
Then ask what the large block of power on line lets other stations do.

acceptedIdeas: It needs very little power to start, less than a steam plant, and then puts a large block on line fast
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It needs very little power to start, less than a steam plant, and then puts a large block on line fast

choices.label: It needs no power of its own to start, so it can restart a dead grid without any outside help
It runs at a fixed output whatever the demand, which holds the frequency steady while others start
It is usually built near cities, so its power reaches customers before the lines are repaired
It needs very little power to start, less than a steam plant, and then puts a large block on line fast

questions.onCorrect: A hydro station starts on very little power and can then bring a big block of generation on line quickly, which lets steam and nuclear stations be started.

misconceptions.feedback: The passage says a hydroelectric station needs only a little power to start, enough to open the intake gates and supply the generator's field current, so it does need some.
The passage says nothing about holding output or frequency. It gives the plant's small starting need and its ability to bring a big block of generation on line quickly.
The passage gives no location. The reasons it gives are the small starting need and the quick large output, which let the plant start fossil-fuel and nuclear stations.

extracts.text: Often hydroelectric power plants are designated as the black-start sources to restore network interconnections. A hydroelectric station needs very little initial power to start (just enough to open the intake gates and provide excitation current to the generator field coils), and can put a large block of power on line very quickly to allow start-up of fossil-fuel or nuclear stations.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.prompt: A tree falls across an 11 kV feeder in an invented town, and a relay opens the feeder's breaker. That cuts supply to 3,000 homes and leaves the feeder's transformer undamaged. How is the relay's action best described in the lesson's terms?
hints: Ask what happened first: the tree, or the relay opening.
Then ask whether the relay did what a relay is built to do, and what that cost the customers on the feeder.

acceptedIdeas: A protective response, because the relay removed the fault and the lost supply is its cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A protective response, because the relay removed the fault and the lost supply is its cost

choices.label: A failure of protection, because customers lost supply and a working system would have kept them on
A trigger, because the loss of supply began at the moment that the relay operated on the feeder
A protective response, because the relay removed the fault and the lost supply is its cost
A weakness, because any device that can cut supply to customers is a hazard to those same customers

questions.onCorrect: The tree was the trigger and the relay isolated the fault as built, so the lost supply is the cost of that response.

misconceptions.feedback: A relay that opens on a fault is doing what it is built to do. In 2016 Wikipedia describes automatic protection isolating plant to protect it, and the blackout followed.
The tree falling across the feeder started the chain, and the relay responded to it. A trigger comes before the protection, and the protection acts on it.
A weakness is a condition already in place that lets a chain spread, such as the wind farm settings. A relay that isolates a fault is a response and not a standing condition.

questions.prompt: As at December 2024, over 4 million Australian households owned rooftop solar connected to the grid. Roughly what share of all the generating capacity in the market did it make up?
hints: A household system is measured in kilowatts, and a gigawatt is a million kilowatts.
Estimate the total for millions of households, then ask what fraction of the market's capacity that would be.

acceptedIdeas: About 25 percent of the market's capacity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 25 percent of the market's capacity

choices.label: About 5 percent of the market's capacity
About 25 percent of the market's capacity
About 60 percent of the market's capacity

questions.onCorrect: More than 22 GW of rooftop solar was 25 percent of all generating capacity in the market, so rooftop solar is a large part of the grid.

misconceptions.feedback: That is too low. The AER counts more than 22 GW of rooftop solar, which is a quarter of the generating capacity in the market.

The AER's figure for capacity is a quarter of the market. The larger shares it reports, such as meeting over half of underlying demand at midday on a sunny day, describe output at one time of day and not capacity.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a grid-tie solar inverter is right?
hints: Think about what the inverter has to read from the grid before it can send any power out.
Then ask what it senses when the grid is dead, and what it does about that.

acceptedIdeas: It matches the grid's voltage, frequency and phase, and it disconnects quickly if the grid goes down
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It matches the grid's voltage, frequency and phase, and it disconnects quickly if the grid goes down

choices.label: It gives the grid the same inertia as a steam turbine, which is why more solar steadies the frequency
It keeps the house running as normal in a blackout, because its panels still produce power
It matches the grid's voltage, frequency and phase, and it disconnects quickly if the grid goes down
It sets the frequency of the grid, which the other generators on the grid then follow

questions.onCorrect: An inverter reads the grid and copies it, so it cannot lead the grid or run without it, and it brings no spinning mass unless its designers add a response.

misconceptions.feedback: A generator connected through an inverter has no rotating mass tied to the grid, so it adds no inertia unless its designers build in a response, as the Hornsdale battery's virtual machine mode does.
A grid-tie inverter will not operate when it does not detect the grid, so a plain system gives the house no supply from its panels during a blackout.
The inverter reads the grid's frequency and phase and copies them. It follows the grid and does not set it.

questions.prompt: Why can the 150 kW of exports be compared directly with a transformer rating given in kVA?
hints: Recall what unity power factor means for the current and the voltage.
Think about how a load's kilowatts and kilovolt-amperes are related by its power factor.

acceptedIdeas: Because the inverters work at unity power factor, where kilowatts and kilovolt-amperes are equal
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because the inverters work at unity power factor, where kilowatts and kilovolt-amperes are equal

choices.label: Because the inverters work at unity power factor, where kilowatts and kilovolt-amperes are equal
Because kilowatts and kilovolt-amperes are two names for the same unit of power at every power factor
Because a transformer's rating counts only real power, so the reactive part is left out of it
Because the rating applies only to power flowing out of the transformer, and not to power flowing back

questions.onCorrect: At unity power factor real power in kW equals apparent power in kVA, so the exports can be added in kW and read against a kVA rating.

misconceptions.feedback: The two are equal only at unity power factor. A kilovolt-ampere is voltage times current, and a kilowatt is that product times the power factor.
A transformer is rated in kVA, the apparent power, because it has to carry the whole current whatever the power factor.
A transformer carries current in either direction, and it is the current that heats it, so the rating is a fair yardstick for the flow back as well.

questions.prompt: The flow of 120 kVA is compared with a transformer rating of 150 kVA. What is the flow divided by the rating?
hints: The ratio asked for is the flow divided by the rating.
Both are in kVA, so the units cancel and the ratio is a plain number.
A ratio below one means that the flow is smaller than the rating.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 120 / 150 = 0.8, so the flow reaches 80 percent of the rating.

questions.onCorrect: The flow is 0.8 of the rating, so it is below the rating and the transformer still has room.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the rating by the flow. The ratio asked for is the flow divided by the rating.
That is the gap in kVA between the rating and the flow. A ratio is a division, and not a difference.

questions.prompt: Is the transformer the first limit on how much solar this second street can export?
hints: Compare the flow with the rating, using the ratio you found.
A limit is reached when the flow gets to the rating. Is it there yet?

acceptedIdeas: No, because the flow is below the rating, so a different limit could be reached first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because the flow is below the rating, so a different limit could be reached first

choices.label: Yes, because any export loads the transformer, and so the flow is already close to its rating
No, because the flow is below the rating, so a different limit could be reached first
Yes, because the exports of twenty houses add up to more than any one of the houses could use
It cannot be told, because the transformer's limit depends on the voltage along the street

questions.onCorrect: The flow is below the rating, so the transformer is not the first limit on this street, and something else may be reached first.

misconceptions.feedback: Exports do load the transformer, but its limit is reached only when the flow gets to its rating. Here the flow is 0.8 of it.
The comparison that matters is with the transformer's rating and not with what one house uses. The flow here is below the rating.
The transformer's limit is its rating, and the flow can be compared with it directly. The voltage along the street is a separate limit, and the next screen turns to it.

questions.prompt: Customers at the far end of a long street report that their solar inverters switch themselves down around midday, while customers near the transformer have no trouble. The panels and inverters are the same models at both ends. What is the most likely cause?
hints: If the equipment is the same, ask what differs between the two ends of the street.
Think about what current along a feeder does to the voltage when houses export at midday.

acceptedIdeas: Voltage rise along the feeder, caused by the exports of the street's own houses at midday
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Voltage rise along the feeder, caused by the exports of the street's own houses at midday

choices.label: The grid frequency is too high at midday, so inverters across the whole street back off
The panels at the far end overheat in the sun, and so lose output before the others do
Voltage rise along the feeder, caused by the exports of the street's own houses at midday
The transformer is too small for the evening load, which caps what the street can export

questions.onCorrect: The exports of every house pass the wiring at the far end, so the voltage there rises most, and inverters back off or trip when it passes their limit.

misconceptions.feedback: Frequency is the same for every customer on a connected street, so it cannot explain a difference between the two ends.
Overheating would not depend on a house's position along the feeder, and the panels are the same models at both ends.
The trips happen at midday, when the issue is exports and not evening load, and a transformer limit would affect every house on it, including those near the transformer.

questions.prompt: A network offers one customer a static export limit of 4 kW. It offers another customer on the same street a flexible limit of up to 8 kW that cuts exports only when the local network is stressed. The offers are invented. Which statement is best supported?
hints: Ask when each limit applies: all the time, or only when the network is under strain.
Then ask what the network still has the power to do under a flexible limit.

acceptedIdeas: The flexible customer exports more when the street has room, and the network can still cut exports
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The flexible customer exports more when the street has room, and the network can still cut exports

choices.label: The static customer exports more, because a fixed limit is guaranteed whatever happens on the network
The flexible customer exports more, because a flexible limit lets the network ignore the street's voltage
Both customers export the same, because each is held by the same street and the same wiring
The flexible customer exports more when the street has room, and the network can still cut exports

questions.onCorrect: A static limit applies all the time and a flexible limit applies when the local network needs it, so the flexible customer can export more at other times.

misconceptions.feedback: A static limit is guaranteed only up to its own figure, 4 kW. The flexible limit allows up to 8 kW at other times, so the flexible customer may export more when the street has room.
Flexible limits exist so that the network can still protect local supply, and the AER says they let the network limit exports when needed. They do not remove the street's voltage limits.
The limits differ, and so do the conditions under which they apply: the static limit applies all the time and the flexible limit only when the network needs it.

questions.prompt: Which street is more likely to have inverters switching down at midday, and why?
hints: Work out how the exports compare with the transformer's rating first, and see whether the transformer would limit them.
Then ask which of the two feeders gives the larger drop of current times resistance.

acceptedIdeas: Street Q, because the same exports through a larger resistance give a bigger voltage rise
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Street Q, because the same exports through a larger resistance give a bigger voltage rise

choices.label: Street P, because its houses are close to the transformer and so are loaded heavily by it
Street Q, because its transformer is overloaded by the exports of its sixteen houses
Street Q, because the same exports through a larger resistance give a bigger voltage rise
Neither, because exports of 40 percent of a transformer's rating are within every limit

questions.onCorrect: The exports are the same and 40 percent of the rating, so the transformer is not the limit, while the larger resistance of Street Q's feeder lifts the voltage more.

misconceptions.feedback: Closeness to the transformer means less feeder resistance between a house and the transformer, so less rise in voltage and not more.
The exports are 40 percent of the transformer's rating, so the transformer is not the limit on either street.
The transformer is only one limit. Voltage rise depends on the resistance of the feeder, and the AER names it as a separate way in which exports are limited.

questions.prompt: An invented street transformer is rated 63 kVA, and each house on it exports 5 kW at midday at unity power factor. What is the largest number of houses that can export together without the flow passing the rating?
hints: At unity power factor the exports in kW can be compared directly with the rating in kVA.
Divide the rating by the export of one house.
Houses come in whole numbers, so check whether the next whole number up still stays within the rating.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 63 / 5 = 12.6, so 12 houses export 60 kW, which is within the 63 kVA rating, and 13 houses export 65 kW, which passes it.

questions.onCorrect: Twelve houses export 60 kW, within the 63 kVA rating, and a thirteenth would take the flow to 65 kW and past it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first number of houses whose exports pass the rating. Thirteen houses export 65 kW, which is more than 63 kVA.
That divides the rating by one house's export, but houses come in whole numbers, and the question asks for the largest whole number within the rating.

questions.prompt: A householder's rooftop system is eight years old and has never been serviced. A friend who is handy with wiring offers to check the inverter and the cabling for nothing. What is the best course, using ESV's advice?
hints: Look for what ESV says about who must carry out a service, and how often.
Ask whether ESV treats a service as a response to a fault or as routine.

acceptedIdeas: Have a licensed A grade electrician service it, since older systems never serviced are where fires occur
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Have a licensed A grade electrician service it, since older systems never serviced are where fires occur

choices.label: Accept, because a friend who knows wiring can check a system whose display shows no recorded faults
Wait for the inverter display to show a fault, since a service is needed only once something has gone wrong
Have a licensed A grade electrician service it, since older systems never serviced are where fires occur
Have the panels washed by a cleaning company, since a clean panel is a safe and well-kept system

questions.onCorrect: ESV says that systems never serviced, particularly older ones, are where rooftop fires occur, and that a licensed A grade electrician must service them.

misconceptions.feedback: ESV says solar servicing is for a licensed A grade electrician, and that inspecting and installing household wiring is work only for one. A friend's check does not meet that.
ESV says fires occur on systems that have never been serviced, and it advises a service at least once every two years, whether or not a fault has shown.
ESV says some companies that claim to service solar panels are nothing more than a cleaning service. A service is an electrician's checks of the wiring, switches, fittings and inverter.

questions.prompt: A retailer says: 'Rooftop solar never shows up in the electricity market, because it is not traded there.' Which reply is best supported by the AER?
hints: Ask what happens to the demand on the market's generators when a house uses its own solar power.
Then ask at what time of day that effect is largest.

acceptedIdeas: It does show up, as lower demand for the market's generators to meet, most of all around midday
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It does show up, as lower demand for the market's generators to meet, most of all around midday

choices.label: It shows up as extra power sold into the market at the midday price, like a power station's
It does show up, as lower demand for the market's generators to meet, most of all around midday
It shows up only on the evenings when grid demand peaks and solar output is at its highest
It does not show up at all, because power used inside the home never reaches the grid or the market

questions.onCorrect: Rooftop solar is not traded in the NEM, and it lowers the demand left for the market's generators, most of all around midday.

misconceptions.feedback: The AER says rooftop solar is not traded through the NEM, except when it is offered as demand response. Its effect is on the demand the market has to meet and not on supply offers.
Evening peaks come when solar generation is minimal or nonexistent, so rooftop solar shows up in the market at midday and not at the evening peak.
Power used inside the home does not reach the grid, and that is exactly how it lowers the demand that the market's generators need to meet.

questions.prompt: A battery is rated 150 MW and 194 MWh. For roughly how long could it deliver its full 150 MW?
hints: A rate of 150 MW means that 150 MWh of energy is delivered in each hour.
Compare the 194 MWh the battery holds with the energy that one hour at full power uses.

acceptedIdeas: A little over an hour before it is empty
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A little over an hour before it is empty

choices.label: Only a few minutes before it is completely empty
A little over an hour before it is empty
About a whole day before it is completely empty

questions.onCorrect: At 150 MW the battery uses 150 MWh each hour, so 194 MWh lasts about 1.3 hours, and the energy figure divided by the power figure is its duration.

misconceptions.feedback: At 150 MW the battery delivers 150 MWh in an hour, and it holds 194 MWh, so it lasts longer than a few minutes.
A whole day at 150 MW would take 3,600 MWh, many times the 194 MWh that the battery holds.

questions.prompt: Using those global figures, roughly how long could each kind of storage run at full power?
hints: Duration is energy divided by power, and gigawatt-hours divided by gigawatts leaves hours.
Work it out for each kind separately, using its own power and energy figures.

acceptedIdeas: Batteries about 2 hours and pumped hydro about 45 hours
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Batteries about 2 hours and pumped hydro about 45 hours

choices.label: Batteries about 2 hours and pumped hydro about 45 hours
Batteries about 45 hours and pumped hydro about 2 hours
Both about the same, since batteries now exceed pumped hydro in power
Batteries about 0.4 hours and pumped hydro about 0.02 hours

questions.onCorrect: Batteries hold about 2.3 hours at full power and pumped hydro about 45, which is why the larger store is pumped hydro even though batteries now have more power.

misconceptions.feedback: That swaps them. Pumped hydro holds far more energy for a smaller power rating, so it runs for the longer time.
More power does not mean more energy. Batteries have the larger power rating and the much smaller energy store, so their duration is the shorter.
That divides the power by the energy. Duration is the energy divided by the power, with gigawatt-hours over gigawatts leaving hours.

questions.prompt: Why does a quantity in megawatt-hours divided by one in megawatts come out in hours?
hints: Read megawatt-hour as megawatt multiplied by hour.
Then ask what is left when you divide that product by megawatts.

acceptedIdeas: Because a megawatt-hour is a megawatt kept up for an hour, so dividing by megawatts leaves the hour
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because a megawatt-hour is a megawatt kept up for an hour, so dividing by megawatts leaves the hour

choices.label: Because a megawatt-hour is a megawatt kept up for an hour, so dividing by megawatts leaves the hour
Because the prefix mega cancels in the division, and the hour is all that remains of either unit
Because hours are the usual unit for time in electricity, so any answer is converted into hours
Because a megawatt is an amount of energy and a megawatt-hour is an amount of time, so they cancel

questions.onCorrect: A megawatt-hour is a megawatt kept up for an hour, so dividing energy by power leaves the time.

misconceptions.feedback: The prefixes do cancel, but that is not why the hour survives. A megawatt-hour is a power kept up for an hour, so dividing by the power leaves the hour.
Nothing is converted. The unit comes straight out of the division, because a megawatt-hour is a megawatt multiplied by an hour.
That reverses them. A megawatt is a rate of delivering energy, and a megawatt-hour is an amount of energy.

questions.prompt: Hornsdale's stability job is 70 MW for 10 minutes. How much energy is that, in MWh, to one decimal place?
hints: Energy is power multiplied by time, and the time has to be in hours.
Ten minutes is ten sixtieths of an hour.
Compare your answer with the 90 MWh of the trading job: a job that lasts only minutes should use far less.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ten minutes is 10/60 of an hour, so the energy is 70 x 10/60 = 11.67 MWh, which rounds to 11.7 MWh.

questions.onCorrect: Ten minutes is a sixth of an hour, so 70 MW for 10 minutes uses about 11.7 MWh.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 70 MW by 10 minutes without changing the minutes into hours. Energy in MWh needs the time in hours.
That changes the 10 minutes into 60 times too much. A minute is a sixtieth of an hour, so divide by 60 and do not multiply.
That divides the 70 MW by the 10 minutes. Energy is power multiplied by time and not divided by it.

questions.prompt: The AER reports that in 2024 negative prices were 15 percent of all prices, against 3.5 percent in 2020, and that they occurred most often around midday. Over the same years prices above $300 per MWh rose from 0.4 percent to 1.8 percent. Which reading is best supported?
hints: Ask what has to be true of supply and demand for the market to settle at a negative price.
Then ask what the rise in prices above $300 per MWh adds, and whether cheaper at midday means cheaper at every hour.

acceptedIdeas: Midday supply has often exceeded demand, so energy is cheap then and storage could shift it later
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Midday supply has often exceeded demand, so energy is cheap then and storage could shift it later

choices.label: Solar has made electricity cheaper at every hour of the day, so storage is no longer needed
Midday supply has often exceeded demand, so energy is cheap then and storage could shift it later
Negative prices mean that generators stop running at midday, so there is no surplus left to store
Negative prices come from a few faulty trading periods, so they say little about supply and demand

questions.onCorrect: Negative prices come when supply exceeds demand, and they were most common at midday, so there is a midday surplus that storage could shift to dearer hours.

misconceptions.feedback: Prices above $300 per MWh also became more frequent, from 0.4 to 1.8 percent of prices, so cheaper at midday does not mean cheaper at every hour.
A negative price is paid when there is more supply on offer than demand, which is a surplus, and the AER links negative prices to midday, when solar output is at its highest.
The AER treats the rise from 3.5 to 15 percent as a trend, and ties it to the midday surplus of solar, so it carries real information about supply and demand.

questions.prompt: Wikipedia names three routes to flexibility. Which route does each case use?
hints: Ask whether each case keeps energy for later, moves when people use power, or links two places.
A link between regions changes where power comes from, which neither storage nor demand response does.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The solar farm and the pumped hydro station are storage, the factory and the retailer's rates are demand response, and the cable and the new line are interconnection.

items.label: A solar farm keeps its midday surplus and sells it after sunset
items.explanation: Energy from one hour is kept for use in another, which is what storage does.

items.label: Water pumped uphill when prices are low runs back through turbines when prices are high
items.explanation: Pumped hydro stores energy as height and returns it later, with some of it lost on the way.

items.label: A factory agrees to move its heaviest running to the hours when supply is plentiful
items.explanation: Demand moves to meet supply, which is what demand response means for industry and commercial customers.

items.label: A retailer offers cheaper rates for using power in the middle of the day
items.explanation: A price that changes when consumers use electricity is a way to shift demand.

items.label: A cable between Tasmania and Victoria lets each state draw on the other when its own supply runs short
items.explanation: Linking regions lets one cover for the other, which is interconnection.

items.label: A new high-voltage line joins two regions so that a calm spell in one can be covered from the other
items.explanation: A link smooths out variation across regions, which is why interconnection counts as a route to flexibility.

questions.onCorrect: Storage keeps energy for later, demand response changes when power is used, and interconnection links regions so that one covers for the other.

questions.prompt: A wind farm in a remote region is curtailed 12 percent of the time because its single line to the city is full. The case is invented. Which change deals directly with that constraint?
hints: Ask where the constraint is: the wind farm's output, the city's demand, or the line between them.
Then ask which option changes the capacity of that part.

acceptedIdeas: A new transmission line from the wind farm to the city
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A new transmission line from the wind farm to the city

choices.label: A large battery installed at the city end of the existing line
A new transmission line from the wind farm to the city
More turbines connected to the same line to add output
A higher cap on the market price that generators may bid

questions.onCorrect: The line is the constraint, so a new line deals with it directly, as the Texas line did when curtailment fell from 8 to 16 percent to near zero.

misconceptions.feedback: A battery at the city end cannot take energy that never reaches the city. The output is held back before the line, so a battery there leaves the line just as full.
More turbines add output to a line that is already full, so more of the output would be curtailed.
A price cap changes what generators may bid. It does nothing to the capacity of the line.

questions.prompt: An invented suburb needs a battery to supply 20 MW for the 3 hours of its evening peak. Which of these batteries fits?
hints: The peak needs a rate and a length of time. Ask which rating gives the rate and which gives the energy.
Work out the energy that 20 MW for 3 hours uses, then check each battery's power and energy against the two needs.

acceptedIdeas: 20 MW and 60 MWh, because it supplies 20 MW and holds three hours of that power
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 20 MW and 60 MWh, because it supplies 20 MW and holds three hours of that power

choices.label: 20 MW and 20 MWh, because its power rating matches the 20 MW that the peak needs
60 MW and 20 MWh, because the larger power rating covers the peak with room to spare
10 MW and 60 MWh, because it holds the three hours of energy that the peak needs
20 MW and 60 MWh, because it supplies 20 MW and holds three hours of that power

questions.onCorrect: The peak needs 20 MW for 3 hours, which is 60 MWh, so the battery needs at least 20 MW of power and 60 MWh of energy, and each other option fails on one rating.

misconceptions.feedback: At 20 MW a battery holding 20 MWh is empty after one hour, so it covers a third of the peak. The energy has to cover 20 MW for 3 hours.
A 60 MW rating gives more power than the peak needs, but 20 MWh at 20 MW lasts one hour, so the energy is still short.
60 MWh covers the energy, but a 10 MW battery can deliver only half of the 20 MW that the peak needs at any moment.

questions.prompt: The AER counts 19,592 home batteries installed across Australia in July 2025, with a combined nominal capacity of 356.6 MWh. About how large was the average battery, in kWh?
hints: Convert the total to kilowatt-hours first, since a megawatt-hour is 1,000 kilowatt-hours.
Divide the total capacity by the number of batteries.
Check that the result is a plausible size for one home, a few to a few tens of kilowatt-hours.
questions.onCorrect: The average is about 18 kWh per battery, which is a nominal figure that includes systems with certificates approved or claimed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer in MWh. The question asks for kWh, and a megawatt-hour is a thousand kilowatt-hours.
That divides the number of batteries by the capacity. The average capacity per battery is the capacity divided by the number of batteries.

questions.prompt: A planner says that every megawatt-hour of curtailed solar is a failure that must be removed. What is the best reply?
hints: Ask what it would cost to use every megawatt-hour, and whether that cost is always worth paying.
Recall what the sources say about building lines or storage in order to avoid curtailment.

acceptedIdeas: Sometimes using every megawatt-hour would cost more than letting the surplus go unused
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sometimes using every megawatt-hour would cost more than letting the surplus go unused

choices.label: Curtailment is cheaper than storage in every case, so it should never be reduced
Curtailment happens only when equipment faults, so it can always be avoided by repairing it
Sometimes using every megawatt-hour would cost more than letting the surplus go unused
Curtailment is the same as load shedding, which is always a sign of a failing grid

questions.onCorrect: Using all available energy may need costly lines or storage, which can cost more than letting the surplus go unused, so some curtailment is the cheaper choice.

misconceptions.feedback: The sources give no cost comparison, and a new line in Texas cut curtailment from 8 to 16 percent to near zero. Removing it is sometimes worth the cost, so 'in every case' goes too far.
Wikipedia describes curtailment as a standard technique used throughout the history of power production, so it is not a fault.
Load shedding cuts demand and curtailment cuts generation. They are different actions.

questions.prompt: A pumped hydro scheme uses 800 MWh to refill its upper reservoir. Taking Wikipedia's efficiency of 75 to 85 percent, roughly how much energy can it return?
hints: Efficiency here is the share of the energy put in that comes back.
Take 75 percent and 85 percent of the 800 MWh.

acceptedIdeas: Between 600 and 680 MWh, because storage returns less than it takes in
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Between 600 and 680 MWh, because storage returns less than it takes in

choices.label: Exactly 800 MWh, because storage returns the energy that was put in
Between 940 and 1,070 MWh, because the height of the reservoir adds energy
Between 600 and 680 MWh, because storage returns less than it takes in
Between 75 and 85 MWh, because the efficiency is a number of MWh and not a share

questions.onCorrect: 75 to 85 percent of 800 MWh is 600 to 680 MWh, so the scheme returns less than it takes, which is the cost of moving energy in time.

misconceptions.feedback: A store's efficiency is below 100 percent, so it returns less than it takes in. Storage moves energy in time and does not create it.
Nothing adds energy. Dividing 800 by the efficiency would give 940 to 1,070, which treats a share below 100 percent as a gain, and it is a loss.
The efficiency is a percentage, a share of the energy put in. A share of 75 to 85 percent of 800 MWh is much more than 75 to 85 MWh.

flashcards.front: A sine wave has a peak of 100 V. What is its RMS value, to the nearest volt?
flashcards.back: 71 V: the RMS value of a sine wave is 0.707 of its peak.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 × 0.707 = 70.7, which is 71 V to the nearest volt.

flashcards.front: What is Australia's nominal mains voltage, and is it a peak, RMS or peak-to-peak value?
flashcards.back: 230 V RMS, an RMS value that heats equally to 230 V DC.

acceptedIdeas: 230 V RMS
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 230 V RMS

flashcards.front: Why do AC supplies quote the RMS value of the voltage?
flashcards.back: The RMS value is the steady DC voltage that would give the same heating, found by squaring, averaging and taking the root. The average of a sine wave over a cycle is zero and says nothing about heating.

flashcards.front: A load takes 8 kW of real power and 6 kvar of reactive power. What is its apparent power, in kVA?
flashcards.back: 10 kVA: the square root of $8^2 + 6^2$, the slope of a 6, 8, 10 triangle.

flashcards.front: Which rating decides the current that a cable or transformer must carry: real, reactive or apparent power?
flashcards.back: The apparent power, in kVA, since it is voltage times the whole current.

acceptedIdeas: apparent power
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: apparent power

flashcards.front: Reactive power is not used up as heat in the load. Why does a supply still have to be sized for it?
flashcards.back: Reactive power is energy that goes out to the load's magnetic or electric field and returns each cycle. The current that carries it still flows along the wires, so cables, transformers and generators heat with it.

flashcards.front: A load takes 6 kW and 7.5 kVA. What is its power factor?
flashcards.back: 0.8: the real power divided by the apparent power.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Power factor = 6 ÷ 7.5 = 0.8.

flashcards.front: What kind of load has a lagging power factor: inductive or capacitive?
flashcards.back: An inductive load, such as a motor or a transformer, since its current lags the voltage.

acceptedIdeas: inductive
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: inductive

flashcards.front: Why is a capacitor fitted close to a motor, and what is wrong with fitting too large a one?
flashcards.back: The capacitor supplies the motor's reactive power locally, so the supply carries less current and loses less. A capacitor that is too large supplies more than the motor needs, which leaves a leading power factor and raises the apparent power again.

flashcards.front: A balanced star supply has 120 V from each line to the star point. What is the voltage between two lines, to the nearest volt?
flashcards.back: 208 V: the line voltage is 1.73 times the phase voltage in a star.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 120 × 1.732 = 207.8 V, which is 208 V to the nearest volt.

flashcards.front: In a balanced star connection, by what factor is the line voltage larger than the phase voltage?
flashcards.back: 1.73, the square root of 3.

flashcards.front: Why does a balanced three-phase load leave almost no current in the neutral?
flashcards.back: The three line currents have the same size and are 120 degrees apart, so they add up to zero at every instant, and the other two conductors act as the return path for each.

flashcards.front: A 100 kVA single-phase transformer has a 230 V secondary. What is its rated secondary current, to the nearest ampere?
flashcards.back: 435 A: the apparent power divided by the voltage.

flashcards.front: Which transformer loss is the same at every load: core loss or copper loss?
flashcards.back: Core loss, since the hysteresis and eddy-current losses are present whenever the transformer is energised.

acceptedIdeas: core loss
